ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 3 1. Overview The Flame Design experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Richard L. Axelbaum of the Washington University of St. Louis’s Dept. of Energy, Environmental & Chemical Engineering . The Co-Investigator (Co-I) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the University of Maryland’s Dept. of Fire Protection Engineering. The ISS research also benefitted greatly from the work of Phillip H. Irace who was a doctoral student at the Washington University of St. Louis throughout the on-orbit operations. Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NA SA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including Flame Design and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University ( CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist.

For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team include d Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. The ISS operations for Flame Design were conducted in two rounds of testing which occurred in April-July 2019 and Oct. 2021 to Feb. 2022 . The two rounds occurred during Increments 59/60 and 66 and respectively featured normal and inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and ethylene (C2H4) while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse flames were ef fectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames. As a notable exception, the first day of testing in the second round was carried out in the normal flame configuration, with propane (with or without nitrogen) flowing into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. The tests on th at day were conducted with the long (near) thermocouple rake to acquire data to calibrate optical measurements of the flame temperature through Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP). Meanwhile, the short (far) thermocouple rake was used on all other Flame Design test days.

Except for the single propane (C3H8) test day previously mentioned, all ISS tests were conducted with the fuel ethylene (C2H4), the inert nitrogen, and the spherical flame configuration. While other conditions had been identified as desired, NASA’s intent was focused rather comprehensive research. 2. Science Overview A. Background This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document (SRD) of April 2010. The majority of practical combustion processes involve nonpremixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been co nsidered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken flames, leading to performance penalties and possible extinction. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 4 these concerns. The approach is termed flame design, as it takes a fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed, designs flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. Flame design involves affecting the basic structure of the flame in that the relationship between the temperature and concentration fields is varied to accomplish a stated objective. The method involves exchanging nitrogen (or any inert, including carbon dioxide) from the oxidizer stream to the fuel stream such that the stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, can be varied with or without affecting adiabatic flame temperature, Tad. The structure of a high Zst flame is substantially different from that of the standard hydrocarbon/air flame, where Zst is relatively low. By varying Zst at constant Tad, flames have been produced that are soot-free at any strain rate (permanently blue) and have extinction scalar dissipation rates up to 40 times those of their fuel-air counterparts.

The nitrogen exchange approach (or some variant of it) has been the subject of many studies by the PI and Co-Is (Du and Axelbaum, 1995, 1996, Chao et al., 1998, Sunderland et al., 2003, 2004, Liu et al., 2005, Chen and Axelbaum, 2005, Kumfer et al., 2006, 2008, Santa et al., 2007a, 2007b, Skeen et al., 2009) and other investigators (Sung et al., 1995; Lin and Faeth, 1996; Kang et al., 1997; Hwang and Chung, 2001). Although these studies have been informative, they typically involved normal -gravity flames, where buoyancy and inherent strain complicated the interpretation of results. For example, these ambiguities have led to different theories to explain the phenomenon of permanently -blue diffusion flames. It is not known whether this phenomenon is due more to a change in the direction of convection a cross the flame or to a change in the detailed structure of the flame. This issue can be addressed by performing microgravity experiments because the unique character of nonbuoyant microgravity flames allows the effects of convection direction and flame s tructure to be independently varied.

By ejecting fuel into an oxidizer in a buoyancy free system, the convective flow across the flame is unambiguously from fuel to oxidizer. Alternatively, by ejecting oxidizer into fuel, the flow is from oxidizer to fuel. Furthermore, the long residence times that can be obtained in the spherical flame geometry will allow for validation of a theory that predicts the sooting limits at the limit of infinite Damköhler number, Da. Studies of the effect of Zst on scalar dissipation rate at extinction have indicated that there is a unique Zst where the flame is most resistant to extinction. These findings also suggest that by employing inert exchange to vary Zst, the peak temperature can be shifted to coincide with the location of radical production, thus allowing the flame to burn at much lower temperatures. The optimum minimum temperature at extinction has led us to propose the concept of a pseudo flammability limit for nonpremixed flames. Again, this fundamental information is most unambiguously demonstrated in quasi-steady, microgravity flames wherein the effects of flame structure can be systematically studied.

The proposed work will also allow, for the first time, a strain-free experimental study of the effects of Zst on soot inception and flame extinction processes. Microgravity experiments will involve gaseous hydrocarbon diffusion flames supported on porous spherical burners and coflow burners.1 Soot inception limits and flame extinction limits will be obtained as functions of Zst, amount of inert, flow direction, and pressure. Extensive analytical and computational modeling

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 5 will support the experimental investigation. Models will include gas -phase and burner -surface radiation. Specifically, soot-inception limits in spherical flames will be measured by establishing a flame at a given Zst and allowing peak temperature to decrease with time until the yellow luminosity is eliminated. The effect of flow direction across the flame will be studied by performing coflow experiments (desired) where the fuel issues into the oxidizer and oxidizer issues into fuel. Gas temperatures will be measured by thin film pyrometry and thermocouples to identify the sootinception temperature. In addition, soot vol ume fraction measurements will be made to evaluate the effects of Zst and flow direction on soot formation and growth, and to better understand the phenomena of permanently-blue flames. Flame extinction limits will also be studied in a manner similar to that of soot inception limits, and temperatures near extinction will be measured.

The experiments and modeling will yield unique data that will allow for an understanding of how Zst affects soot -inception and flame extinction and how Zst can be used to design optimum flames. In addition, the effects of flow direction will also be studied and the importance of flow direction and flame structure to permanently-blue flames will be assessed. Finally, the proposed concept of a pseudo-flammability limit for nonpremixed flames will be evaluated and these limits will be ascertained for the test fuels. These results will be useful for the development of future combustion devices that will ta ke advantage of oxygen enrichment technology to design more stable and less polluting flames. __________________________ 1 The coflow flame experiments are desired. This means that many critical goals of the experiments can be obtained without these exper iments but they would add great value to the results. B. Rationale for Microgravity This is the ‘Justification for Extended Duration Microgravity’ section (2.5) of the experiment’s SRD from April 2010. References and the appendices are not included in this document but can be found in the SRD.

The included equation is formatted differently in this copy. Previous ground-based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the value of the spherical, burner-supported nonpremixed flames for flame studies. The one -dimensional flame offers a simple, fundamental configuration to improve our understanding of nonpremixed flame behavior and to explore such effects as radiation and thermophoresis, which are more pronounced under microgravity conditions (Atreya et al., 1992, Law et al., 2001). The burner-supported spherical flame is in some respects similar to droplet burning but it holds the advantages that larger flames are possible and, with sufficiently long time, can approach quasi -steady state. Furthermore, the proposed microgravity coflow flames allow the direction of convection across the flame to be varied. Although the spherically -symmetric flame geometry has many advantages, it is not practical to produce such a flame at normal gravity. The reason for this can be understood by considering the Richardson number, Ri, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial force and is given by

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 6 Ri = g (ΔT L) / (T u2) . (2.1) Here g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u burner surface, and ΔΤ = (Tad – Tb), we find that Ri is on the order of 1000 in normal gravity. In fact, it is much higher than this because the more appropriate length and velocity scales are the flame diameter and the velocity at the flame, respectively. The value of Ri can be reduced by judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity. However, Ri for these flames is still on the order of unity, implying that while the flames appear spherical, natural convection is still present. Furthermore, hydrogen must be used as a fuel and be supplied in the ambient so such flames are not relevant to this study. A reduction in Ri can be achieved by reducing the flame size, but substantial reduction in L is not practical because our goal is to produce a flame that is sufficiently large that its structure can be characterized. Furthermore, heat loss to the burner would be excessive for small flames.

Consequently, for general fuels and inerts the only practical method of obtaining Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This can be accomplished in a number of microgravity environments, including ground-based facilities, e.g., drop towers for short times, as well as flight experiments, e.g., the International Space Station for longer times. A quantitative evaluation of the acceptable g levels for these experiments is given in Appendix A and is discussed below. The drop-tower results detailed in Section 1.3 have demonstrated the value of the sphericallysymmetric burner stabilized flame. The ability to reverse flow direction has helped to elucidate the dominant mechanism responsible for permanently -blue flames, yet the results are not conclusive because transient effects could dominate these observations. Transient effects arise from two sources: the ignition process and the long times required for spherical microgravity flames to reach quasi -steady state. The ignition process is not spherically symmetric and thus there is an asymmetry imposed by ignition that must be damped out.

More importantly, soot particles that are created during ignition can be trapped in the interior of the flame due to thermophoresis. The particles are trapped for the same reasons that a soot shell is produced in microgravity droplet combustion (Choi et al. , 1991, Avedisian and Callahan, 2000). Thus, it is possible for soot to exist in flames after the ignition event e ven though the flame has ceased producing soot. The reason the spherically-symmetric burner-stabilized flame takes so long to reach quasi-steady state is that the radial velocity scales with 1/r2. Thus, at only a few burner diameters away from the sphere, diffusion is the dominant mechanism of transport. Since the characteristic diffusion time τd is given by r2/D, τd is on the order of tens of seconds a few centimeters from the burner. Decreasing the flame size will decrease the size of the thermal field and, consequently, the time to reach quasi-steady state, but there are limits to the minimum flame size that is possible. These limits are imposed by the need to avoid heat loss to the burner and ensure flame sphericity.

Experiments performed in the 5 s drop facility indicate that for many of the run conditions needed for the proposed experiments the flame is still growing significantly after 5 s. Analytical (see Appendix A) and numerical calculations predict that up to 30 s of jitter -free (less than 10 -5 g) microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these run conditions. No ground-based facilities are available to accomplish this. In some ways, the spherical flame experiments are the nonpremixed analog to premixed flame balls because in both systems diffusion dominates the development of the far field temperature distribution. Therefore, this work is subject to the same needs as SO FBALL (Ronney et al., 1998)

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 7 in that long duration microgravity is needed and g -jitter must be negligible because the thermal field is very large and convection is small, i.e., Ri is large even for small g. To provide a quantitative assessment of the acceptable gravity level, an analysis was performed, as detailed in Appendix A. In this analysis, the acceleration induced on a fluid packet by natural convection is formulated by considering a gravitational acceleration given by a sinusoidal function. The resulting acceleration function for the fluid packet is next integrated to obtain the gravity induced flow velocity. This velocity can be converted to an additional mass flux that transports the flame front and causes distortion of the flame. By specifyin g the maximum percentage of distortion allowed in the experiment (10% here), the acceptable gravity level is determined, and this result is given in Fig. 2.1 for the four flames of Table 1.1. As shown, the required g levels are on the order of 10 μg. This is too for microgravity aircraft, but is consistent with the anticipated environment of the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).

Finally, it is important to emphasize that the proposed experiments illustrate an important and novel use of microgravity for combustion research. In microgravity we are able to hold Zst fixed and in coflow tests vary the direction of convection through the flame. There are no analogous experiments at 1g that can accomplish this. Experiments have been performed in normal gra vity coflow flames to understand the effects of flame structure and flow direction on soot formation (Kumfer et al., 2006, 2008, Skeen et al., 2009). As mentioned previously, owing to the effects of buoyancy on the flow field, the flow direction cannot be prescribed in normal gravity coflow flames as it can in microgravity spherical flames or microgravity coflow flames. For example, it is well known that for fuel issuing into an ambient of air, buoyancy accelerates the flow field and causes the streamlines to be from oxidizer to fuel in the lower regions of the flame and from fuel to oxidizer in the upper regions (Santoro et al., 1987). The importance of buoyancy to the flow field will vary with Zst because the velocity and thus Ri are strongly affected by dilution.

In other words, the relative amount of entrainment will vary with Zst in buoyant flames. Thus, normal gravity flames have ambiguities with respect to flow direction as Zst is varied. Nonetheless, coflow flames have been valuable in confirming the role of Zst on flame structure and the effects of residence time on soot inception (Kumfer et al., 2006, 2008, Skeen et al., 2009). Microgravity gas jet flames in quiescent surroundings have been observed in drop towers and the Space Shuttle and the results have revealed significant differences between the two in terms of

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 8 sooting behavior, suggesting that the drop tower results were far from steady state (Urban et al., 1998). Velocities in coflow flames are similar to those in gas jet flames in quiescent environments. Therefore the impact of buoyancy on coflow flames is expected to have a similar impact to that reported in Urban et al. (1998). Thus, drop tower coflow experiments are not a viable option for studying quasi-steady microgravity coflow flames. The characteristic times in these flames are long and thus the scalar fields develop much slower that in normal gravity, indicating that long duration microgravity is needed. C. Hardware Overview A. General Description Except for limited updates and clarifications in the boxed notes, this section is copied from section 2.A of the April 2021 version of ‘ACME Engineering Implementation’ which should be consulted for additional details. This section provides a general description of the ACME engineering from the ‘3.0 Experimental’ section of the following 2014 conference paper: Dennis P. Stocker, Fumiaki Takahashi, J. Mark Hickman, and Andrew C. Suttles, “Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station ,” Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Tulsa, OK, 16– 18 March 2014. IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper, from which this section was extracted, proceeded completion of the spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017. As a result, it does not accurately describe the final engineering in some regards . Therefore updates, clarifications, additional details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the original description. As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none were cropped.

As prev iously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners. Besides the chamber ins ert, other ACME-unique hardware includes a high -definition color camera and an avionics package, which is for data acquisition and control.

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 10 Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS. ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 t o 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew -exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper -motor drive will allow for precise positioning.

Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 11 However, only the larger gas -jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are addressed in detail in section 3.C of the ACME Engineering Implementation report. Unfortunately, the spherical burners did not always yield spherically symmetric flames, presumably because of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching. Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted using a loop ig niter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with a coil igniter tip, where that included the CFI-G investigation and the second-round testing for Flame Design, Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) , and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame), with the exception of the latter’s first day testing. For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D of the ACME Engineering Implementation report.

The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery system enables on -orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments. Gases can also be delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as the blending of different fuel gases. CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) that can be released into the combustion chamber. ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent.

Furthermore, the fuel diluted with helium (for s-Flame) was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer flows of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a maximum of 5 slpm. ACME did not use gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as in dicated above; the bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control. ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot volume fraction; and operational sup port. However, it is unlikely that all functions would be exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high -definition digital camera mounted outside of the chamber and a stan dard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning mirror).

Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations. Light emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 12 support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue -green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23 -24]. Alternately, CH* imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430 -nm bandpass filter with a 10 -nm full width at half -maximum transmissi on (FWHM). A 450 -nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission.

However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame conditions. The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, was not archived in space. The video was instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. Its gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction. The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second. But as an alternate, it was sometimes instead used with high gain values. The clear “filter” is of fused silica. Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it does not balance the intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature determination.

Meanwhile, rather than the 450 -nm bandpass filter described above, the high -definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions. For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A). Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band. This camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second (fps). Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss through the LCTF. Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where ACME is equipped with a crew -replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers. The fibers are orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video.

During set up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal t o either ACME’s color digital camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF. An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24].

TFP tests were conducted with 14-micron fibers spaced apart by 5 mm for a total span of 20 mm (in the case of 5 intact ceramic fibers), neglecting optional translation of the array. Tests were conducted using arrays with and without the platinum wire in the furthest do wnstream position. Tests were also sometimes conducted with some of the fibers broken and subsequently removed, leaving only three fibers in the final testing for the BRE and Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiments and for all CFI-G testing.

CIR has a second HiBMs camera, without a filter, that will be used in combination with CIR’s illumination package for alternate measurements of the soot volume fraction. This will be accomplished via an extinction technique previously employed in microgravity [3,6,26], where the camera and the collimated light source (with its two fiber-coupled laser diodes) are positioned at opposite windows. The images are recorded at 1024x1024 and 30 fps. Thus far, the primary purpose of this combined system has been the measurement of the droplet diameter for determination of the droplet burning rate. A HiBMs camera without the Liquid Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF) was used throughout ACME’s operations. In the first round of the CLD Flame experiment, it was used without a filter for flame imaging, but this proved to be largely unsuccessful because the camera is very insensitive to blue. Through the remainder of ACME testing, it was equipped with a red filter corresponding to the CIR illumination package for the rest of the ACME testing.

Unfortunately, that filter is sufficiently broad that significant incandescence can pass through the filter limiting its utility for determinations of soot volume fraction via light extinction, e.g., through the technique described in the following papers: D.L. Urban, Z.G. Yuan, P.B. Sunderland, K.C., Lin, Z. Dai, and G.M. During ACME operations, the HiBMs camera was typically archived at 15 fps because of data limits for transfer and downlink operations. And because operations were constrained by data limits, image data from this camera were sometimes deleted without downlinking to enable additional testing.

And in some testing, HiBMs images weren’t even acquired given their lesser value. Unfortunately, the HiBMs backlight illumination is significantly obstructed by the bracket for the electrode mesh further limiting its utility for the E -FIELD Flames experiment. This was a design

CIR’s Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL -UV) package is a monochrome camera with an intensifier (for 280-700 nm) and a 310-nm bandpass filter (with a 10-nm FWHM) for OH* imaging. Again as a result of the signal loss through the filter, binning is employed such that the OH* images are recorded at 512x512 and 30 fps. During ACME operations, the LLL -UV camera was only used for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment. While not discussed in the preceding section, another intensified camera was used throughout ACME testing, although its image data was sometimes deleted or not even acquired to allow the performance of additional tests. This was the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) camera which was generally configured with its CH* filter, where exceptions included CFI-G and s-Flame testing with particularly dim flames. Due to design trade-offs, its Field of View (FOV) was partially obstructed by the arms of the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array when it was moved inwards to the flame.

More information about th e CFI intensified camera can be found in its characterization report, CIR-RPT-4600. The ACME chamber insert will also be equipped with non -imaging optical diagnostics including both thermopile radiometers and Photomultiplier Tubes (PMTs). There is a crew -exchangeable linear array of radiometers of which there are two versions supporting the initial set of experiments. The array has a fixed position which is parallel to the chamber axis and centered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows and thus most of the other instrumentation. One array is equipped with a single wide -view radiometer with two narrow view radiometers that are downstream and two more that are upstream, where all views are orthogonal to the chamber axis, as depicted in Figure 4. The n arrow-view radiometers are intended to support studies of gas -jet flames, where ACME can accommodate shorter burners, making the “lower” detectors useful. The other array, also seen in Fig. 4, provides for three wideview measurements of the flame, where one view is masked to nominally block radiant emission from the burner.

It was specifically designed for the BRE experiment but will be a resource available to other ACME experiments. Given that the radiometer array can be exchanged by the crew, alternate arrays could be developed.

The third PMT will be equipped with a neutral density filter to prevent saturation. Like many other components, the PMT array can be removed from the chamber insert by the crew. Factors which led to the limited use of the short thermocouple rake included the need for crew time to switch between rakes and the potential adverse effects, such as heat loss and quenching, of the long (close) rake. The short (far) rake’s thermocouple tips should nominally be at 45, 60, 100, and 100 mm from the spherical burner center.

Meanwhile, the thermocouples of the long (near) rake should nominally be at 13, 25, 50, and 100 mm from the spherical burner center. For thermocouples at the same distance from the burner center, the angle between the rays from the burner center to the two thermocouples should be 90 degrees. The bead size of the thermocouples was not measured, but it is undoubte dly at least twice the size of the 0.2 mm diameter wire. For example, to accommodate the E-FIELD Flames experiment, the insert is equipped with a high -voltage supply and a crew-removable electrode mesh which can be set between +10 and -10 kV. The circular mesh is orthogonal to the chamber axis and is positioned (during set up) at either ~35 or ~50 mm downstream of the insulated burner. The ion current between the burner and electrode mesh will be determined via measurement of the voltage drop a cross a known resistor and application of Ohm’s Law.

Additional supporting measurements will be made, where the chamber pressure is a simple example. The ACME experiments will use the CIR’s gas chromatograph for pre - and post-test analysis of the chamber atmosphere, e.g., for oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and fuel gases. Acceleration measurements will be provided by the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) [27], which is the primary instr ument for such measurements on ISS and previously served that role for the space shuttle. The CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) was not used for the CFI-G, CLD Flame, or E-FIELD Flames investigations but was sometimes used during BRE, Flame Design, and s-Flame testing. Its use require d significant time and as such effectively reduce d the number of

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 18 tests that c ould be conducted. However, estimates of the chamber contents were computed assuming that the fuel in a normal flame test (for example) was either fully or not at all oxidized, e.g., for unsustained ignition in the latter case. The CIR facility was equipped with a 3-axis SAMS sensor head and the acceleration measurements, along with relevant documentation, are accessible via the home page for the Principal Investigator Microgravity Services (PIMS) , https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/. To be clear, the acceleration measurements are not archived with the ACME experiment data in the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) website, www.nasa.gov/PSI. All ACME experiments will be constant volume (i.e., rather than constant pressure) studies, where the chamber’s free volume will be about 90 liters. Burner flows will generally be constrained to limit the pressure rise, and tests will typically be 0.5-2 minutes in duration. The chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed hardware. The ACME experiments will be configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.

Instead, the experiments will be commanded from the ground, specifically from the Telescience Support Center (TSC) at the NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio. They can be conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre -programmed scripts. However, it will also be possible to effectively operate the experiments in a “manual” mode, where changes can be made in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, a flow rate could be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. Step and ramp changes can be made in the flow rate(s) or electric field pot ential. The TFP fiber array can be translated uniformly through a soot -free flame to get a continuum measurement of the temperature field. In summary, ACME’s experiment control will allow for broad flexibility. The TSC is now also referred to as the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). ACME tests were always conducted in a nominally automated mode. B.

Hardware Shortcomings From the Flame Design PI, Rich Axelbaum: “The only significant disappointment with the project was with the diagnostics, particularly with respect to gas temperature and soot volume fraction. They were not at the level that the team would have hoped. Much of this was due to the fact that the diagnostics were outdated by the time they were used in our experiments on the ISS, and thus the diagnostics and calibrations were not at the level that we expect in a laboratory experiment. Of course, the ISS has constraints that limit the ability to incorporate stateof-the-art diagnostics, and this likely made this weakness unavoidable, but it would have been valuable to have had more flexibility in terms of being able to upgrade the diagnostics with more modern cameras and instrumentation.” ACME’s sintered spherical burners did not always yield spherically symmetric flames which are centered on the burner’s center, where that combination is important for true spherical symmetry. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center bec ame increasing offset from the burner center as the flow rate was increased.

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 19 itself because the flame is seen to be shifted toward the supp ly tube. There was significant improvement when the starting burner (serial number 1002) was replaced mid -way through round 1 with an alternate burner (serial number 1003), which continued to be used for spherical flame testing throughout the remainder of ACME operations. Nonetheless, the symmetry was not perfect, which is a shortcoming of the Flame Design data. On 27 Dec. 2021 (GMT 361), it was determined that the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array was not aligned to the ACME Data Camera (DataCam ) as intended, i.e., so that the fibers would be orthogonal relative to the camera. Unfortunately, this was the fourth day of testing in which the fiber array wasn’t aligned, where it regrettably wasn’t recognized earlier. Given the importance of the TFP-derived measurements of the flame temperature, testing was halted until the array was aligned (with other crew tasks) by astronaut Raja Chari on 17 Jan. 2022 (GMT 017).

The signal from the standard ACME radiometer array used in round 1 of Flame Design testing was saturated for nearly every test, yielding non -useful data. For round 2, that sensor array was replaced with the one designed for Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI -G) which yielded satisfactory measurements. ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer did not always perform adequately, where the flow rates were not always appropriately steady or at the intended value. However, the resulting effects on the flame behavior are tentatively assumed to be minor. In addition to sections 3.A-B, shortcomings are discussed in Appendices B and C of this report and in the ACME Engineering Implementation document. The latter document includes discussion of deviations and waivers (in section 4.B), etc. 4. Preliminary Results A. Changed Test Plans A change was made to the CIR combustion chamber’s pressure limit on 17 Jan. 2022 (by astronaut Raja Chari) to enable Flame Design testing at chamber pressures of up to 3 atm in the final round- 2 test days, whereas the limit had been 1.5 atm in preceding testing.

In his request for this change, Flame Design PI Rich Axelbaum explained: “One of the fundamental goals of Flame Design is to achieve sooting limits. We are unsure if we will be able to attain a range of sooting flames with the current ambient fuel constraints. One way to increase soot formation, and thus the range of the test matrix, is via higher pressures, so this capability can help to ensure we me et our science goals. Another fundamental goal of Flame Design is to understand flame extinction. Our recent analysis suggests that pressure is a critical variable when predicting flame extinction, and in can influence flame chemistry in ways that we had not anticipated. Obtaining extinction data over a wide range of pressures could also be valuable for spacecraft fire safety.” An additional normal-flames test day was added to the start of the second round of testing (even though that was focused on inverse flames) to acquire data useful for calibrating the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) measurements. With that goal, the added test day, conducted on 28 Oct. 2021

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 20 (GMT 301), was carried out with the long (near) thermocouple rake, where all other Flame Design tests were conducted with the short (far) rake. In his request for this additional test day, the PI stated in part: “The ability to validate the TFP is very important for most of the ACME experiments. Thus, measuring the near-field temperatures under conditions where we have TFP data would be highly desirable, almost required. … These results would be the only measurem ents ACME has with a direct comparison with TFP, and since we already know exactly which flames to run to get good data, we know that we will be successful in obtaining this data and validating the TFP data. … Reiterating, this extra day would directly benefit all of the temperature data of Flame Design, and all of the spherical flame ACME experiments, by providing at least one direct validation of the TFP method.

As you know, we have uncertainties about the accuracy of the TFP technique we are using in the ACME rig, and having these T/C measurements could have a profound impact on the ACME results.” As discussed in the previous section, the decision was made to use the CFI-G radiometer array in Flame Design’s second round of testing rather than the standard ACME array that often saturated in the earlier testing. Coiled igniter tips were also used in the second round of testing instead of the loop igniter tips used in the first round, where the coiled were believed to be more robust. The narrative description of the experimental procedure is an excerpt from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of the following conference paper. Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D.

Dunn -Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. While the paper was written for the Electric -Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E -FIELD Flames) experiment, much of the discussion applies to ACME in general, including the Flame Design investigation. The figure referenced in this excerpt is not i ncluded herein. Clarifications and additional information, not in the conference paper, are included in boxed notes like this. The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Thus far, ACME’s activity has included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities. Most often the astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips. In the latter case, the igniter tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the crew already has changes to make changes in the interior of the insert. While these activities may seem mundane, the crew play a critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment.

As an extreme example, there were crew activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. In contrast, only two crew days were required to reconfigure the

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 21 hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner. Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. As a correction, including two maintenance activities, there were 11 crew days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to prepare for the initial CLD Flame testing on the space station. All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically , four to six people staff four consoles during the testing. The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console. Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many pre - and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM.

A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks. On intervening weekdays, the image dat a is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both gas bottles. Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2 -shift day for the RO and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew activity. As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week. A team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR a nd ACME console staff, and the daily operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing. The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding.

In the case of E -FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters. That te am does not see the telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e -mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files. In advance of the test day, the UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camer a settings. It is also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit.

Provisions were made to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely view the analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the operations center. All ACME flame tests, including those for Flame Design, were conducted in a nominally automated manner using software scripts and extensive parameter files. Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low rate results from several unavoidable factors. After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz nonimaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team. A small sample of images are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 22 those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples. The review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for the given fl ame conditions. After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed. Midway through a day’s E -FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minu tes through a filter cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) System. Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic communication outages with a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite to another) or can last as long as 30 minutes.

An average of 16 tests were conducted per Flame Design test day, where ignition was typically unsuccessful (e.g., un-sustained) in a couple of tests. In contrast to E-FIELD Flames, recirculation during Flame Design inverse-flame test operations was only conducted prior to venting at the end of a test day. During normal -flame testing, it was usually conducted once in the midst of testing, as done with E-FIELD Flames. Exceptions were test days 19115, 19123, and 19137 (the first three days with flames); 19161 (when no flames were ignited); 19206 (the last test day in the first round of testing), and 21301 (the first day of the second round of testing). Another exception was on 19150 when it was carried out duri ng the midst of testing and then again when the combustion chamber was vented and refilled for additional tests on the same day. A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis. The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material flammability.

That follow -on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing. Although it requires additional crew time, these allotments are split into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from testing for careful review of the early results so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of their second round. This paper reports on early results from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests. For E -FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010. At that time, NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited objectives rather than comprehensive experiments. As s uch, the general target was 50 tests per experiment. For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber.

This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing). The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion chamber. Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant). For E -FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 10 tests typically completed per day.

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 23 The maximum limit of 999 seconds for the valve safety timers was used for all ACME testing. Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, such as the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours. When necessary for the research, NASA does have continuous 24 -hour/day operations for some non -CIR experiments. But as discussed, the ACME tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is almost always limited to the planned durations. Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on -orbit hardware can store a limited amount of data. More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two shift transfer and downlink day. Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where image data from select cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge. Nonetheless, the limit sometimes forces decisions to abandon recorded images. This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME experiments are conducted.

Summary of Preliminary Results Abstract for Critical temperature and reactant mass flux for radiative extinction of ethylene microgravity spherical diffusion flames at 1 bar (2023): In microgravity combustion, where buoyancy is not present to accelerate the flow field and strain the flame, radiative extinction is of fundamental importance, and has implications for spacecraft fire safety. In this work, the critical point for r adiative extinction is identified for normal and inverse ethylene spherical diffusion flames via atmospheric pressure experiments conducted aboard the International Space Station, as well as with a transient numerical model. The fuel is ethylene with nitrogen diluent, and the oxidizer is an oxygen/nitrogen mixture. The burner is a porous stainless-steel sphere. All experiments are conducted at constant reactant flow rate. For normal flames, the ambient oxygen mole fraction was varied from 0.2 to 0.38, burner supply fuel mole fraction from 0.13 to 1, total mass flow rate, mtotal , from 0.6 to 12.2 mg/s, and adiabatic flame temperature, Tad , from 2000 to 2800 K.

For inverse flames, the ambient fuel mole fraction was varied from 0.08 to 0.12, burner supply oxy gen mole fraction from 0.4 to 0.85, mtotal from 2.3 to 11.3 mg/s, and Tad from 2080 to 2590 K. Despite this broad range of conditions, all flames extinguish at a critical extinction temperature of 1130 K, and a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2 s for normal flames, and an oxygen- based mass flux of 0.68 g/m 2-s for inverse flames. With this information, a simple equation is developed to estimate the flame size (i.e., location of peak temperature) at extinction for any atmospheric-pressure ethylene spherical diffusion flame given only the reactant mass flow rate.

Flame growth, which ultimately leads to radiative extinction if the critical extinction point is reached, is attributed to the natural development of the diffusion limited system as it approaches steady state and the reduction in the transport properties as the flame temperature drops due to increasing flame radiation with time (radiation-induced growth.) Abstract for On the existence of steady state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames in the presence of radiation heat loss (2023): Whether steady-state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion exist in the presence of radiation heat loss is an important fundamental question and has important implications for spacecraft fire safety. In this work, experiments aboard the International Space Station and a transient numerical model are used to investigate the existence of steady -state microgravity spherical diffusion flames. Gaseous spherical diffusion flames stabilized on a porous spherical burner are employed in normal (i.e., fuel flowing into an ambient oxidizer) and inverse (i.e., oxidizer flowing into an ambient fuel) flame configurations. The fuel is ethylene and the oxidizer oxygen, both diluted with nitrogen.

The flow rate of the reactant gas from the burner is held constant. It is found that steadystate gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames can exist in the presence of radiation heat loss, provided that the steady-state flame size is less than the flame size for radiative extinct ion, and the flame develops fast enough that radiation heat loss does not drop the flame temperature below the critical temperature for radiative extinction (1130 K). A simple model is provided that allows for the identification of initial conditions that can lead to steady -state spherical diffusion flames. In the spherical, infinite domain configuration, the characteristic time for the diffusion controlled system to effectively reach steady -state is found to be on the order of 100,000 s. Despite a narrow r ange of attainable conditions, flames that exhibit steady -state behavior are observed aboard the ISS for up to 870 s, even with the constraint of a finite boundary. Steady state flames are simulated using the numerical model for over 100,000 s.

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 26 Abstract for Observations of long duration microgravity spherical diffusion flames aboard the international space station (2021): Spherical diffusion flames of gaseous fuels supported on a porous spherical burner are investigated experimentally in microgravity for long durations aboard the International Space Station (ISS). Experimental results are compared with a transient numerical model. The experiments involve normal spherical diffusion flames (i.e., fuel flowing into oxidizer) burning ethylene in an oxygen/nitrogen mixture at atmospheric pressure. The stoichiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature are varied by diluting the fuel with nitrogen and varying the oxygen concentration in the ambient. The diagnostics consist of color v ideo, thin-filament pyrometry for gas temperature, thermocouple measurements of burner temperature, and photomultiplier tube measurements of broad and narrow-band flame emission. Burn times range from 28 –336 s. All flames grow monotonically after ignition . Peak gas temperature generally decreases with time.

Radiative extinction is observed when, at constant reactant flow rate, the flame expands until radiation heat loss approaches the chemical heat release. Before a flame experiences complete extinction, i t may enter an oscillatory mode in which part of the flame partially extinguishes and then reforms. The oscillations grow in magnitude until complete extinction. Sufficiently small flames with low radiation losses exhibit quasi -steady behavior, but burner heating is significant, and the experimental duration is dictated by the temperature limit of the porous sphere. Impacts, Benefits, and Products The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low.

For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame , leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. Introduction The Flame Design experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to impr ove the understanding of soot inception and control, in order to enable the optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and the ‘design’ of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free. An outside review panel declared that Flame Design “… could lead to greatly improved burner designs that are efficient and less polluting than current designs."

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 32 Flame Design investigates the soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames created with porous spherical burners. Tests are co nducted with various concentrations of both the fuel (e.g., ethylene) and oxygen in order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot inception. More specifically, Flame Design has the following experimental objectives which are listed here in priority order. It must be emphasized that NASA does not currently plan to carry out the desired or highly desired testing with carbon dioxide, pressure as a variable (except to a limited degree), coflow flames, or methane. A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2**), and pressure** for C2H4 and CH4* flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames**. B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi -steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4*.

Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2**), and pressure** on flame te mperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames. Obtain similar measurements for inverse and normal coflow flames**. C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2**), and pressure** for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 * flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Identify the presence of radiative or kinetic extinction. Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames. Measure blowoff limits for inverse and normal coflow flames**. *desired; **highly desired The majority of practical combustion processes involve the non -premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient, and the resulting emissions must be low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided.

Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken flames, leading to performance pen alties and possible extinction. The Flame Design study considers an innovative method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed flame design, as it takes a fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inh erent constraints imposed, designs flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. Flame design involves affecting the basic structure of the flame, in that the relationship between the temperature and concentration fields is varied to accom plish the desired objective. This method involves shifting the nitrogen from the air (or oxygen/nitrogen mixture) to the fuel stream, such that the mixing that occurs at the flame can be varied with or without affecting the flame temperature. [This can a lso be done with inerts other than nitrogen and oxygen/inert

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 33 mixtures other than air.] Such nitrogen exchange has enabled the production of the flames that are soot-free at all flow conditions, i.e., which are ‘permanently blue.’ The Flame Design experim ent involves gaseous hydrocarbon diffusion flames supported on a porous spherical burner. Soot inception limits and flame extinction limits are obtained as functions of the nitrogen exchange, flow direction, and pressure. Extensive analytical and computational modeling support the experimental investigation, where they are facilitated by the spherical flame shape enabled by the microgravity environment. Models include gas -phase and burner-surface radiation. Buoyant gravity-driven flow complicates the interpretation of the existing results and has led to different theories to explain the permanently-blue diffusion flames. It is not known whether this phenomenon is due more to a change in the direction of convection across the flame, or to a change in the detailed structure of the flame.

The challenges of normal-gravity studies are avoided by performing the tests on the International Space Station (ISS), where the non -buoyant microgravity flames allow the effects of convection direction and flame structure to be independently varied. By ejecting fuel from the burner into an oxidizer (e.g., air) in a buoyancy free system, the convective flow across the flame is unambiguously from fuel to oxidizer. Alternatively, by ejecting oxidizer from the burner into an atmosphere of fuel, the flow is from oxidizer to fuel. Furthermore, microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal -gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity -driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi -steady flames in microgravity. Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum -dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.

Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stab ility behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. Flame Design should yield unique data that allows for a better understanding of how nitrogen exchange affects soot-inception and flame extinction, and how it can be used to design optimum flames. In addition, the effects of flow direction are also studied, and the importance of the flow direction and flame structure to permanently-blue flames is assessed.

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 34 II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol Flame Design and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is comma nded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘ manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, the flow rate can be adjusted to approach a flame’s soot limit. This was not done during Increments 59 and 60, where the console commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished.

Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. III. Results A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight The first round of Flame Design tests, during which a total of 188 flames were ignited, was conducted during Increments 59 -60, more specifically from April -July. These tests featured normal flames, where gaseous fuel was ejected from a porous spherical burner into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. In contrast, the upcoming second round will feature tests with inverse flames, where the oxidizer is ejected from the burner into a fuel/nitrogen atmosphere. As a result, the second round flames will be ‘inside out.’ It is currently expected that the second round of tests will be conducted during Increment 63.

The ‘interruption’ in the Flame Design testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. Flame Design does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with the gaseous fuel ethylene (C2H4). It is a simple hydrocarbon gas for which the chemistry is well understood and it is typically highl y sooting because of its carbon double bond. The tests were conducted with both pure fuel

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 35 and fuel mixed with nitrogen. In the latter case, the ACME hardware allows for simultaneous flow of fuel (from a launched bottle) and ISS nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations. No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for Flame Design; all of the ISS results were electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME experiments.
