text: Furthermore the soot formation/oxidation times are believed to be greater than the time necessary for diffusion of reactants. 27 If chemical kinetics is practically instantaneous, then residence time becomes the dete rmining factor for soot formation and oxidation. It has also been suggested that the ratio of soot formation and soot oxidation times also determines when the smoke poin t will occur. Lautenberger et al. 27 describe this process for buoyant laminar flames. “Increasing the flame height increases the residence time and allows more time f or the flame to produce soot. Once formed, this soot requires additional time to oxidize in the upper parts of the

source: Reports SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES DotsonThesis
text: 5 flame if it is to be entirely consumed below the fl ame tip. As soot travels through the flame (in a Lagrangian sense), it radiates away energy and cools the flame gases.” Also corroborating what was mentioned previously ab out a limiting temperature at which soot oxidation ceases, typically at the smoke point flame height, the radiative heat loss from the flame by soot radiation is about 30% of the total heat release rate of the flame. 28 The cooled flame gases can no longer oxidize the s oot and one could consider the soot formation/oxidation time to appro ach the diffusion time. 27 Smoke is then released from the tip of this flame and it has just surpassed its characteristic smoke point because the required time for soot oxidation is now less than the time the soot is capable of being oxidized post flame sheet. Important review articles on soot formation mechani sms are available from Frenklach 29 , Mansurov 30 , and Glassman. 31 Richter and Howard 32 in a particularly detailed fashion reviewed the formation of PAHs and their growth to soot. Soot oxidation is well covered by Stanmore et al. 33 1.3.

text: Fuel and Diluent Effects For diffusion flames, work by Schalla and McDonald 34 showed that fuel sooting propensity decreases with hydrocarbon family in the following order: aromatics > alkynes > alkenes> alkanes. According to Glassman 31 , increasing the molecular weight of the fuel increases the soot formation rat e by increasing the radical concentration and the Arrhenius pre-exponential factor for the overall rate coefficient. In premixed flames, the number of carbon-carbon (C- C) bonds determines the critical

source: Reports SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES DotsonThesis
text: 6 sooting equivalence ratio in a predictable fashion. However, the number of C-C bonds is only an indirect measure of the pyrolysis rate of the fuel. In diffusion flames H radicals are important to the fuel pyrolysis process, facilitating the initial pyrolysis of the virgin fuel as well as the subsequent attack on fuel intermediates. H radicals facilitate abstraction reactions much faster than hydrocarbon radicals do. Despite this importance of H radicals, Schug et al. 4 have shown that the initial overall carbon-hydrogen (C/H) atom ratio of the fuel does not determine the sooting propensity. Nevertheless the degree of mole cular unsaturation correlates with higher sooting propensity, perhaps likely due to th e greater ease these molecules can form acetylenes and PAHs. In over-ventilated coflow diffusion flames, additio n of inert to the fuel stream typically reduces sooting propensity. Longer smoke points result. However the addition of inert can also alter the flame temperat ure. This occurs by the inert acting as a heat sink, this effect depending on the heat c apacity of the inert.

Additionally , the temperature field of the flame can be altered through transport effects. Ine rt species with high thermal diffusivities have their volumetric dilution effect s countered by a thermal effect of extending the high temperature range where soot for mation is possible. 36 The temperature of the pyrolysis zone determines the so ot propensity and correlates well

Buoyancy Effects Soot is transported in flames primarily by convecti on, modified slightly by thermophoresis. The primary difference between a bu oyant and nonbuoyant jet flames is that, in general, a buoyant flame, the fl ow is accelerating, while for a nonbuoyant jet the flow is decelerating. This is of course neglecting volumetric expansion from combustion related heating. In gener al, for a buoyant flame the flow streamlines move towards the flame axis, while for the nonbuoyant flame the flow streamlines are drawn outwards from the flame axis. 16 Therefore in a buoyant flame, once soot is nucleated in the soot production regio n near the flame sheet, it is drawn into the fuel rich core, allowing continued growth. In a nonbuoyant flame as the flow is drawn outwards, the soot moves in a more direct path to the flame sheet and oxidative region downstream. 16 It had been predicted that smoke points would not o ccur in nonbuoyant gas-jet flames.

Velocity Field Effects By varying the burner diameter, coflow velocity, an d fuel dilution, flame shape and residence times in the soot formation and soot oxid ation regions can be changed. Reductions in the burner (fuel jet exit) diameter i ncrease the mean fuel jet velocity, reducing overall flame residence time, assuming tha t flame length only depends on the mass flow rate of fuel. There has not been subs tantial research into the burner diameter effect on smoke points. The work of Kent a nd Wagner 25 showed that reducing burner diameter (increasing fuel jet veloc ity) shifts the centerline sootvolume-fraction profile downstream, without modifyi ng peak values.

text: 12 Chapter 2. Theoretical and Numerical Methods 2.1. Flame Shapes Faeth and co-workers 42,43,44 applied the flame shape analysis of Spalding 45 to still flames. This is a similarity solution approach that assumes the following for a steady, axisymmetric laminar jet diffusion flame at constan t pressure in a still environment: (1) no buoyant forces (2) no viscous dissipation (l ow Mach number), (3) the flame has a large aspect ratio so that diffusion of speci es, momentum and energy in the streamwise direction is small, (4) all chemical rea ctions occur in a thin flame sheet with an infinite reaction rate, (5) diffusivities o f mass of all species, momentum, and energy are all equal (unity Lewis number), (6) all transport properties and heat capacities are constant and equal throughout the fl ame, (7) effects of radiation are small, and (8) constant density. An additional cav iot is that rather than matching the initial conditions at the jet exit, integral conser vation of species is maintained. This approach is more suited to predicting conditions in the far-field where similarity is likely to be satisfied.

Quantitative correlations may also be possibl e from an examination of radiative losses, which have been observed to be 20-30% for n ormal-gravity smoke point flames and increase with adiabatic flame temperature. 5 As a first approximation, the velocity field of a n on-reacting axisymetic jet flow was investigated to estimate residence times for the mi crogravity flames in this study. Much of the literature assumes constant velocities throughout the flow field of jet flames for residence time estimation. It is more ap propriate to consider theoretical velocity decay from a jet. There has not been an ad equate theory developed for the velocity field of a laminar jet in coflow. The lite rature focuses on jets into a still environment (simple jets), 49,50,51,52,53,54 turbulent jets in a slow moving coflow 55 , or even jets in a counterflowing stream 56 . The only experimental study on jets in a coflowin g stream (including jets in the laminar regime) utili zed contraction nozzles to produce an initial uniform velocity profile (plug flow), ra ther than fully developed Poiseuille flow.

text: 22 Chapter 3. Experimental Procedure All of the tests performed required determining when the s moke point condition was reached. The smoke point is a transition between two different flame behaviors, nonsmoking and smoking. There are several indicators of t he smoke point. A nonsmoking flame does not have any obvious smoke product ion, and it is helpful to view the flame against a white or black background to determ ine this. Generally a white background it best for observing smoke production visual ly. A non-smoking flame has a relatively sharp luminous boundary at its lumin ous flame tip. This is somewhat dependent on overall soot concentrations within the fl ame. The tip is usually closed, though soot ‘wings’ are also typically present. These horn-like structures at the luminous flame tip are produced in an annular region c ontaining the majority of the flame sheet. The luminous flame tip is also bright, an d orange or yellow in color. A sooting flame usually opens up at its tip and is usu ally not sharply defined. The tip also darkens and becomes redder due to the cooling of t he soot. 3.1.

text: 40 Chapter 4. Results and Discussion 4.1. Microgravity Smoke Points Smoke points were obtained for five fuels, as summarized in Table 3.1. Smoke points could not be obtained for methane before the flames wou ld impinge on the copper plate at the end of the duct. These flames did not sh ow any signs of approaching their smoke points before impinging on the plate. Also show n in Table 3.1 are the ranges of various parameters for which microgravity smoke points were observed. Some smoke points, for propane and ethylene in particu lar, were identified by the onset of gradual dimming and reddening of the luminous flame tip in the downstream direction. Rounding of the flame tip was also associa ted with the smoke point for these flames. Conversely the brightest flames did not a lways display significant reddening or darkening near their tips, except when well above the smoke point. This occurred for the pure propylene and propylene mixtures, a nd the smoke point was identified by the rapid transition to an open-tipped, soot emitting flame. For conditions sufficiently above the smoke point, quench ed soot could be seen leaving the flame.

source: Reports SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES DotsonThesis
text: Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were found to be generally more luminous than those of methane, ethylene, and propane , resulting from their higher propensity to form soot. Periodic flame motion was observ ed in some flames, especially those with high coflow, long length, and low fuel velocity, and this is

source: Reports SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES DotsonThesis
text: 41 attributed to non-uniform coflow. Propane flames appeared t o be especially susceptible. However, this effect was small and did no t prevent clear measurement of the flame length. For ethylene and 1.6 mm burner propane flames, the smoke point transition was not surpassed to a large degree so there is some uncertainty whether these points are smoke points, or that the actual poi nt could be slightly higher. The present smoke points were found to be repeatable, e xcept for propylene with the 0.41 mm burner. Testing on different days yielded differen t smoke points for this combination. This is attributed to a change in the duct exit system, which became partially clogged with soot and required higher fan vol tages to obtain a given coflow air velocity reading. The lower smoke points were obt ained with a relatively clogged exit, and the highest smoke point was found after the exit was vacuumed clean. For all of these tests, the air coflow rate was set based o n the hot-wire anemometer velocity reading. The flow restriction in the exit may have altered the coflow in some manner and also the measured smoke points.

text: Other smoke points collected on these two dates did not exhibit this same discrepancy so t his coflow quality effect may only affect flames of this smallest burner diameter. It could b e surmised that the coflow is less uniform for the case of higher fan voltage for a particu lar flow rate. Figure 4.1 shows images for representative flames near the ir smoke points. Two sequences are shown, and in both the smoke point oc curs between the third and fourth flames. In the top sequence, coflow velocity decreases from left to right at a constant fuel flow rate. This increases luminous flame length an d reduces the smoke point,

text: 42 leading to soot emission. The luminous length decrea ses in the fourth image because it was taken at a shorter shutter time. In the bottom sequence fuel flow rate is increased at a constant coflow velocity, increasing fl ame length as expected. As seen in Figure 4.1, luminous length is more sensitive to c hanges in fuel flow rate than to changes in coflow velocity. In Figure 4.2 the measured smoke point lengths are plo tted with respect to coflow velocity. For a given choice of fuel and burner diamete r, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke point length. This behavior could be attributed Figure 4.1. Color still camera images of 75% C 3H6 flames with (top) decreasing coflow velocity at a constant fuel flow rate, and (bottom) increasing fuel flow rate at a constant co flow velocity. text: 43 to decreased residence times in the soot formation regi on as the coflow velocity is increased. Alternatively, if soot oxidation in the pos t-flame-sheet region is limited by oxidizer transport into the region, then increases in co flow velocities would increase the rate of soot oxidation. This would delay the smo ke point transition to higher fuel flow rates until the rate of soot formation overcomes the rate of soot oxidation. text: 64 Chapter 5. Conclusions Smoke points of microgravity and normal gravity gas-jet diffusion flames were observed. Microgravity conditions emphasized small burn ers and effects of coflow velocity. These flames allow extensive control of resid ence time, which may be important in smoke point phenomena. An increase in co flow velocity increases the smoke point length. A decrease in burner diameter incre ases the smoke point length. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. The effect of coflow velocity could also be explained by in creased O 2 transport if soot oxidation downstream of the flame sheet is transport lim ited. The fuel sooting propensities in these flames are as fol lows: propane < ethylene < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene, however ethy lene is less sooty than propane for the 0.76 mm burner. To the first order, luminous length at the smoke point is proportional to fuel mass flow rate, consisten t with past theory and experiments. A second-order effect is that this length increases for low ua,o / u f,o velocity ratios.

For the smaller burner tests in a confined coflow environment, sm oke point length increased with an increase in coflow velocity or a decrease in no zzle diameter. For a very large burner in an unconfined coflow, the smoke point length decreased with increasing

This, and results of a previous study showing domains where the s moke point is invariant to changes in coflow velocity, indicate that the relatio nship of smoke point to coflow velocity and nozzle diameter is more complicated than initially expected. It has been hypothesized that the different responses may be due to different soot oxidation regimes, transport-limited, kinetics-limited, and residen ce-time-limited. Simplified analysis of the residence time and soot forma tion time to soot oxidation time ratio of the SPICE microgravity flames failed to yi eld substantial collapse of the smoke point data or a residence time related criticalit y. This may be due to the simplified nature of the analysis, such as neglecting combustion related volumetric expansion. COMSOL® simulations have shown that the simplified Schlichting-based analysis does not adequately predict the centerline v elocity decay of air jets with initial air to fuel velocity ratios larger than around 0.2 – 0.5.

text: Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment “SPICE” Microgravity Science Glovebox Increment 19-20 (30 Day Report) Investigators: David Urban NASA GRC, Peter Sunderland: Univ. Maryland Project Scientist: Zengguang Yuan, National Center for Space Exploration Research Project Manager: Robert Hawersaat NASA GRC I. Introduction A. Hypothesis The hypothesis of the SPICE investi gation is that smoke point behavior will be observed for co-flowing flames and that it will show dependence on nozzle diameter and coflow velocity. B. Objectives of Investigation The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions. C. Previous Mission Experience N/A D. Background/History of Project (Optional) The SPICE experiment was an outgrow th of the Laminar Soot Processes Experiment (LSP) which flew on STS 83, 94, and 107.

SPICE utilized the design heritage and modified the hardware from the Enclosed Laminar Flames Experiment (ELF) which flew in the Middeck Glovebox on STS 87. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velo city, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Appr oximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support crew in Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. After the tests the video record was analyzed to identify sm oke point conditions. The associated coflow and fuel flow rates were obtain ed from digital data recorded in the video. The smoke point lengths, LSP, we re obtained from the video record and are the measured distance from the burner tip to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis.

III. Results A. Introduction Soot formation is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 50,000 prem ature deaths in the U.S. [1] a nd is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting [2]. Radiation from soot in flames allows reading by candlelight but also contributes to he at loads in engines and the spread of unwanted fires. Smoking flames emit carbon monoxide, which is the major cause of death in fires [3]. The smoke point is the condition (or length) where a flame begi ns to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous a nd condensed fuels [4–9].

Laminar smoke points have been found to correl ate with soot volume frac tions [10] and radiative loss factions [11] of turbulent diffusion flames. Yang et al. [12] found that gas turbine soot em issions correlate very well with a threshold sooting i ndex (TSI) based on fuel molecula r weight divided by the laminar smoke point. Smoke points have been shown to co rrelate with the smoke release from turbulent buoyant flames [13] and have been applied to developing general soot models for computational combustion simulations [14] and heat release measurements [15]. In a 1988 paper [16], Glassman predicted that smoke points would not occur in nonbuoyant gasjet flames. He based this on the assumption that residence time scales with the square root of fuel flow rate in normal gravity but is independent of flow rate in microgravity flames. Subsequent work [17] observed smoke points of nonbuoyant fl ames aboard a parabolic aircraft and used numerical predictions to show that residence time increases with flame length for nonbuoyant flames without co-flow. Urban et al. [18] reported smoke points of microgravity flames observed on a space shuttle.

2 owing to g-jitter and in drop facilities owing to limited test times. Attributing smoke point behavior to total resi dence time helps with qualitative explanations of smoke point behavior but to date has not yielded successful quant itative correlations [8]. This may be because smoke points arise from a comp etition between the times available for soot formation and soot oxidation. De lichatsios and co-workers suggest ed that smoke point length is proportional to soot formation time [19–20]. Quantitative correlations may also be possible from an examination of radiative losses, which have been observed to be 20 – 30% for normal-gravity smoke point flames and to increase with adiabatic flame temperature [5]. Soot is transported in flames by convection and thermophoresis. By varying the burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel dilution, flame shape and residence times in the soot formation and soot oxidation regions can be changed. A decrease in coflow velocity will generally increase entrainment of flow towards the flame axis.

Kent and Wagner [21] found that smoke burn out in the oxidat ive region of the flame ceases when the tip of a buoyant diffusion flame cools to approximately 1300 K. Urban et al. [22] found that the tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) fl ame reaches 1000 K at its smoke point. In buoyant flames this decrease in temperature is attr ibuted primarily to he at conduction, while in nonbuoyant flames it is attributed largely to ra diative quenching [23]. The radiative quenching effect causes a visible tip openi ng in nonbuoyant smoke points of flames of relatively long residence time [22]. A recent 2.5 s drop tower study by Jeon et al. [24] found that for small coflow velocities the soot volume fraction increases with coflow velocit y. This was attributed to an increase in temperature. Lin and Faeth [7,25] studied the effects of coflow velocity on weakly-buoyant flames near the smoke point. They observed flam es in normal gravity, but at low pressures to reduce the effects of gravity. They found that increasing the coflow velocity reduced soot volume fractions and increased the smoke point le ngth. This was attributed to decreased flame residence time and modified soot pathlines. Thus motivated, the objectives of this study are: 1. to measure nonbuoyant smoke points of propane, ethylene, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures, 2. to identify the effects of coflow velocity and burner diameter on the smoke points, and 3. to correlate the luminous flame lengths. 2. Experimental The Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPI CE) module was brought to the International Space Station (ISS) in 2008. It was operated in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) by various crew members in 2009. Smoke points were at tempted for all fuels for fuel jet diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm. The conditions for which smoke points were found are summarized in Table 1. In some cases (e.g., te sts involving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted before desired smoke points could be found, as the supply was limited to two 75 cc bottles of each fuel at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa, depending on the fuel. The SPICE module contains a rectangular duct th at has an approximately 76 mm square cross section with rounded corners. A DC fan supplie s coflowing air from the glovebox contents.

The air passes through a honeycomb and screen to reduce swirl and then enters the duct. The air and combustion products leave the duct through a pe rforated copper plate followed by a copper screen. The screen is 50 mm upstream of th e burner discharge and the plate is 120 mm downstream. Fan voltage is varied to control the coflow velocity, which is measured with a hotwire anemometer between the inlet honeycomb a nd screen. This anemometer was calibrated in normal gravity using a hot-wire anemometer 36 mm downstream of the duct entrance. Fuel flow rate was adjusted manually and controlled with a mass flow meter. The flames were ignited with a hot-wire ignitor. Video was recorded with an analog color video camera and downlinked in real time. Still images were recorded with a 12 bit Nikon™ D100 single-lens reflex color digital still camera (with 3008 × 2000 pixels) with a 60 mm lens. Most of the tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support crew in Cleveland.

Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. After the tests the video record was analyzed to identify smoke point conditions. The associated coflow and fuel flow rates were obtained from digital data r ecorded in the video. The smoke point lengths, LSP, were obtained from the vi deo record and are the measured distance from the burner tip to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not sharply defined in most images, but rather involved a transition from bright yellow to black across an axial distance of 2 – 5 mm. Flame hei ght was thus measured to the point where the centerline grayscale intensity changed most rapidly between these yellow and black regions. This helped reduce the sensitivity of measured flame height to camera exposure settings. Smoke points were obtained for five fuels, as summarized in Table 1. Smoke points were

4 attempted with methane, but could not be obtained before the flames impinged on the plate at the end of the duct. Also shown in Table 1 are the ranges of various parameters for which microgravity smoke points were observed. 3. Results and Discussion Some smoke points, propane and ethylene in part icular, were identified by the onset of gradual (rather than sharp) dimming and reddening of the luminous flame tip in the downstream direction. Rounding of the tip al so was associated with th e smoke point. For conditions sufficiently above the smoke point, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flame. The brightest flames did not always display significant redden ing or darkening near their tips, except well above the smoke point. This occurred for the pu re propylene and propylene mixtures, and the smoke point was identified by the rapid transition to an open-tipped, soot emitting flame. The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than those of methane, ethylene, and propane, attribut ed to their higher propensity to form soot.

The smoke point transition was more abrupt in th e propylene-based fuels than for propane or ethylene. Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with high coflow, long length, and low fuel velocity, and is attributed to non-uniform coflow. This effect was small and did not prevent clear measurement of flame length. Figure 1 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. Two sequences are shown, and in both the smoke point occurs betw een the third and fourth flames. In the top sequence, coflow velocity decreases from left to right at constant fuel flow rate. This increases luminous flame length and reduces the smoke poi nt leading to soot emission. The luminous length decreases in the fourth image owing to incomplete combustion. In the bottom sequence fuel flow rate is increased at constant coflow velocity, increasing flame length as expected. As seen in Fig. 1, luminous length is more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in coflow velocity. Table 1.

ii Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) Abstract The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the luminous flame length) where a flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels. Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss fractions of turbulent diffusion flames. SPICE project measured laminar smoke points in non) buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co)flowing air aboard the International Space Station. Fifty)two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co)flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter, and co)flow velocity. Increasing co)flow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co)flowing flames.

These trends can be explained qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The measured smoke point lengths were found to correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity. A model of residence times in coflowing flames is developed, and although residence time helps explain many of the observations, it does not correlate the measured smoke points. The measurements yielded estimates of sooting propensities of the present fuels in microgravity diffusion flames. Acknowledgments The authors acknowledge G.M. 1 INTRODUCTION SPICE project, from it was rewarded in 1997 to it w as conducted onboard ISS in 2009, covered more than a decade time span. During these years, t he project experienced a few cycles of active and inactive status. A brief project history is given b elow. SPICE project was awarded on December 3, 1997 by the Microgravity Science and Application Di vision of NASA Headquarters to Professor Gerard M. Faeth of the University of Michigan for h is proposal titled as Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Nonbuoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames in response to NASA’s 1996 Solicitation for Glovebox Investigations issued in late 1996. The or iginal proposal of Professor Faeth was meant to be a supplement to the Laminar Soot Processes Exper iment which was a combustion project under NASA Grant No. NAG3-1245, conducted onboard STS-73 and STS-94 in 1997. In the awarding letter, the experiment was planned to be carried out onboard STS-107, for which the launch date was then scheduled in May 2000. From December 1997 to t he end of 1999 was the first phase of the project.

In this period, the experiment was planned to be conducted in the Middle Deck Glove Box of a Space Shuttle and the SPICE hardware was fabri cated and assembled in GRC. Various project reviews necessary for the flight project, were comp leted. In addition, significant efforts on science side were made to explore proper camera settings fo r different flame conditions by conducting reduced gravity experiment in parabolic flight on board the KC-135 aircraft. From the end of 1999 to March 2002, the project was inactive. The second p hase of the project was from March 2002 to January 2005. In this period, SPICE was a part of MRDOC contract to ZIN Inc., for a potential UF-1 Flight. Since the target facility of SPICE was swit ched from Space Shuttle’s Middle Deck Glove Box to the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), ZIN’s major effort was to retro-fit hardware for use with MSG in International Space Station (IS S), which included: designed and assembled Power/Video Unit to support MSG video interfaces, d esigned and fabricated a new mechanical camera supports, redesigned fuel bottle assemblies and developed new cabling. Project was cancelled again at the end of 2004.

ZIN developed s torage plan for hardware which was presented to NASA in December, 2004. The SPICE apparatus was put in storage in January 2005 and all the documents were archived waiting for future flight o pportunities. At that time, the LSP project and the re-flight LSP-2 were completed, thus the object ives of SPICE were later changed to a standalone investigation of smoke point of jet diffusion flames with coexistence of air flows. One important event soon after the SPICE became inactive again was the sudden death of Professor Faeth of the University of Michigan, the PI of the projec t. It was not until March 2006 that the SPICE was resurrected in May, 2006 as part of the Small Paylo ads Projects Task under MRDOC that Dr. David Urban, the Co-I of the project, succeeded Professor Faeth as the PI of the project. In addition, Professor Peter Sunderland of University of Marylan d, former Ph.D. student of Prof. Faeth was recruited as a Co-I of the project. An updated Scie nce Requirement Document was edited. The test matrix was finalized. Additional tests in camera were conducted. Minor hardware modifications were made and a number of project reviews were conducted.

The SPICE hardware was shipped to KSC on June 18, 2008 and later lifted up to ISS by ULF-2 in October 2008. SPICE experiments were finally conduc ted in ISS MSG from February through June of 2009. What Follows is the science significance and justification of the SPICE project. Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an i mportant unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S. 1 and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting. 2 Radiation from soot in flames is beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires. 3 Knowledge of Soot formation is needed for developing computational combustion.

2 The differences between soot processes in buoyant a nd nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames can be seen by comparing their soot production regions as plotted in Fig. 1. Soot formation in diffusion flames generally is limited to fuel-equivalence rat ios, φ, in the range 1-2, which are marked on the plots. Unlike gases, which both convect and diffus e, soot mainly convects with the flow velocity so that it moves along the streamline. For buoyant fl ames, the dividing streamline generally is inside the soot formation region so that most of the soot initially forms near the flame sheet, where φ, =1, and then moves radially inward toward cooler region s having higher fuel concentrations. The soot formation process for nonbuoyant flames is complete ly different: most of the soot initially forms near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the fl ame sheet. Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Lamin ar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be subs tantially different form that seen in normal gravity.

The removal of buoyancy induced accelerat ion can cause the smoke point phenomenon to be dominated by radiative heat losses for condition s of low overall flame velocity. Under these conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effe ct, it is still possible to have flames that either emi t soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate. Figure 1. Soot path lines through buoyant and non-b uoyant flames The information of smoke-point properties and flame shapes is needed to improve our understanding of heat and mass transfer mechanisms for different flame conditions. Unfortunately, while the laminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffu sion flames at normal gravity are well known, corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of soot generation and oxidation processes under micro gravity conditions are critical to devise better fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration activities.

In addition, the improved understanding of soot processes in laminar flames will help us, by analogy, to gain better understanding of soot processes in practical turbulent flames. The objectives of the SPICE experiments is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames for several fuels unde r different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the

3 flame shapes under co-flow conditions. In particula r, the experiments are planned to be conducted under the following conditions: six types of fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, 75% propylene mixed with 25% nitrogen in moles, and 50% propylene mixed with 50% nitrogen in moles; three nozzles: 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 mm ID and two air v elocities: 100% and 50% of the maximum air flow velocity (near 50cm/s). The operation procedur es are as such that the air velocity is set first, then start the fuel flow and ignite the flame. Fuel flow rate is adjusted until the smoke point is reached. Thus, for each combination of a fuel and a nozzle size, two smoke point fuel flow rates are obtained. One is under 100% air velocity and the ot her is under 50% air velocity. Then in the case of 50% air velocity, the fuel flow rate is reduced to 50% of the smoke point fuel flow rate to get a flame length with that fuel flow rate. SPICE EXPERIMENT SETUP A.

SPICE FLIGHT TESTS The actual SPICE tests were conducted in SMG in twelve sessions from February 14, 2009 to June 23, 2009. In each session, the SPICE science team and engineering team were in the TeleScience Center (TSC) in GRC to support the tests conducted on MSG. Real-time flame images were available as long as air-to-ground communication channel was available. In addition, the team was able to communicate with the astronaut who conducted the experiment to answer questions or to clarify any ambiguities.

Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow vel ocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support team in TSC. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS c abin air. The oxygen mole fraction of this cabin air is maintained within 19 – 24%. After the tests the video record was analyzed to id entify smoke points. The smoke point lengths, L SP , (and the flow conditions) were obtained from the vi deo record and are the measured distance from the burner to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not sharply defined in most images, but rather transiti oned from bright yellow to black over an axial distance of 2 – 5 mm. 17 DISCUSSION Although it is convenient to classified all flames, laminar vs. turbulent and diffusion vs. premixed, into two categories based on their soot emission co nditions, i.e., soot emitting flames and non-soot emitting flames, the conditions delineating the two or the conditions of onset of soot emission are difficult to define. Up to date, these conditions h ave been documented solely based on experimental observations. Many efforts have been made to dev elop a universal method of defining the onset of soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer to parameters used to set the flame, not those gene rated by the flame. The primary parameters of jet diffusion flames include fuel type, fuel and oxidiz er supply rates, ambient temperature and pressure, and configuration of the device where the flame takes place, such as nozzle diameter and dimensions of the combustion chamber.

The flame temperature, g as velocity and species distributions as well as flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat ge neration and heat loss, are the parameters generated by the flame which is not considered as p rimary parameters. If a method that relates smoke point to those primary parameters were found, we would be able to predict whether a flame emits soot or not based on the planned flame condit ions. In the course of pursuing such a universal method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of so ot emission have been proposed to associate smoke point with certain flame generated parameters . Those surmises served as a middle step in hoping to help further development of the aforement ioned method. The first surmise, and least controversial, is that smoke points occur when soot temperature drops below a critical temperature prior to soot burnout. This temperature is about 13 00 K in normal gravity 8,9 and 1000 K in microgravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiati ve loss fraction reaches 0.2 – 0.4 for normal-gravity flames 12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames.

This ratio increase s with flow rate. Once it reaches about 2, smoke poin t occurs. 15,18,19 The last surmise suggests that smoke point correlates with the centerline flame re sidence time. This is the most complex 8-11,17,18,20- 24 surmise because flame residence time affects the s oot processes in twofold. An increase in residence time can lead to soot emissions by increa sing the time available for soot formation. Because this generally also increases the time avai lable for soot oxidation, it has been proposed that smoke points are associated with conditions where t he time available for soot formation exceeds that for soot oxidation to certain extent. 21 This is difficult to prove because to evaluate the flame residence time requires the velocity distribution a lone the centerline and the flame length, both of which are resulted flame parameters, not readily av ailable from primary parameters of the experiment.

In addition, the soot formation time an d oxidation time are conceptually defined. Practically, these times are not measurable and the y might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles ma y happen simultaneously. Because of these difficulties and ambiguities, the fame residence ti me theory cannot be proved or disproved rigorously. However, these obstacles do not preven t us from checking the residence time theory against the observed smoke point data with the help of some approximated velocity distribution and flame length information. More detailed discussion of this effort can be found in the publications resulted from the SPICE project listed in Appendice s B through F. The results showed that although residence time is helpful in understanding the pres ent smoke points, it does not yield quantitative correlations. CLOSING REMARKS Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion f lames in coflowing air were measured in earth orbit. The conditions emphasized small burners and the effects of coflow velocity. These flames allow extensive control over residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena.

The major conclusions are as follows: 1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. 3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. 4. The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtur es in microgravity increase according to ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane. 5. Consistent with past theory and experiments, lumino us length at the smoke point is proportional to fuel mass flow rate. However there is a slight increase in luminous length as u a / u f decreases. 6. Although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative correlations of smoke points. 7. The present smoke point lengths scale with d –0.91 uair 0.41 . 1 Executive Summary This work examines how microgravity conditions on spacecraft change the development of smoke aerosol relative to smoke on Earth. We perform simulations of particle formation and growth with the goal of capturing smoke dynamics similar to those realized in experiments performed aboard the International Space Station. The simulations provide detailed information about ﬂuid/thermal/particle interactions that cannot be acquired experimentally on orbit. A surrogate material, dibutyl pthalate, is expelled from a hot surface in a rectangular chamber while ambient air is blown through the domain, convecting the developing smoke downstream. The study considers two ﬂow rates, two geometric con- ﬁgurations, and the isolated effects of gravitational particle settling and thermophoresis. In Earth gravity, buoyancy produces asymmetries in all ﬁelds of interest and ampliﬁes vapor-to-particle conversion near room temperature surfaces at the upper boundary of the simulation domain. Gravitational settling removes large particles from the aerosol, limiting the maximum particle size to ∼ 40 µm and the mode particle size to∼ 5µm.

Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmetric and contains very large particles (> 40µm). A bimodal particle size distribution results in microgravity when prominent recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source. The distribution is comprised of large particles (> 20µm) associated with long residency time, vapor rich, high temperature recirculation, and smaller particles (< 10µm) that originate farther downstream of the hot vapor source. A distinct large particle mode does not appear in microgravity ﬂows that do not have prominent high temperature recirculation, although the aerosol still contains large particles. Without recirculation, the mode particle diameter in microgravity is∼ 10µm, or approximately twice that of terrestrial smoke. Results show that future experiments should carefully consider and quantify surface interactions and the presence of hot, recirculating vapor, in order to control geometry-dominated features of the particle size distribution. A manuscript based on this work will be submitted to the journal Aerosol Science & Technology. The ﬁnal document, when accepted, will be provided to NASA.

2 Introduction Gravity affects the evolution of aerosols by introducing buoyancy and particle settling. Buoyant convection modiﬁes the time-temperature history of the aerosol, as well as the spatial distribution of particles, condensing vapor, and thermal energy. Gravity also causes the settling of large particles out of the aerosol, provided the chemistry and vapor concentrations allow for the generation of large particles with appreciable settling velocities. These factors combine to increase particle residency times in high temperature, vapor rich regions in microgravity systems relative to terrestrial or Earth gravity systems (Urban et al., 1998, 2005). As a result, smoke particles produced in microgravity tend to be larger than those produced on Earth (Ku et al., 1995, Urban et al., 1998). Measurements suggest microgravity smoke particles to be 2− 8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles (Urban et al., 2005). Moreover, large particles (not only smoke particles) persist in microgravity, with mass concentrations of particles with diameter > 100 µm measured at ten-times that of a nominal terrestrial environment (Liu et al., 1991).

Total particulate mass concentrations are also more than ﬁve times greater in microgravity (Liu et al., 1991). Understanding gravitational effects is of practical interest because it assists in the design of mission-critical smoke detection systems for use in microgravity environments, including the International Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015); systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities (Urban et al., 2005). The present work uses numerical simulation to explore the inﬂuence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. We simulate the formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments. We utilize direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015). The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the ﬂuid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences.

This study considers two cross- ﬂow velocities of sufﬁciently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity. Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and ﬂow geometry. The paper is organized as follows: we introduce the simulation and modeling methodology, followed by a description of the ﬂow geometry and the parameter space under consideration; we then examine differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower of two ﬂow speeds; next, we present and discuss instantaneous scalar ﬁelds as a means to describe particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the hot vapor source; after developing an understanding of how the particle ﬁelds interact with the ﬂuid dynamics for the low speed cases, we consider the effects of thermophoresis, particle settling, ﬂow geometry, and the higher ﬂow speed; we conclude with a discussion of the results, summarize ﬁndings relevant to future experimentation, and outline directions for future work.

4 Results 4.1 FLOW CONFIGURATION We simulate the formation and growth of DBP particles in air ﬂowing over a heated sample that expels DBP vapor. The simulation mimics the smoldering or pre-conﬂagration stage of a ﬁre studied in experiments performed aboard the ISS (Mulholland et al., 2015). A schematic of the computational domain is shown in Fig. 1. Room temperature air enters a long chamber and ﬂows over a heated rectangular sample. Vapor released from the sample nucleates into particles that grow and are subsequently collected downstream for analysis. The ﬂow is laminar and steady, allowing the two-dimensional representation to present physical characteristics largely representative of the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015). DBP is used as the surrogate material because its properties are known and its use in modeling is well-established (unlike the materials used in the SAME experiments). 4.2 PHYSICAL CONDITIONS Constant ﬂuid properties for air and DBP are provided in Table 1, and variable DBP properties are provided in Table 2. The enhancement factor required for the nucleation expression, Eqn.

(20), is deﬁned for DBP ascnuc = 3.2× 10−4 (Nguyen et al., 1987, Pyyk¨onen and Jokiniemi, 2000). The thickness of the heated DBP source serves as the reference length scale,Lo = 0.0044 m (illustrated in Fig. 1), which is representative of the length scale in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015). The air enters from the left with velocity Uo and temperature To = 300 K . We consider two inlet velocities: Uo = 0.08 m/s, the velocity considered in the SAME experiments, and a slightly faster ﬂow ofUo = 0.10 m/s. The upper and lower boundaries are impermeable, no-slip, iso-thermal surfaces (Twall =To). The heated rectangle is also no-slip, has a ﬁxed temperature ofTs = 473.2 K, and releases DBP vapor at a constant mass ﬂux ofq′′ = 8.4× 10−5 kg/m2· s. The mass ﬂux has been selected to be representative of the mass loss data presented by Mulholland et al. (2015). Zero-derivative conditions are imposed for all species and particle ﬁelds at the inlet and outlet. The gravitational acceleration is considered at terrestrial (go = 9.81 m/s2) and microgravity (go = 0 m/s2) conditions.

The inlet velocities and the gravitational accelerations considered represent four cases with varying Reynolds and Froude numbers. A summary of the simulations performed at the two ﬂow speeds and gravitational levels is given in Table 3. The ﬂags “EG” and “MG” identify the “Earth gravity” and “microgravity” conditions, while 1 and 2 identify the Uo = 0.08 m/s andUo = 0.1 m/s conditions, respectively. Case 1MG is therefore deﬁned to have an inlet velocity of Uo = 0.08 m/s and go = 0 m /s2, corresponding to a Reynolds number Re = 22.3 and a Froude numberFr =∞. In addition to the four base cases listed in Table 3, we examine the aerosol development sensitivity to: (1) particle settling, (2) thermophoresis, and (3) the ﬂow geometry. For this purpose, a series of additional cases, deﬁned in Table 3, are constructed by modifying the setup of Case 1MG and/or Case 1EG. Case 1EG-NS (where NS stands for “no settling”) is identical to Case 1EG, but the settling mechanism has been neglected. Case 1MG-NT (where NT stands for “no thermophoresis”) is identical to Case 1MG, but the thermophoresis transport mechanism has been neglected.

Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R (where R stands for “rotated”) are identical to Cases 1MG and 1EG, except the heated vapor source has been rotated 90◦. In all cases, data is collected and presented at a time oft = 7 seconds. 4.3 NUMERICAL SPECIFICATIONS The domain is non-uniformly discretized by 960 grid points in the x direction and 240 grid point in the y direction. The governing equations are solved on this computational mesh with a second-order MacCormack scheme. The particle size space is discretized by 45 particle nodes, with the volume of each successive node increased by a factor of 2.25, i.e.vk = 2.25×vk−1. The volume of the ﬁrst node is selected to be the volume of a DBP molecule, v1 =vm = 4.44× 10−28 m3. Both the air and the condensing vapor are considered calorically perfect gases with constant properties deﬁned in Table 1. • The Mach number M is only important for ﬂows with M ≳ 0.3. Although the physics are insensitive to variation in Mach number when the Mach number is small, the ratio of sound speed to convective speed imposes a large computational burden. The computational challenge is often remedied with a Boussinesq approximation, but this approach is not valid in the presence of large density variations.

Additionally, an elliptical solve for pressure is computationally intractable for the number of iterations required to resolve the particle time scales. We instead use a scaled dynamic pressure as the reference pressurePo =ρo (c1Uo)2, such thatP⋆ = ραRαT Po , wherec1 is speciﬁed to reduce the effective speed of sound to 8 m/s. The ﬂow ﬁeld was found to be independent of c1 for the values used. • All particles are assumed to be spherical. • Condensed phase DBP properties are deﬁned by their continuum values. • There is no momentum exchange between the particles and the ﬂuid (the air/DBP vapor mixture); the particle velocity equals the ﬂuid velocity, augmented by the thermophoretic velocity and the stokes settling velocity. The stokes settling velocity is assumed to apply for all particles in the domain (including the large particles). • The ﬂuid and particles are in thermal equilibrium and have the same temperature. • Particle diffusion coefﬁcients decrease rapidly with diameter. This poses a numerical challenge due to the lack of a physical mechanism for diffusing numerical errors.

For this reason, the minimum diffusion coefﬁcient considered in the particle mass fraction transport equations corresponds to the ﬁfth particle size node – any node greater than the ﬁfth node is assigned the particle diffusion coefﬁcient of the ﬁfth node. • The mass ﬂux of DPB from the heated rectangle is spatially uniform and all surfaces have spatially uniform temperature. • Particles that impact a solid surface “stick” with 100% efﬁciency, and are removed from the ﬂow. • The aerosol does not achieve a rigorous steady-state because particle evolution continues (slowly) in regions of the ﬂow with recirculation, particularly behind the hot vapor source. The recirculation is characterized by high temperatures, long particle residency times, and the continuous introduction of additional vapor. The hydrodynamic and thermal ﬁelds, conversely, become steady after only a few seconds. Although a rigorous steady-state does not exist, all aerosol features develop and effectively stabilize shortly after the hydrodynamic ﬁelds. We therefore present all results at timet = 7 seconds, which is considered to be the effective steady-state.

4.5 FLUID FLOW, TEMPERATURE, AND MASS FRACTION The velocity ﬁeld controls the convection of thermal energy, condensible species vapor, and particles. Vorticityω, deﬁned as the curl of the velocity vector ω =∇× u, (31) is positive in regions of the ﬂow where ﬂuid rotates counterclockwise, and is negative in regions where the ﬂuid rotates clockwise. The sign and magnitude of vorticity therefore identiﬁes the location, orientation, and intensity of vortices and boundary layers. Figure 2 shows the steady dimensionless vorticity. Panel (a) shows Case 1MG and panel (b) shows Case 1EG. The grey rectangles represent the heated vapor source. Red ﬂuid rotates counterclockwise (positive vorticity) and blue ﬂuid rotates clockwise (negative vorticity). Immediately upon entering the channel, the ﬂuid at the walls is brought to rest by the no slip condition, signiﬁed by the large vorticity gradients in the upper and lower left corners of panels (a) and (b). As the ﬂuid travels downstream from left to right, boundary layers develop symmetrically on the upper and lower walls due to viscous diffusion.

Further downstream, the heated rectangle reduces the cross-sectional ﬂow area, and the pressure ﬁeld accelerates the ﬂuid through ﬂow paths above and below the heated vapor source. The microgravity case in panel (a) remains symmetric near the heated vapor source, whereas the Earth gravity case in panel (b) develops an asymmetry with the majority of ﬂuid passing below the heated vapor source (indicated by larger vorticity magnitudes below than above). Comparatively low vorticity values on the downstream side of the rectangles indicate the presence of low speed, recirculating wakes. The microgravity wake in panel (a) is symmetric, whereas the Earth gravity wake in panel (b) is asymmetric. As the ﬂuid continues to ﬂow downstream, the boundary layers thicken in both cases and the ﬂuid exits the domain to the right. Variations in density due to heat transfer from the rectangle have inﬂuenced the vorticity ﬁelds via baroclinic torque and buoyancy. Because there is no gravity in Case 1MG in panel (a), density variations due to heating do not disturb the symmetry of the ﬂow ﬁeld. The asymmetry apparent in panel (b) is due to buoyancy effects.

5 Summary We have simulated smoke formation and growth in microgravity and Earth gravity to examine how buoyancy and particle settling affect thermal/ﬂuid/particle interactions and the resultant smoke particle size distributions. The simulated geometry emulates the SAME experiments performed aboard the International Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015). Dibutyl pthalate (DBP) vapor is released from a heated rectangular sample, which serves as a surrogate for the smoldering material used in the SAME experiments. Large particles (> 30µm) are present in the wake region downstream of the heated vapor source, and large particle number densities (∼ 1010 m−3) occur inside the wake vortices. The wake contains large particle number densities because dividing streamlines prevent the particles from being convected away, and the particles continue to grow as condensation consumes all available DBP vapor. The particles simultaneously grow via coagulation. Downstream of the wake, two parallel particle streams contain high number densities of both large and small particles.

No particles are present far downstream with diameter< 400 nm because nucleation only occurs for a short distance downstream of the heated vapor source. The particle size distributions contain local maximums near dp = 5µm and dp = 35µm for both ﬂow speeds. The faster ﬂow conditions present a slightly larger wake but this does not manifest as a meaningful difference in particle size distribution. Thermophoresis prevents particles from contacting the heated surface, which has been demonstrated by turning off the thermophoresis mechanism. Without thermophoresis, particles contact the heated vapor source and undergo evaporation. With respect to the particle size distribution, this has the effect of decreasing the number of large particles and increasing the number of small particles – this supports an assertion that the wake is responsible for producing the largest particles in the system. When gravity is present, all ﬁelds become asymmetric due to buoyant convection. Upward convection in the faster ﬂow brings DBP vapor into close proximity with the cool upper surface, resulting in locally high nucleation rates near the upper wake vortex and the upper surface.

Large particle number densities (∼ 1011 m−3) are present along the upper surface, and slightly lower number densities are present in the upper wake vortex. Comparably few particles are present in the lower wake vortex, where the diameter of average mass is maximized. Downstream of the wake vortices, gravitational settling eliminates all particles with diameter> 35µm. Unlike the microgravity case, the 8 cm/s Earth gravity case is not bimodal, with a single local maximum at dp = 5µm. Without particle settling, a bimodal distribution results with two local maximums at particle diameters comparable to the microgravity case. Rotating the heated vapor source 90◦ dramatically reduces the wake volume, and no particles appear in the small wake. Rotating the heated vapor source does not affect the Earth gravity case as signiﬁcantly as the microgravity case. Increasing the ﬂow speed from decreases the prominence of buoyancy, delays interaction with the upper surface until further downstream, widens the particle size distribution to include particles on the nanometer scale, and introduces a second local maximum to the PSD neardp = 30µm.

Microgravity smoke presented in this study contains larger particles than terrestrial smoke. When the microgravity PSD is bimodal, the larger mode contains particles with dp > 35µm, while the terrestrial PSD contains effectively zero particles in this size range. Alternatively, the microgravity PSD can be unimodal with a mode diameter of dp = 10 µm – roughly twice that of the terrestrial case. Results exhibit three primary mechanisms that differentiate the microgravity and Earth gravity smoke: (1) different recirculation geometries and volumes modify the time-temperature-concentration history of the aerosol in regions of high temperature and high vapor mass fraction; (2) particle settling eliminates large particles from Earth gravity smoke, which reduces the maximum particle size and modiﬁes aerosol development by changing coagulation and condensation rates of the remaining particles; (3) buoyant convection can transport condensible species toward relatively cool surfaces, increasing vapor-to-particle conversion. Each of these factors tend to increase the size of particles in microgravity relative to Earth gravity.

However, each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent: (1) the wake dynamic becomes unimportant if nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake, or if there is a time dependent ﬂow without a stable recirculation region; (2) particle settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms particles that are too small to settle (the DBP considered in this work forms large particles); (3) if smoke is produced in an open environment, there may not be cool surfaces nearby to increase nucleation rates. In these situations, microgravity and Earth gravity smoke are hypothesized to be more similar. The simulation data is organized in PSI in “Experiment Data” on the “Data” tab, in two high level categories: • Earth Gravity Figure Data • Microgravity Figure Data The simulation data is further categorized into specific cases: • Case 1 with inlet velocity: U o = 0:08 m/s • Case 2 with inlet velocity: Uo = 0:1 m/s Additional test parameters and conditions are located in Table 3 of the Final Report: Where EG = Earth Gravity; MG = Microgravity; U o = Inlet Velocity; go = Gravitational Acceleration; Re = Reynolds number; Fr = Froude number.

In addition to the four base cases listed in Table 3 of the Final Report, and as shown above, the data is further categorized as the researcher examines the aerosol development sensitivity to: • Particle settling • Thermophoresis • The flow geometry For this purpose, a series of additional cases, defined in Table 3 of the Final Report, and as shown above, are constructed by modifying the setup of Case 1MG and/or Case 1EG. • Case1-Earth Gravity-NS: (where NS stands for “no settling”) is identical to Case1-Earth Gravity except the settling mechanism has been neglected. • Case1-Earth Gravity-R: (where R stands for “rotated”) is identical to Case1-Earth Gravity except the heated vapor source has been rotated 90 o. • Case1-Microgravity-NT: (where NT stands for “no thermophoresis”) is identical to Case1- Microgrativy except the thermophoresis transport mechanism has been neglected. • Cases1Microgravity-R: (where R stands for “rotated”) is identical to Case1-Microgrativy except the heated vapor source has been rotated 90o. In all cases, data is collected and presented at a time of t = 7 seconds.

text: vi ABSTRACT The primary scientific explorations of this thesis work are to better understand (a) microgravity fire-suppression of untested extinguisher, (b) co mbustion kinetic model refinement of renewable fuel butanol (C 4H9OH) isomers, and (c) directly induced cool flame dynamics of higher n-alkane fuels from an isolated small droplet combustion perspective employing computational fluid dynamics with compreh ensive chemical kinetics. The chronological development of the research directi on shifts from a relatively small fuel like methanol (CH3OH) to heavier straight paraffinic fuel n-decane (n-C 10H22). The first installment of the thesis is directed towards answeri ng the feasibility of thennewly considered fire suppressa nt xenon (Xe) for microgravity s pace application by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Methanol was used as model fuel to assess the combustion behavior under xenon-rich environ ment. The comprehensive analysis revealed that xenon promotes longer burn ing time and higher flame temperature compared to existing other diluents/extinguis hers and can support hot flame with much lesser oxygen cont ent than its counterparts.

text: Th e exceptionally low thermal diffusivity of xenon is identified to be responsible fo r the significantly higher peak gas temperature and prolonged burn time. This detailed ana lysis clearly debilitates the potential of xenon as a next- generation fire-suppressant for microgravity applications and helped NASA in safeguard financial investment for International Space Station (ISS) experiments using xenon.

text: vii The second installment of the thesis outlines the efforts direc ted towards improving the gas phase kinetic m odel of butanol isomers based on droplet combustion experiments and computations. This is a unique contribution whe re the traditional gasphase experiment/theory-driven kinetic model is further refined in light of critical recommendations from the droplet combustion analysis. The compr ehensive kinetic model of Sarathy et al. ( Combust. Flame, 2012) is one of the two widely used model for b u t a n o l i s o m e r s w h i c h h a s b e e n e x t e n s i v e l y v a l i d a t e d a g a i n s t h omogeneous gas phase experiments. The numerical simul ation of the butanol droplet co mbustion experiments at atmospheric conditions predicted t he faster burning rate and la rger flame diameter using the above model. An exhaustive p erturbation analysis is carried on chemical, thermodynamic and transport parameters influences (while simult aneously isolating their cross-influences) to pinpoint the root cause of faster burning tendency of the model.

text: The synthesized results from this huge variable-matric perturbation revealed that the isomerspecific species transport parameters were culpable, and recomm endations were made to update those Lennard-Jones potential parameters. Once updated, the computational predictions significantly improves for the Sarathy et al. model based on the feedback from droplet combustion. The final segment of the thesis discusses the direct initiation o f c o o l f l a m e combustion for submillimeter-sized higher n-alkane droplets (n- heptane and n-decane) for possible terrestrial experiments without the necessity of r adiative extinction as frequently encountered onboard the ISS experiments. It has been found that the dimensionality of the droplet (D o = 0.5 mm) statistically reduces the possibility of achieving direct cool flame burn for the droplet by simply vary ing the ignition energy

source: Reports Dissertation Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka
text: viii initiation. Therefore, it was con ceptualized that a combination of a reduced ignition source and induction chemistry modulation may hold the possibil ity of direct initiation of cool flame for n-C 7H16 and n-C 10H22 even in ground-based drop tower experiments. To facilitate this idea, we numerically investigate the droplet co mbustion under selective ozone (O 3) augmented ambient where O 3 serves as an induction chemistry modulator through its liberation of atomic O via molecular decomposition. The available atomic O then reacts with the surrounding fuel producing OH radical, and eventually water and heat. This latter heat input acts as a secondary thermal feedba ck to the droplet surface maintaining steady surface burning rate which then stabilizes the cool flame very near the droplet surface. It was found that the fuel physical properties , especially flash point, play a decisive role in determining the nature of the initial cool f lame dynamics and the ozone requirements. Higher flash point fuel (here, n-C 10H22) is likely to undergo initial dumped cool flame oscillation than its lower value counterpart (n-C 7H16) and will require higher O3 loading under identical ambient.

Analyses further indicate that the dynamic interact ion of degenerate chain branching and chain terminati on/propagation reaction classes of QOOH (Q=C nH2n) species associated with the low-temperature kinetic regimes, an d continuous fuel leakage across the flame location contribute to the ever-increasing tre nds of the oscillation magnitude.

text: 2 1.1 PROBLEM STATEMENT The efficient conversion of fossil fuels to useful energy has b een an active area of research ever since the development of steam engine by Sir Jame s Watt and the postindustrial revolution [1]. Since then, fossil fuels have incred ibly the preferred choice of energy production in the form of ‘ shaft output’ from the prime movers (i.e., engines, gas turbines, propellers, boilers and so on). Consequently, it is a nticipated that the fossil fuels (gaseous and condensed phase) will also remain the automatic ch oice of ground, marine and aviation transportation systems for forth-coming future [2]. Such a prolific use of fossil fuels is primarily due to their extraordinary energy density ir respective of any defined metric (unit mass or volume basis) as illustrated in Figs. 1.1 and 1.2. Therefore, despite the resurgence of renewable energy sources in recent times (solar, wind, tidal, biomass etc.), combustion technology will remain the principal source of energy conversion for centuries. Figure 1.1 Comparison of energy content per unit volume for different fossil fuels and battery types (normalized against the conventional gasoline).

text: 3 Figure 1.2 Comparison of volumetric energy density for differen t energy sources. The plot is recreated after the reported data in reference [3]. Data for wind is for 5 m/s. However, the boon of combustion technology is not a singular en tity and is often rationally criticized for contri buting to the harmful emissions , posing detrimental effects on the environment as well as human health. Therefore, modern c ombustion technology simultaneously aims for higher conversion efficiency and lower perilous emission to tackle the ever stringent regulatory co nstraints [4, 5]. In relation t o the fuel combustion, its ignition, flame development, and pollutant formation are inevit ably interconnected. Therefore, the fundamental insights regarding the flame dynamics and species evolutions (including the harmful ones) are typically studied in standardi zed combustion and/or oxidation settings at desired thermodynamic states (P, T). Hist orically, such fundamental endeavors are carried out extensively using shock tubes [6], fl ow reactors [7], jet-stirred reactors [8], rapid compression machines [9], burner stabilized premixed flames [10] and opposed diffusion flame burners [11].

text: Although these test faci lities are far from practical ideality for combustion devices, they offer unique opportunitie s to individually study ignition, flame characteristics and species evolution (i.e., re action kinetics). In addition,

source: Reports Dissertation Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka
text: 4 due to their simplified flow field, the detail kinetic analysis is possible for these zero- or one-dimensional problems. While these experimental platforms an d associated kinetic analyses serve as the foundational stage for the combustion research, they have two major concerns- (a) the studies have to be conducted in gas phase reactant mixtures, and (b) they are either steady state [7, 8, 10, 11] with transport effect, o r transient in nature [6, 9] ignoring altogether the transport effect. Therefore, there exists a natural gap in studying the fuel combustion considering both the unsteady flame dynamics an d the transport effect. The investigation of isolated single fuel droplet combustion in absence of (under significantly reduced) gravity offers a unique opportunity to probe liquid fuel combustion under unsteady transport dependent environment [12]. With such an advantageous canonical configuration, the physical problem becomes classical Stefan flow problem [13] where enthalpy and species transports are one-dimensional in ra dial coordinate.

text: Computationally, such a facile reacting fluid domain can be modeled with detailed kinetics [14, 15], even to validate asso ciated submodels, e.g., radiatio n model [16, 17], transport model (multicomponent vs. mixture average) [18] and water disso lution model [15, 19- 21]. Interestingly, although one-dimensional droplet combustion may appear simple in configuration, it has relevance to the complex spray environment by incorporating moving boundary effects, unsteady heat conduction and mass diffusion i n the droplet and surrounding gas, variable properties (dependent on temperature and composition), phase equilibrium at the interface, radiation dynamics, and a detailed kinetic mechanism for the combustion process. Traditionally, isolated droplet combustion studies (with or without the gravity) are conducted to understand the fuel ignition, burning rate characteristics, flame

source: Reports Dissertation Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka
text: 5 dynamics and spreading [22-24]. Therefore, there is a need to e xplore the outer regime of conventionality to apply droplet combustion approach, namely- (a) fire extinguishment, (b) kinetic model validation and improvement, and (c) new combustion technology study. This thesis work is dedicated to expl oring these less- ventured pathways where computational droplet combustion can enhance the understanding of liquid fuel combustion. 1.2 LITERATURE REVIEW Study of single isolated or array of isolated droplets has exi sted nearly seven decades since the pioneering work of G.A.E. Godsave [25, 26]. These initial investigations were primarily empirical in nature, therefore covering a wide range of fuels, e.g., benzene, tertiary butyl benzene, decalin, n-heptane etc. Along the line, Kumagai and coworkers were the forerunners in studying the combustion behavior of isolated droplet under reduced gravity environment [27, 28]. These investigators are the first to conduct research on spherical diffusion flames in absence of gravity and formulated a theoretical framework to study it numerically.

text: In an inde pendent study, Goldsmith and Pe nner [29] improved the simplified model of Godsave and also performed extensive experi mental investigations [30] to delineate the role of in creased ambient oxidizer, press ure and temperature on burning rate. To further excel in understanding the droplet com bustion in terms of highpressure, Spalding [31] proposed a transient theoretical model t o d e t e r m i n e t h e f r a m e locations and burning rate at elevated pressure conditions. By deploying statistical formulations, Willams [32] then tried to predict the droplet growth, new droplet formation, collision and aerodynamic forces on droplets under spray condit ion. He further explored the validity of typical droplet burning steady-state assumption s and showed that these

source: Reports Dissertation Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka
text: 6 simplifying assumptions can lead up to 20% error in predictions [33]. In contemporary time, researchers also engaged continuous photography and video recording techniques [34] to understand the dynamics of droplet combustion. As the i mportance of droplet combustion became more prominent from spray perspective, resear chers like Hottel et al. [35] experimentally pursued the combustion behavior of different heavy fuels. The pivotal works of the fifties (i.e., till 1960) played an in strumental role to motivate the researchers to study droplet combustion with multifaceted research objectives. Combustion of the droplet and its subsequent burning behavior has been studied for rocket combustor application [36], high-pressure systems [37-39], denotation configuration [40], super-critical condition [41], evaporation model development [42] and for the ignition and extinction of droplets [43, 44]. Kassoy and Williams are the fi rst to propose a theoretical formulation accounting for variable property effect on droplet combustion along with finite rate chemistry [45], and showed that numerical predictions impr oved significantly over constant fluid property approach.
