text: A critical evaluation of the pre sented studies suggests that wh ile these improved our understanding of droplet com bustion, they are based either convective experiments (forced or/and natural) or simplified computations, both of which required further research to address complicated spray envir onment. Consequently, there h ad been a necessity to address more practically relevant droplet combustion studies. I n their innovative experiments, Faeth and Lazar [ 46] conducted tests for droplet c ombustion of alcohol and paraffinic fuels in the downstream of the flat flame burner to emulate droplet burning under gaseous product distribution environment. These authors also ex tended their research efforts towards bipropellant dr oplet combustion near critical p oint condition [47]. In an

text: 7 independent study, Kumagai et al. [48] conducted a ‘ paradigm-shift’ study of isolated droplet combustion under free-fall condition retaining the spherical flame configuration to decoupling the role of external convective perturbation. Concur rently, Aldred and coworkers [49] experimentally exp lored the transient dynamics o f relatively smaller droplet combustion with a conclusion of the inadequacy of the-t hen existing theoretical models. In the form of theoretical treatment, Law [50] proposed an asymptotic analysis of ignition and extinction of liquid fuel droplet which was then f urther improved to account the internal mixing considering the unsteady effect of multicomponent droplet [51]. Based on this contributing works, Law and Sirignano [52, 53] develope d fully transient droplet combustion model. Crespo and Linan [54] also deployed asymptoti c analysis to explore the effect of unsteady effects of droplet combustion and evapor ation. In pursuit of developing more realistic theoretical models, Law et al. [55] i mproved their previous formulations incorporating the convective effect to unsteady mu lticomponent model.

text: By the late 1970s, an emulsion of water-fuel mixture received attention across the combustion communities due to its relevance to practical application, and it was venture as a binary mixture under droplet configura tion [56-58]. At this point, the research direction steered towards a better understanding of the role of reaction chemistr y on droplet combustion through finite rate kinetics [59, 60]. Expressing the hot flame chemistry with single irreversible reaction step, Siri gnano [61, 62] refined the prev iously developed single droplet theory under convective environment. Comprehensive deta ils of the literature discussed so far can also be found in the review article of Law [63] and Faeth [64]. With the advancement of computational tools and diagnostics cap abilities, freely falling [65] and micro- and/or re duced-gravity [66-68] droplet combustion gained

source: Reports Dissertation Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka
text: 8 popularity due to its geometrical c onstraint with well-defined boundary conditions. The works lead by F.L. Dryer at the Princeton University were the first to deploy computational fluid dynamics (CFD) in analyzing sphero-symmetric droplet comb ustion invoking detailed kinetics [69, 70]. Thes e authors have successfully dem onstrated the necessity of detailed kinetics in reproducing the experimental targets against reduced- or micro-gravity tests [71]. At this point in tim e, a careful synthesis of four decades of droplet combustion research (1950s-1990s) illustrates that the research thrust was first initiated by the empirical terrestrial experimentation (with or without gravity) which simultaneously led to the theoretical development of isolated droplet combustion phenomena. Subsequently, the role of chemistry was included in numerical consideration throu gh single-step finite rate chemistry, and finally the development of CFD analysis with detailed kinetics. Beginning in the early nineties (the 1990s), the research direc tion with isolated droplet combustion shifts from global observational and/or fund amental targets to individualistic physical phenomena base understanding.

However, a careful reexamination of all these major studies shows that the isolated droplet comb ustion can be further deployed to harness deeper insi ght for (a) fire suppressant eff ectiveness, (b) improving/refining detailed chemistry to complex fuels, and (c) oscillatory behavior of low temperature driven cool flames. This existing knowledge gap w as the main intrinsic motivation to pursue this dissertation work in the field of iso lated droplet combustion employing high fidelity CFD code with detailed kinetics. 1.3 SCOPE AND ORGANIZATION OF THE THESIS WORK Since the seminal works of Godsave [25, 26], attention for iso lated droplet has been given exclusively for large diameter droplets (order of several millimeters, analytical/experimental/computational) including the experiment s conducted onboard the international space station [89].

text: To facilitate a gravityless e nvironment for large diameter droplets, testings were primarily conducted in either space shu ttle experiments or in the ISS as a terrestrial test site would demand very high drop towe r free-fall height. To the contrary, smaller droplets (D o < 1.0 mm) require much less drop hight, thus opening the opportunity to do the testing in g round-based facility avoiding the expansive space-based testing [94]. This thesis work focuses on the numerical analysi s of small diameter droplet combustion for a variety of practical fuels to extend the potentiality of droplet combustion in understanding the fire dynamics, reaction kinetics, and cool flame combustion.

text: 11 Chapter 6 shifts the research direction towards the numerical exploration of a concurrent new research topic- ‘cool flame’ from multiphase dro plet perspective. Cool flame phenomena in droplet configuration have been investigated previously for large diameters only with a preceding extinction of the precursor hot flame. Here, we advance the mechanistic concept of directly instituted cool flame for sub-millimeter sized n-alkane (n-C7H16, n-C10H22) droplets without the necessity of radiative extinction of the hot flame. Subsequently, in chapter 7, the cool flame has been studied in a near-limiting condition where a quasi-steady cool flame transitions to an ever-increasi ng oscillatory flame. The inception, growth, and dynamics of such an oscillatory flame are discussed at length in this chapter. Coupled mass, energy and species transport equations are simultaneously solved in both the phases liquid and gas phases. text: 34 ordinary differential-algebraic equations in time. Spatial disc retization is performed according to a node-centered finite volume scheme with a second-order accuracy. The gasliquid interface demarcates the volume boundaries for which the inner zone represents the condensed phase liquid fuel and the outer zone represents the g as phase ambient and the far field. The discretized mass flux is represented on cell interfaces and not cell centers, in the manner traditionally referred to as a staggered grid to avo id oscillatory solutions. Numerical integration of the fin al set of discretized equations is performed using a fifth order backward difference formula and a variable time step util izing a fully implicit multipoint interpolation. This method is appropriate for the large range of time scales and overcomes stability constraints imposed by a chemically reactin g system and automatic time-step variation.

text: 39 3.1 ABSTRACT The ‘FLame EXtinguishment’ (FLEX) program conducted by the Nati onal Aeronautics and Space Administra tion (NASA) onboard the Interna tional Space Station (ISS) has been assisting in devel oping fire-safety protocols fo r reduced gravity applications through microgravity droplet combustion experiments. A wide range of fuels including alcohols and alkanes have been studied under differen t ambient conditions encompassing the deployment of different diluents with compositional variation. A prime focus of this on-going research endeavor has been to assess the relative effectiveness of atmospheric composition and pres sure changes on fire suppressio n under ‘reduced’ gravity conditions. This chapter compiles the results of detai led numerical simulations investigating the combustion and extinction characteristics of isolated sphero-symmetric methanol droplets burning in xenon (Xe) enriched environments. Subsequently, comparative analysis of diluen t behaviors under identical condi tions using argon (Ar), carbon dioxide (CO2) and helium (He) as an alternative diluent choice to nitrogen (N2) is also reported.

It is found that xenon augmented ambient re sults in reduced burning rate, larger extinction diameter and counter-intuitively, prolo nged burning time. The limiting oxygen index (LOI) for xenon is found be significantly lower than argon, carbon dioxide or helium. The numerical analyses also indicate that th e lower thermal diffusivity of xenon is the principal factor responsible for the remarkably lower LOI. In addition, the

It is concluded that the combined ob servation of elevated peak gas temperature, exceptionally slow diffusive heat loss and the lower LOI value associated with xenon as a diluent all detract from its utility for suppressing fire concerns in reduced gravity applications. 3.2 INTRODUCTION Combustion of sphero-symmetric isolated fuel droplets under qui escent conditions provides well-characterized oppor tunities to obtain fundamental data on the coupling of chemical kinetics and transport in diffusion-limited combustion . It also strengthens our understanding of elementary combustion properties such as burni ng rate, flame structure, extinction phenomena, and limiting oxygen index. Moreover, mode ling aspect of isolated, spherically symmetric combustion configuration offers opportunities to include substantial detail in the sub-model components describing chemi cal kinetics, diffusive transport, and radiative interactions.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 3 1. Overview The Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the Department of Fire Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The two Co-Investigators (Co-Is) are Profs. Richard L. Axelbaum and Forman A. Williams who are respectively from the Washington University of St. Louis and the University of California, San Diego (UCSD). Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NA SA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including CFI-G and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team include d Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU.

The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted from March to Oct. 2021 in two sequential rounds of testing. The two rounds occurred during Increments 64 -65 and 65 -66 and respectively featured normal and inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse flames were effectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames. Although it was in the second round, the final day of CFI -G testing was carried out in the normal flame configuration, with gaseous fuel (with or without nitrogen) flowing into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. This was an added test day carried out under conditions in which low-temperature combustion occurred during the first round of testing. CFI-G was a late addition to ACME, where the experiment was jointly selected for spaceflight by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) rather than NASA.

The selection was notably announced after the core ACME hardware had launched to the ISS and just weeks before ACME’s on-orbit operations began. It is effectively an extension of ACME’s Flame Design experiment for which the PI and Co-I are respectively Axelbaum and Sunderland. And it is likewise a follow-on to the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI), led by Williams, in which liquid droplets were burned rather than gaseous fuel. Although CFI-G wasn’t selected for spaceflight by NASA, its ISS operations and the development of its unique hardware, software, and procedure were carried out by the same teams of personnel as the other ACME experiments, primarily from ZIN Technologies, Inc.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 4 2. Science Overview A. Background This background is the Project Summary from the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. Overview: Cool diffusion flames were discovered in 2012 aboard the ISS. This spawned a rapidly growing research field, but only a small number of measurements at limited conditions are available. Consequently, cool flame kinetics m echanisms cannot be adequately tested or advanced. This could be impeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines. It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by porous spherical burners fed with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. Normal and inverse flames will be considered for a broad range of dilution conditions and pressures. The ISS is the ideal platform for observing cool diffusion flames because they typically require 20 s to establish and they could burn indefinitely. Tests will be performed using the ACME insert in the CIR.

Minimal hardware development will be required because the spherical porous burners and gas delivery system will be those used by the Flame Design flight experiment, w hile the diagnostics will be those used by the CFI flight experiment. The objectives are to observe diverse cool diffusion flames aboard the ISS, to simulate the tests with an advanced CFD model, and to identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism th at accurately models these conditions. Intellectual Merit: Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chem istry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The proposed experiments will take advantage of many state -of-the-art diagnostics that are already available on the ISS. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. An advanced CFD model will simulate the flames and will aid the testing and development of cool flame kinetics models.

Observing cool flames burning as steady spherical diffusion flames will yield valuable insight into cool flame chemical kinetics. The measurements proposed cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. Broader Impacts: The research will be disseminated widely to the combustion research community and to industry. It should advance the state-of-the-art in cool flame kinetics mechanisms, which in turn could lead to cleaner, more efficient internal combustion engines. This project will have several educational impacts. Graduate students will conduct much of the

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 5 research. The research results will be integrated into three combustion courses taught by the PI. The PI will team with two organizations at UMD - the Women in Engineering Program and the Center for Minorities in Science and Engineering - to foster interest in science and engineering among female and minority secondary school students. A day -long flame laboratory will be developed for secondary school students that will foster their interest in combustion and scientific inquiry. B. Rationale for Microgravity This is the ‘Justification for Testing Aboard the ISS’ section (3.1) of the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion a nd Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth . The included equation is formatted differently in this copy. Previous ground -based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the scientific value of spherical, burner -supported diffusion flames.

These one -dimensional flames offer a simple, fundamental configuration to improve the understanding of diffusion flame behavior and to explore such effects as transport, kinetics, soot formation, and radiation , which can be more pronounced under microgravity conditions (Atreya et al. 1992; Law et al. 2001; Lecoustre et al. 2012). Spherically-symmetric flames are not generally practical in normal gravity. This can be explained by considering the Richardson num ber, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial force, Ri = g (ΔT L) / (T u2) , (1) where g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u is the characteristic velocity. Taking as representative values L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K, Ri = 1300 in normal gravity. Ri can be reduced with a judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity using low pressure hydrogen inverse flames. However for typical spherical diffusion flames the only way to obtain Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This requires a microgravity environment.

Available microgravity drop tower facilities do not offer sufficient time to observe quasi -steady spherical diffusion flames, let alone their radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Experiments performed in the 5 s drop facility confirm that typical spherical diffusion flames continue growing during 5 s (see Fig. 2). Observations of cool flames in the FLEX, FLEX -2, and CFI droplet experiments involved or will involve burn times of up to 60 s. Analytical work supports these observations of slo w flame development. Radial velocities in spherical diffusion flames scale with 1 / r2, where r is radius. Thus, at only a few burner diameters distance from the sphere, diffusion is the dominant transport mechanism. The characteristic diffusion time is r2/D, where D is mass diffusivity. For r = 25 mm and D = 20 mm2/s, this diffusion time is 30 s. Decreasing the flame size can reduce this time, but will not permit the observation of radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Our analytical and numerical calculations indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these flames.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 6 C. Science Objectives The objectives text presented here is the ‘ Hypotheses and Objectives’ section (1.3) of the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a d ecrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. The research objectives of the proposed work are as follows. 1. Plan and support flight testing on the ISS. 2.

Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n -butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. 5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. In contrast to objective 2 (and hypothesis 3), it was not feasible with the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and ACME chamber insert to conduct tests with n-pentane as proposed (because of its low vapor pressure) and testing was instead conducted with ethane as an alternate. 3. ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 7 IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper from which this section was extracted proceeded completion of the spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017. As a result, it does not accurately describe the final engineering in some regards . Therefore updates, clarification s, additional details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the original description. As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none were cropped. As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners. Besides the chamber insert, other ACME-unique hardware includes a high -definition color camera and an avionics package, which is for data acquisition and control. Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS.

ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew -exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper -motor drive will allow for precise positioning.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 8 Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm. However, only the larger gas -jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are addressed in detail in section 3.C. Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded sph erically symmetric flames, presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching. Two types of igni ter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR.

However, some tests were conducted with a coil igniter tip, where that included the CFI-G investigation and the second-round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames ( s- Flame) experiments, with the exception of the latter’s first day testing. For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), wherea s much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery system enables on -orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments.

Gases can also be delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as the blending of different fuel gases. CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME will sometimes use smaller bottles as a haz ard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) that can be released into the combustion chamber. Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent. Furthermore, the fuel diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer flows of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 9 maximum of 5 slpm. ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control. ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot volume fraction; and operational support. However, it is unlikely that all functions would be exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high -definition digital camera mounted outside of the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the ch amber insert (with a turning mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations.

Light emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue -green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24]. Alternately, CH* imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430 -nm bandpass filter with a 10 -nm full width at half -maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450 -nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission.

However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course rep roducible flame conditions. The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, is not archived in space. The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. Its gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction. The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second. The clear “filter” is of fused silica. Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a re duction in the red, so it does not balance the intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature determination.

Meanwhile, rather than the 450 -nm bandpass filter described above, the high definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions. For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A). Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusi on Flames (s-Flame) experiment was particularly challenging with these, if not all, cameras.

This camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second (fps). Hardware Shortcomings CFI-G’s two primary challenges were in initiating cool flames and discerning their presence. Based on the findings of the earlier studies with droplet combustion, non-premixed cool flames can be directly ignited by limiting the ignition energy or can occur after the self -extinguishment of (normal) hot flames. Tests intended to directly ignite cool flames sometimes unintentionally resulted in hot flames. Meanwhile, evidence of cool flames was first discovered in review of the data a few days after the testing.

During that testing, it wasn’t known that the cool flames were present after hot flame extinction and the tests were terminated, which unknowingly and sadly shortened the duration of the cool flame combustion. In later testing with the long/near thermocouple, two of the tests exhibited repeated hot flame quenching and reignition, which resulting from intervening low -temperature combustion. It appears that the closest thermocouple, approximately 1 cm from the burner surface, was a factor in the reignition. The exposed type-B thermocouple includes platinum, a catalyst for the oxidation of hydrocarbons. The catalysis contributed to the rapid reignition limiting the duration of the lowtemperature combustion in these tests. A challenge for cool flame detection was concern about potential damage to the CFI intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter, while the intensifier gain was set high. There were also issues with the Image Processing and Storage Units (IPSUs) which affected CFI-G operations. On 30 Aug.

However, the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules and radiometers were closer to the flame than the windows and might had been adversely affected by soot.

When at a small fraction (e.g., less than 10%) of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during CFI -G testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed from that desired. Meanwhile, at high flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.

Thus far, ACME’s activity has included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities. Most often the astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips. In the latter case, the igniter tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the crew already has changes to make changes in the interior of the insert. While these activities may seem mundane, the crew play a critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment. As an extreme example, there were crew activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. In contrast, only two crew days were required to reconfigure the hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner. Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. As a correction, including two maintenance activities, there were 11 crew days in Sept.-Oct.

2017 to prepare for the initial CLD Flame testing on the space station. All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in Clevel and, Ohio. Typically , four to six people staff four consoles during the testing. The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console. Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many pre - and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM. A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks. On intervening weekdays, the image data is do wnlinked and the crew often swap one or both gas bottles.

Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2 -shift day for the RO and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 19 activity. As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week. A team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing. The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding. In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters. That team does not see the telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e -mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files.

In advance of the test day, the UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera setti ngs. It is also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. Provisions were made to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely view the analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the operations center. All ACME flame tests, including those for CFI-G, were conducted in a nominally automated manner using software scripts and extensive parameter files. Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low rate results from several unavoidable factors. After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz nonimaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team.

A small sample of images are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples. The review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for the given flame conditions . After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed. Midway through a day’s E -FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only conducted when both Ku and S band communi cation is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) System. Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic communication outages with a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite to another) or can last as long as 30 minutes.

Typically, on the order of 12 tests were conducted per CFI-G Flame test day. In contrast to E-FIELD Flames, recirculation during CFI-G test operations was only conducted prior to venting: (1) at the end of a test day and/or (2) between atmospheres, where the latter was limited to days with normal-flame testing.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 20 A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis. The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material flammability. That follow -on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing. Although it requires additional crew time, these allotments are split into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from testing for careful review of the early results so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of their second round. This paper reports on early results from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests. For E -FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010. At that time, NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited objectives rather than comprehensive experiments.

As such, the general target was 50 tests per experiment. For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber. This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing). The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion chamber. Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant). For E -FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 10 tests typically completed per day. The maximum limit of 999 seconds for the valve safety timers was used for all ACME testing. Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, such as the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours. When necessary for the research, NASA does have continuous 24 -hour/day operations for some non -CIR experiments.

But as discussed, the ACME tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is almost always limited to the planned durations. Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on -orbit hardware can store a limited amount of data. More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two shift transfer and downlink day. Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where image data from select cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge. Nonetheless, the limit sometimes forces decisions to abandon recorded images. Summary of Preliminary Results Abstract for Spherical Gas-Fueled Cool Diffusion Flames : An improved understanding of cool diffusion flames could lead to improved engines. CDFs are investigated here using a spherical porous burner with gaseous fuels in the microgravity environment of the International Space Station. Normal and inverse flames burning ethane, propane, and n-butane were explored with various fuel and oxygen concentrations, pressures, and flow rates. The diagnostics included an intensified video camera, radiometers, and thermocouples. Spherical CDFs burning gases were observed for the first time. However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39. The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large. An analytical model is presented that combines previous models for steady droplet burning and the partial -burning regime for CDFs. The results identify the importance of burner temperature on the behavior of these CDFs.

They also indicate that the observed CDFs reside in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53. Abstract for Cool Diffusion Flames in a Stably Stratified Stagnation Flow: Cool diffusion flames have been a growing research topic since their discovery in 2012. Until now their study has been hindered by the high cost of the experimental systems used to observe them. A method is presented here for observing CDFs inexpensively using a pool of liquid n-heptane and parallel plates heated so as to produce a stably stratified stagnation flow. The flames were imaged with a color camera and measurements included gas phase temperatures, fuel evaporation rates, and formaldehyde emissions. These are the first observations of CDFs burning near the surface of fuel pools. The measured peak temperatures were between 705 – 760 K, whic h corresponds to an increase in gas temperature of 70 K. Autoignition first occurred at 550 K. Cantera autoignition simulations for homogeneous mixtures with the CRECK mechanism predicted a cool flame temperature of 885 K, which is significantly higher than observed. Publications: • M. Impacts, Benefits, and Products Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportatio n. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra -lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. Introduction Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI -G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were disco vered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 29 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. CFI-G had the following experimental hypotheses and experimental objective when it was proposed in 2017: Hypotheses The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5.

Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. Experimental Objective A. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. where Zst and Tad are respectively the stochiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature. However, it was later determined that the CIR facility could not support testing with pentane because of the fuel’s low vapor pressure so the test matrix was revised to instead include testing with ethane in addition to the propane and n-butane. The additional research objectives are as follows, where CFD stands for Computational Fluid Dynamics. B. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. C. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. D. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.

The experiment is carried out using the same spherical burner configuration as ACME’s Flame Design and s -Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) experiments. The instrumentation is the same as that used for Flame Design except that an alternate radiometer array was developed for CFI -G. Furthermore, the CFI -G tests were conducte d using the

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 30 formaldehyde filter on the CFI intensified camera rather than the typically used CH* filter. In this regard, the CFI camera was developed for the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) which preceded ACME and studied non-premixed cool flames in the combustion of liquid droplets. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal -gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum -dominated flames, which are important for most practical com bustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.

The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The CFI-G investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC).

The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre -programmed scripts. No CFI -G tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fi re or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

This was just the beginning of testing, which is expected to continue through most if not all of Increment 65. The CFI-G experiment does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with various gaseous fuels, including ethane, propane, and n-butane. These are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the hot flame chemistry is reasonably well understood, where there is more to be learned about cool flame chemistry. No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for CFI-G; all of the ISS results were electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME experiments. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data CFI-G’s two primary challenges are in initiating cool flames and discerning their presence. Based on the findings of the earlier studies with droplet combustion, nonpremixed cool flames can be directly by limiting the ignition energy or can occur after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames. Tests intended to directly ignite cool flames sometimes unintentionally resulted in hot flames.

A challenge for cool flame detection is concern about potential damage to the CFI intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter, while the intensifier gain is set high. When at a small fraction (e.g., less than 10%) of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during CFI -G testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed from that desired. Meanwhile, at high flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. During Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) testing on 23 Dec.

2020, it was discovered that the lowest of the 14 -micron silicon carbide fibers on the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array had broken. Recovery plans were developed and enacted on 18 Jan. 2021 to remove the broken fragments from the harp -like array. Unfortunately, the next fiber was broken during the delicate operations where the fibers are only spaced 5 mm apart. Although ACME does have alternate arrays, it also has months of remaining testing, so the decision was made to continue testing with only 3 fibers (instead of 5) for the final BRE testing, the subsequent CLD Flame tests, and at least

Completeness/Quality of Data Only the first 3 of 22 CFI-G test days were conducted during Increment 64, so only a small fraction of the test matrix has been completed. In this regard, CFI -G testing is expected to continue through most of Increment 65. The cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels g radually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post -processing, they are a degradation of the image quality. It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there is not obvious indication of this; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). Recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some image data to allow additional tests to be conducted.

This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the project constraints. D. Status of Data Analysis [provided by the U. of Maryland investigator team and lightly edited by Stocker] Data sets of spherical diffusion flames as a function of the fuel mass flow rate , atmospheric O2 concentration, fuel dilution, and pressure were obtained. The raw test measurements made from devices - such as thermocouples, photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), gas flow meters, and radiometers - were saved in a csv file format per each test. The data rate of the non-imaging measurements was 125 per sec. The raw data was processed to transform it into scientific measurements. The transformed data were visualized as plots for further analysis. In addition, test images recorded in tiff and ho bj formats respectively for the CFI intensified camera and ACME DataCam have been analyzed to find flame diameters. Of these the intensified camera is of most value and all of its images to date have been converted to video files and reviewed.

Particular attention has been given to the PMT -2 measurements due to its sensitivity to wavelengths of 230 – 700 nm for CH2O* to investigate the presence of cool flames. PMT-2 measurements have been analyzed to determine flame durations as well.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 34 Burner temperature s will be analyzed to find their correlation to the cool flame diameters. E. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by the U. Maryland investigator team] The first three days of testing have yielded dozens of flames, some lasting several minutes. Based on the output from the photomultipliers, radiometers, and intensified camera images we do not believe any self -sustained cool flames were created. While it is possible that momentary cool flames were created, these are difficult to detect without increasing the gain on the intensified camera before the hot flames extinguish, which is planned. The video record will furnish excellent measurements of flame diameter versus time for a broad range of fuels and conditions. These will be compared with a si mple analytical model and detailed CFD simulations using Sphdif. Thin -filament pyrometry has been performed and the results will soon be analyzed. F. Introduction Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI -G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CI R) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 36 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cet ane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. CFI-G had the following experimental hypotheses and experimental objective when it was proposed in 2017: Hypotheses The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5.

Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. Experimental Objective A. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. where Zst and Tad are respectively the stochiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature. However, it was later determined that the CIR facility could not support testing with pentane because of the fuel’s low vapor pressure so the test matrix was revised to instead include testing with ethane in addition to the propane and n-butane. The addi tional research objectives are as follows, where CFD stands for Computational Fluid Dynamics. B. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. C. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. D. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.

The experiment is carried out using the same spherical burner configuration as ACME’s Flame Design and s -Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) expe riments. The instrumentation is the same as that used for Flame Design except that an alternate radiometer array was developed for CFI -G. Furthermore, the CFI -G tests were conducted using the

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 37 formaldehyde filter on the CFI intensified camera rather than the typically used CH* filter. In this regard, the CFI camera was developed for the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) which preceded ACME and studied non-premixed cool flames in the combustion of liquid droplets. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal -gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum -dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.

The long residence times in microgravity fla mes can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. VI. Methods/Research Operations B. Discussion of Method/Protocol The CFI-G investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC).

The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre -programmed scripts. No CFI -G t ests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight A total of 280 hot flames were ignited (or in some cases naturally reignited) for the CFI-G experiment during Increments 64 -66, where 33, 225, and 22 flames were ignited in the three increments, respectively. Testing began near the end of Increment 64 and the final test day was conducted at the start of Increment 66. Cool flame evidence was seen in some tests and 15 cool flames, listed and discussed later, have been identified thus far. The CFI-G experiment does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests were instead conducted burning various gaseous fuels, including ethane (C 2H6), propane (C3H8), and n-butane (n-C4H10). These are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the hot flame chemistry is reasonably well understood, but where there is much remaining to be learned about the cool flame chemistry. No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for CFI -G; all of the investigation’s data was electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all current ACME experiments.

Mission anomalies On Aug. 30 (GMT 242), the primary Image Processing and Storage Unit, used to record the imaging from both the ACME DataCam and CFI intensified camera (IPSU -G, also known as IPSU5), caused issues and eventually stopped working. Only the first two tests on that day were successful, where two tests aborted due to an IPSU error, and three tests failed to ignite. In closing checkout, it was determined that the hot -wire igniter tip had also failed. With the IPSU-G failure, the test day was nearly a total loss. Except for a small number of sample images downloaded during the midst of testing, the primary image data from even the successful tests was lost. Furthermore, there was no more propane available for use in inverse-flame testing, so the test day could not be repeated. However, astronaut Mark Vande Hei replaced the failed igniter tip on Sept. 8 and the failed hard drive in the IPSU -G on Sept. 10, and CFI -G testing successfully resumed on Sept. 13, just 2 weeks after the double failure.

Looking back t o Increment 64, the Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU1) used with the High Bit -depth Multi -spectral (HiBMs) camera and the opposed CIR illumination package ceased functioning on March 29 (GMT 088). Tests 21088M1-M3 aborted due to an error with IPSU1 communication, where test M4 was successful when the test was run without use of the HiBMs camera. The troublesome IPSU1 was replaced by astronaut Megan McArthur on May 18 (GMT 138), but it was not available during the intervening test days. However, this wasn’t particularly a loss to CFI-G because that camera, with its red filter, is only sensitive to the red backlight from the CIR illumination package and visible thermal radiation, e.g., from glowing soot particles. Furthermore, the illumination cou ld make it more difficult to discern cool flames, so the HiBMs camera, illumination package, and IPSU1 were rarely used for CFI-G. The principal exception was during the second round of testing. With the inverse-flame tests, the soot is generated outside of the flames, so this photography was used to track potential soot deposition on the chamber windows, etc.

However, the end-of-day imaging did not appear to change over time, suggesting that the soot was not an issue for the chamber windows. However, the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules and radiometers were closer to the flame than the windows and might had been adversely affected by soot. 4. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data CFI-G’s two primary challenges are in initiating cool fla mes and discerning their presence. Based on the findings of the earlier studies with droplet combustion, non premixed cool flames can be directly ignited by limiting the ignition energy or can occur after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames. Tests intended to directly ignite cool flames sometimes unintentionally resulted in hot flames. Meanwhile, evidence of cool flames was first discovered in review of the data a few days after the testing. During that testing, it wasn’t known that the cool flames were present after

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 42 hot flame extinction and the tests were terminated, which unknowingly and sadly shortened the duration of the cool flame combustion. In later testing with the long/near thermocouple, two of the tests exhibited repeated hot flame quenching and reignition, which resulting from intervening low temperature combustion. It is likely that the closest thermocouple, approximately 1 cm from the burner surface, was a factor in the reignition. The exposed type -B thermocouple includes platinum, a catalyst for the oxidation of hydrocarbons. The catalysis contributed to the rapid reignition limiting the duration of the low temperature combustion in these tests. A challenge for cool flame detection was concern about potential damage to the CFI intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter, while the intensifier gain is set high. When at a small fraction (e.g., less than 10%) of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during CFI -G testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed from that desired.

Meanwhile, at high flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow r ates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non -spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. During Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) testing on 23 Dec. 2020, it was discovered that the lowest of the 14 -micron silicon carbide fibers on the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array had broken. Recovery plans were developed and enacted on 18 Jan. 2021 to remove the broken fragments from the harp -like array. Unfortunately, the next fiber was broken during the delicate operations where the fibers are only spaced 5 mm apart.

Although ACME does have alternate arrays, it also had months of remaining testing, so the decision was made to continue testing with only 3 fibers (instead of 5) for the final BRE testing and the subsequent CLD Flame and CFI-G tests. This was a minor loss, where the fiber array was only o ccasionally used in CFI -G testing.

Completeness/Quality of Data The experiment’s proposal to CASIS and NSF stated: “It is assumed here that approximately 50 ISS flames can be conducted. These will include approximately 12 chamber fills following evacuation.” Far more testing was carried out for this experiment, where that included the ignition of 280 hot flames in 23 days of ISS testing, some of which included multiple chamber fills. Although some of the flames were short lived, the testing far exceeded the quantity that had been proposed. The cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post -processing, they are a degradation of the image quality. It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there is not obvious indication of this; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). Recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed per test day.

Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some image da ta to allow additional tests to be conducted. This is intentionally done to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the project constraints. J. Status of Data Analysis [provided by the U. of Maryland investigator team and lightly edited by Stocker] Data sets of spherical diffusion flames as a function of the fuel mass flow rate (for normal flames), the oxidizer mass flow rate (for inverse flames), O 2 concentration, fuel dilution, and pressure were obtained for all the normal and inverse flame test days. The raw test measurements made from devices - such as thermocouples, photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), gas flow meters, and radiometers - were saved in a csv file format per each test. The data rate of the non-imaging measurements was 125 per sec. The raw data was processed to transform it into scientific measurements. The transformed data were visualized as plots for further analysis.

In addition, test images recorded in tiff and hobj formats respectively for the CFI intensified camera and ACME DataCam have been analyzed to investigate the presence of cool flames and to find flame diameters. Of these the intensified camera is of most value, and all of its images to date have been converted to video files and reviewed. Since the intensi fied camera images were taken under the maximum possible gain applied, the images were averaged and filtered to decrease the overall noise level, and the intensity of the images was increased by a factor of 50 to facilitate the search of intensity peaks.

Preliminary Research Findings [provided by the U. of Maryland investigator team and lightly edited by Stocker] A total of 280 hot diffusion flames were observed. Among them, 189 flames experienced radiative extinction, and the rest were e xtinguished when their flow was terminated, either because the preset flow time was out or the burner overheated. Of those that extinguished radiatively, 15 subsequently reignited as cool diffusion flames.

These cool flames were observed only with the following conditions: a) concentrations of 30 vol% nbutane and 40 vol% O2, b) normal flames, c) a pressure of 2.03 bar, and d) mass flow rates between 0.75 – 1.5 mg/s. Cool diffusion flames were initially identified by the readings of radiometers after th e radiative extinction of hot flames. Unlike the heat flux shown in Fig. 1(a), Fig. 1(b) shows that the radiant heat flux did not drop to zero after the radiative extinction of a hot flame. Instead, it decreased to a certain level and stayed at that level until the fuel stopped flowing. Figure 1(c) shows multiple hot -cool flame transitions. The first cool flame, the first drop of the radiant heat flux, followed the radiative extinction of the first hot flame. In a few seconds, the heat flux abruptly inc reased due to reignition of a hot flame. This cycle of radiative extinction, transition to a cool flame, and reignition of a hot flame continued until the flow was terminated. The observed cool flames are summarized in Table 3. Cool flames were also identified by processed images taken from the intensified camera.

When cool flames appeared after the radiative extinction of the hot flames, no flame luminosity was evident for about 1 s, after which cool flames appeared. For test points 21174C3, C4, C6, and F1, the cool flames lasted for approximately 14 s and disappeared as soon as the fuel flow stopped. For the tests of multiple hot -cool flame transitions, 21291A1 and 21291C1, the first cool flame lasted longer than the following cool flames. The intensified camera images of hot and cool flames were used to find flame radii as well. The radii of hot flames were measured at the time just before the flame oscillation. Representative images of a hot flame and a cool flame are presented in Fig. 2. It is shown that the hot flame is brighter and larger than the cool flame. While a flame sheet is clearly indicated in the hot flame image, the intensity of a cool flame gradually decreases from the peak along radial direction, which implies that the reaction zone of the cool flame is

ABSTRACT Title of Dissertation: BURNING EMULATIONS OF CONDENSED PHASE FUELS ABOARD THE INTERNATIONAL SPACE STATION Parham Dehghani, Doctor of Philosophy, 2022 Dissertation directed by: Professor Peter B. Sunderland, and Professor James G. Quintiere Department of Fire Protection Engineering Little is known about the fire hazards of solids and liquids in microgravity. Ground-based tests are too short to overcome ignition transients and testing dozens of condensed fuels in orbit is prohibitively expensive. Burning rate emulation is one way to address this gap. It involves emulating condensed fuels with gases using a porous burner with embedded heat flux gages. This is a study of microgravity burning rate emulation aboard the International Space Station. The burner had porous round surfaces with diameter of 25 mm. The fuel mixture was gaseous ethylene, and it was diluted with various amounts of nitrogen. The resulting heats of combustion were 15 – 47.2 kJ/g. The flow rate, oxygen concentration in the ambient, and pressure were varied. Heat flux to the burner was measured with two embedded heat flux gages and a slug calorimeter.

The effective heat of gasification was determined from the heat flux divided by the fuel flow rate. Radiometers provided the radiative loss fractions. A dimensional analysis based on radiation theory yielded a relationship for radiative loss fraction. RADCAL, a narrow-band radiation model,

yielded flame emissivities from the product concentrations, temperature, flame length, and pressure. Previously published analytical solutions to these flames allowed prediction of flame heights and radius, and when combined with the radiation empirical relationship led to corrections of total heat release rate from the flames due to radiative loss. Average convective and radiative heat flux were obtained from the analytical solution and a model based on the geometrical view factor of the burner surface with respect to the flame sheet, that were used to calculate heats of gasification. All flames burning in 21% by volume oxygen self-extinguished within 40 s. However, steady flames were observed at 26.5, 34, and 40% oxygen. The analytical solution was used to quantify flame steadiness just before extinction. The steadiest flames reached more than 94% of their steady-state heat fluxes and heights. A flammability map as a plot of heat of gasification versus heat of combustion was developed based on the measurement and theory for nominal ambient oxygen mole fractions of 0.265, 0.34, and 0.4.
