Introduction The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Spac e Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention. More specifically, BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial -gravity environments. A flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liq uid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent.

A small number of gaseous fuels (including mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and alcohol by matching properties including the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface temperature, and smoke point. The experiment’s results can establish fuel properties that

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 46 directly relate to fire hazards in spacecraft, and if effective in microgravity could provide an efficient, safe, and comprehensive technique for assessing flammability and selecting fire resistant spacecraft materials. BRE’s specific experimental objectives are as follows, where it must be emphasized that NASA does not currently plan to carry out the desired tests for objective B. A. Observe burning behavior in long -duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA -considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. B. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). C. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits. The observations will enable quantification of the microgravity behavior of condensed fuels (i.e., liquids and non-charring plastics).

Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy -driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi -steady flames in microgravity. Le ngth scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend t o have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong so ot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II.

Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not c onducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 47 response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted after quasi -steady data has been collected. But testing has not been conducted in a ‘manual’ mode thus far for BRE or ACME in general. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. III. Results A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, where a total of 45 flames were ignited during Increment 58. That round was completed in April 2019, where the latter portion will be covered in the upcoming Increment 59-60 report. Meanwhile, the second round of BRE testing is expected to begin near the end of Increment 60 and continue into Increment 61.

The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. All of the first round of tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen. The tests were carried out at a range of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats. More specifically, testing was especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with nitrogen and any incomplete combustion products (e.g., water vapor and carbon dioxide) from preceding tests. BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experimen t, but the tests are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.

Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon double bond. Tests are conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen, where the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch for some cases. But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on -orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.

Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often saturated. Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors. Estimates had been made of the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the flame in the absence of buoyancy and the reby remain within the view of the radiometers. As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity. The estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been sufficiently tracked in the hardware development.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 49 times the duration of the drop tests. With the fixed amplification of the radiometer signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge that the limits were exceeded. An engineering review failed to identify an acceptable solution and BRE testing continued unchanged. From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere: The radiometry array proved problematic as its sensors were mostly out of range and quickly became saturated. However, for some of the small size flames, these data were complete. Those data will be vital to assessing the role of flame and combustion product radiation in the destiny of the flames. Ignition was not always successful, where BRE tests were sometimes conducted under conditions, e.g., for igniter activation and deactivation, which led to momentary flashes without sustained ignition. Given that unplanned crew time is required to replace failed igniter tips, the BRE ops team li mited - to varying degrees - the igniter voltage and the time that it was energized within the flame. The latter was known from earlier research in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to degrade the hot-wire igniter tip and hasten its demise.

It is nota ble that the flashes of flame (across the burner surface) sometimes continued briefly after the igniter was deactivated and retracted. In one case on the first day of testing, there was excess fuel and a ‘fireball’ was ignited which promptly quenched. Ig nition also sometimes failed due to a software limitation where the fuelFlowIgnitionDeltaMs parameter which specifies the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation must be evenly divisible by 100 (ms). This limitation wasn’t initially unders tood and the igniter didn’t energize as a result. From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere: It was realized that the igniter for the burner gases could only be applied for up to 4 seconds, on insertion and retraction. This produced an unanticipated problem, as the time for the burner gases to reach the igniter could be 10s of seconds depending on the set flow rate. Also, after the first test, the burner would contain that fuel mixture minus diffusion with the chamber. Thus the burner would need to be flushed with nitrogen before the second fuel mixture was initiated. Intense communication with the NASA team proceeded the day before the first test.

The gas volume of the burner along with the feed pipe volume was supplied by NASA. Accordingly ground experiments at Maryland were conducted with an identical NASA BRE burner along with its piping volume from the flow valve. These experiments and theory were used to develop an algorithm for determining the relative timing of the igniter and gas flow activation that will result in ignition. Day 1 was conducted with rough estimates made on the fly, and fortunately nearly all of the tests led to a satisfactory ignition. By Day 2 an algorithm was established

This algorithm will need to be refined and applied for the larger 50 -mm diameter burner that will be used in Round 2. The second day of flame testing was delayed to allow for the development of a new ignition procedure, where concerns arose that the mixture of gas flowing from the burner wasn’t sufficiently well understood, i.e., in terms of concentrations. This concern had to do with the burner’s large internal volume relative to that of the burners used for the other ACME experiments. To be clear, this issue had to do with the analysis of results rather than the achievement of ignition. Re -planning was also necessary early in BRE testing because the test durations were often much longer than had earlier been envisioned by the investigators. While these factors didn’t directly interfere with the acquisition of test data, they did slow progress.

While it rarely occurred, BRE tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling software script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter. As a result, there is little lost other than the time associated with the failed test attempt. Such aborts typically occur because of communication issues with an Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU). D. Status of Data Analysis (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere) All of Round 1 tests have had the thermopile sensor data reduced using their original calibrations. As presented immediately below, the data must be continually processed to address the effect of the combustion product water and any paint degradation.

The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from the flame to the burner surface. In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass flow rate per unit area of the fu el mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated fuel. The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix). Th us achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than a candle flame, this has not been shown before.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 52 The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface. One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center. The resulting data suffered from two possible effects. The first effect is the condensation of water vapor. As the sensors are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the fla me grows, water from its combustion products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor. This occurs, as the dew point for combustion products is about 60 – 70 oC, and the sensor begins at ambient temperature and can achieve temperatures over 100 oC. Thus condensation can occur at temperatures below the dew point that leads to added heat to the sensor. Above the dew point, the condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor. Once the sensor is dry, it will only measure the heat flux from the flame gases as intended. We have duplicated this condensation effect in 1 -g laboratory experiments with our duplicative NASA BRE burner. The figure below (Fig. 1) shows an illustration of the condensation and evaporation effect in the ISS tests.

The offset sensor in red shows a clear jump increase when the water fully evaporates. More analysis is needed to properly correct for this effect. Fortunately by the end of the test shown here (and for all of the other data), this water effect is gone. Figure 1. E. Preliminary Research Findings (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere) Despite having much data to digest and completely analyze, there is a profound conclusion from these tests. The burner has definitively shown that steady burning is possible for real solids with a flat surface of 25 mm diameter.

Up to now most flammability studies in microgravity have focused on flame spread with a w ind for concurrent spread and at least a self-induced wind for opposed flow spread. We already knew that this would be possible from 1 -g research. The burning of liquids, as in a wick of a candle flame and small droplets, has been shown to produce stead y flames. However, in the case of droplet burning cool flames could sustain normal burning, and normal burning would extinguish. The extinction has been shown to result from the radiative cooling of the flame. We see this as well in the extended ISS microgravity tests. However this extinction was predominately seen for atmospheric conditions of 21 %

Introduction The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. BRE is focused on spacecraft fire preventio n. More specifically, BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments. A flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 61 alcohol by matching properties including the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface temperature, and smoke point. The experiment’s results can establish fuel properties that directly relate to fire hazards in spacecraft, and if effective in microgravity could provide an efficient, safe, and comprehensive technique for assessing flammabilit y and selecting fire resistant spacecraft materials. BRE’s specific experimental objectives are as follows, where it must be emphasized that NASA does not currently plan to carry out the desired tests for objective B. D. Observe burning behavior in long -duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA -considered atmosphere for human space missions will be e xamined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. E. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). F.

Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits. The observations will enable quantification of the microgravity behavior of condensed fuels (i.e., liquids and non-charring plastics). Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy -driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi -steady flames in microgravity. Length scales are increased in microgra vity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.

The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the compl ex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 62 All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the operations center at the NASA Glenn Research Center. The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted after quasi -steady data has been collected. But testing has not been conducted in a ‘manual’ mode thus far for BRE or ACME in general. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. III. Results A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, whe re a total of 45 flames were ignited during Increment 58.

That round was completed in April 2019, during the beginning of Increment 59, when an additional 17 flames were ignited. As such, a total of 62 flames were ignited in the first round of testing. Meanwhile, the second round of BRE testing is expected to begin near the end of Increment 61 and continue into Increment 62. The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial resul ts in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. All of the first round of tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen. The tests were carried out at a range of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats. More specifically, testing was especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen. In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with nitrogen and any incomplete combustion products (e.g., water vapor and carbon dioxide) from preceding tests.

An exception is tests conducted after the chamber atmosphere was vented and refilled, such as the first test of the day. But the atmosphere was typically refreshed once during each of testing. BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests a re independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting

There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collec ted for BRE, where all of the ISS results are electronically transmitted to the ground. Mission anomalies There were no significant anomalies hindering BRE operations during Increment 59, but there was one in Increment 58 during the preparations for BRE testing began (that was mistakenly not addressed in the 3 0-day report including that increment). It was discovered on Feb. 4 (GMT 035) that the pressure was low in a check gas bottle for the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). The bottle had been on the space station for 9 years, and the lo w pressure was attributed to a nominal leak rate. The check gas was for calibration of the GCIP measurements and not needed for regular operations which proceeded unhindered. The bottle was replaced on June 13 to enable the necessary calibration. 2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often saturated. Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors.

Estimates had been made of the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby r emain within the view of the radiometers. As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity. The estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been sufficiently tracked in the hardware development. Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60 times the duration of the drop tests. With the fixed amplification of the radiometer signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge that the limits were exceeded. An engineering review failed to identify an acceptable solution and BRE testing continued unchanged. From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere: The radiometry array proved problematic as its sensors were mostly out of range and quickly became saturated. However, for some of the small size flames, these data were complete. Those data will be vital to assessing the role of flame and combustion product radiation. Ignition was not always successful.

As previously discussed, it wa s discovered on April 1 (GMT 091) that the hot -wire igniter tip had failed on the preceding test day, preventing further flame testing until it could be replaced. While such circumstances are uncommon for ACME operations, BRE tests were sometimes conducte d under conditions, e.g., for igniter activation and deactivation, which led to momentary flashes without sustained ignition. Given that unplanned crew time is required to replace failed igniter tips, the BRE ops team limited - to varying degrees - the igniter voltage and the time that it was energized within the flame. The latter was known from earlier research in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to degrade the hot-wire

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 65 igniter tip and hasten its demise. It is notable that the flashes of flame (acro ss the burner surface) sometimes continued briefly after the igniter was deactivated and retracted. In one case on the first day of testing, there was excess fuel and a ‘fireball’ was ignited which promptly quenched. Ignition also sometimes failed due to a software limitation where the fuelFlowIgnitionDeltaMs parameter which specifies the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation must be evenly divisible by 100 (ms). This limitation wasn’t initially understood and the igniter didn’t energiz e as a result. From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere: It was realized that the igniter for the burner gases could only be applied for up to 4 seconds, on insertion and retraction. This produced an unanticipated problem, as the time for the burner gases to reach the igniter could be tens of seconds depending on the flow rate. Also, after the first test, the burner would contain that fuel mixture mixed with the chamber gas. Thus the burner would need to be flushed with nitrogen before the second fuel mixture was initiated.

Intense communication with the NASA team proceeded the day before the first test. The gas volume of the burner along with the feed pipe volume was supplied by NASA. Accordingly ground experiments at UMD were conducted with an identical NASA BRE burner along with its piping volume from the flow valve. These experiments and theory were used to develop an algorithm for determining the relative timing of the igniter and gas flow activation that will result in ignition. Day 1 was conducted with rough estimates made on the fly, and fortunately nearly all of the tests led to a satisfactory ignition. By Day 2 an algorithm was established and successfully used for the remainder of the testing. This algorithm will need to be refined and applied for the larger 50 mm diameter burner that will be used in Round 2. A document on the development of the algorithm and its refinement for the larger burner is being prepared and will be shared with the NASA team to facilitate round 2.

The second day of flame testing was delayed to allow for the development of a new ignition procedure, where concerns arose that the mixture of gas flowing from the burner wasn’t sufficiently well understood, i.e., in terms of concentrations. This concern had to do with the burner’s large internal volume relative to that of the burners used for the other ACME experiments. To be clear, this issue had to do with the analysis of results rather than the achievement of ignition. Re -planning was also necessary early in BRE testing because the test durations were often much longer than had earlier been envisioned by the investigators. While these factors didn’t directly interfere with the acquisition of test data, they did slow progress.

However, the image quality is less than was hoped for. The ACME ops camera provides video, but only offers 0.3 megapixels of resolution, a nd for many flames it is too zoomed out. Status of Data Analysis (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral student Parham Dehghani) All measured transient raw data (e.g., heat flux sensors, thermocouples, radiometers, mass flow meters and chamber pressure sensor) have been converted to engineering units and plotted using the calibrations provided in ACME’s Software Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). All of the round 1 tests have had the heat flux sensor data reduced using their original calibrations. As presented below, the data is being processed to address the effect of the combustion product water and paint degradation. The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from the flame to the burner surface. In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasif ication of the emulated fuel. The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix).

Thus, achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than for a candle flame, this has not been shown before. The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface. One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center. The resulting data suffered from two possible effects. The first effect is the condensation of water vapor. As the sensors are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its combustion products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor. This occurs, as the dew point for combustion products is about 60 -70oC, and the sensor begins at ambient temperature and can achieve temperatures over 100oC. Thus, condensation can occur at temperatures below the dew point that leads to added heat to the sensor. Above the dew point, the condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor.

Fortunately, by the end of the test shown here (and for all of the other data), this water effect is gone. Figure 1. Typical net heat flux of the heat flux sensors. This was the original manufacturer’s paint, instead of that used for the copper top. The copper paint appears fine. We are working with the heat flux gage manufacturer to explore the effect of heat damage on the calibration of the sensors.

Preliminary Research Findings (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral student Parham Dehghani) Despite having much data to digest and analyze, there is a profound conclusion from these tests. The burner has definitively shown that steady burning is possible for real solids with a flat surface of 25 mm diameter.

Up to now most flammability studies in microgravity have focused on flame spread with a wind for concurrent spread and at least a self -induced wind for opposed flow spread. We already knew that this would be possible from normal -gravity research. The burning of liquids, as in a wick of a candle flame and small droplets, has been shown to produce steady flames. However, many droplet flames were found to extinguish owing to radiative cooling of the flame. We see this as well in the extended ISS microgravity tests. However, this extinction was predominately seen for atmospheric conditions of 21% oxygen and 14.7 psia. At conditions of 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia and 34% oxygen, 8.2 psia, the flames generally persisted for 2 minutes or more. These are all atmospheric conditions that NASA is considering for future spacecraft. Some examples are shown below to illustrate these results. Figure 5 shows a typical test of ignition and flame growth. Although extinction occurred at 45 s with the flame still growing, the heat flux was nearly steady by 30 s. Therefore, a heat of gasification (L) could be estimated.

This was done in a preliminary estimation by using the center heat flux sensor as the net average heat flux. If the heating is just due to diffusion, theory indicates that the average heat flux is double the center value. Hence such an estimated heat of gasification could be low by 50%. On the other hand, if the sensor is degraded in its calibration and radiation is a significant component of the heat flux, then the estimate will also be low. Hence, using the center heat flux sensor directly gives a conservatively low estimate of the heat of gasification in the emulation of real solids. This will be significant when the totality of results for the 25 mm flat burning surface is displayed over its spectrum of conservatively low values for L.

The investigation is being carried out in two separate rounds, where the first round was cond ucted during Increments 58 and 59 and the second round began in Increment 63 and should be completed in Increment 64. Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker ( dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project Scientist, who is the primary contact for BRE and ACME information. Principal Investigator (PI): Prof. James G. Quintiere, University of Maryland, College Park, MD Co-Investigator (Co-I): Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, U. of Maryland, College Park, MD Co-Investigator (Co-I): Dr. John L. de Ris, FM Global (retired) Collaborator: Prof. Alexander Yu.

Snegirev, Peter the Great St. Petersburg Polytechnic University, St. Petersburg, Russia Project Scientist (PS): Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH PS team member: Dr. Uday G. Hegde, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH I. Introduction The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention. More specifically, BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials fla mmability, such as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial -gravity environments. A flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent.

A small number of gaseous fuels (including mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and alcohol by matching properties including the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 80 temperature, and smoke point. The experiment’s results can establish fuel properties that directly relate to fire hazards in spacecraft, and if effective in microgravity could provide an efficient, safe, and comprehensive technique for assessing flammability and selecting fire resistant spacecraft materials. BRE’s specific experimental objectives are as follows, where it must be emphasized that NASA does not currently plan to carry out the desired tests for objective B. G. Observe burning behavior in long -duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA -considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel co nditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. H. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). I. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.

The observations will enable quantification of the microgravity behavior of condensed fuels (i.e., liquids and non-charring plastics). Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, whi ch is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi -steady flames in microgravity. Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.

With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. text: ACME Critical Design Review– 24 Glenn Research Center ZIN Technologies PDR RFA-004 Disposition RFA # 04 Originator: Al Linne Originator Concurrence: 7 November 2013 Statement of Concern Recommended Action Closure Rationale A detonation analysis has not been completed. Perform a detonation analysis on the expected ACME gas mixtures. This should be done prior to the ACME Phase 0/1 Flight Safety Review, since it may inform some of the hazard analysis. Also, the results of this analysis could drive the consumables usage and could limit the amount of science performed. An ACME detonation analysis has been performed for the Inverse Flame Experiment, which is the the worst case hazard. It was chosen because of the possible oxygen interaction with ACME CIA hardware (i.e. materials compatibility). The analysis validated that the present configuration could safely meet requirements. The analysis has not impacted the design. A full detonation analysis of all experiments will be completed prior to the Phase 2 Flight Safety Review.

19 May 2018 Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) PURPOSE: ACME is focused on advanced combustion technology via fundamental microgravity research. The primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion. A secondary objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. RESEARCH: ACME includes six independent experiments investigating laminar, gaseous, non -premixed flam es. They are being conducted with a single set of modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). STATUS: ACME set-up and check-out was carried out by the ISS crew in Sept.-Oct. 2017, where science test ing began in November. The first round of testing for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment of Marshall B. Long et al. was completed in Feb. 2018, where 130 methane flames (at a range of concentrations) were ignited. The first round of testing for the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment of Derek Dunn-Rankin et al. was completed on May 18 , where 1 20 coflow flames were ignited .

On May 20, b urners and additional hardware for the next three ACME experiments are scheduled to launch . The ACME hardware should be reconfigured on May 22 by astronaut Ricky Arnold (NASA) for CLD Flame ’s second round , where the ethylene flame testing should begin later in the week. 20 August 2018 Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) PURPOSE: ACME is focused on advanced combustion technology via fundamental microgravity research. The primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant emission in practical terrestrial c ombustion. A secondary objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. RESEARCH: ACME includes six independent experiment s investigating laminar, non-premixed flames of gaseous fuels . The experiments are being conducted with a single set o f modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS) . While the ISS astronauts set up the experimental hardware, the ACME tests are remotely commanded from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center. STATUS: ACME setup and checkout were carried out by the ISS crew in Sept. -Oct. 2017 . Thus far, a dozen astronauts from Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States have supported the ACME research. Since November 2017, over 300 flames have been ignited for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) and Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E -FIELD Flames) experiments led respectively by Profs.

Marshall B. Long (Yale University) and Derek Dunn-Rankin (University of California, Irvine). A second round of CLD Flame tests is currently underway and should end in September when the testing will transition back to the E-FIELD Flames experiment. In late 2018, the hardware will be reconfigured for the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment led by Prof. Jim Qui ntiere (University of Maryland). While the first two ACME experiments are focused on improving practical combustion on Earth, BRE is aimed at improving spacecraft fire safety. U.S. astronaut Ricky Arnold cleaning soot from the coflow burner used by both the CLD Flame and E -FIELD Flames experiments. The cleaning was carried out with a toothbrush, piece of insulated wire, vacuum sweeper , flashlight (for burner inspection), dust mask, and gloves. CONTACT: Dennis Stocker, ACME Project Scientist NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 216-433-2166, dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov Lifted flames (detached from the burner) as a function of the matched fuel and air velocity from the CLD Flame experiment. The false color indicate s the CH* concentration as function of the radius and height above the burner . CH* is an excited species and emits blue light as it drops to a lower energy level in a process known as chemiluminescence.

It is the primary source of the blue that is the natural color of hydrocarbon flames (neglecting the broadband thermal radiation from the soot). Diffusion flames with a weak air coflow as a function of the electric field strength, where an open copper mesh above the flame is negatively and positively charged in the top and bottom rows, respectively . Flames naturally include ions which can be affected by a powerful electric or magnetic field. In ACME’s E-FIELD Flames experiment, the copper mesh is energized up to 10,000 volts. This technology could be used to stabilize fuel-lean flames under conditions which are less polluting.

Internal Interfaces (which includes Tables 15-17*) *where Table 17 describes channels A0-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board as discussed in 8.1 below. 8.0 Output FILES 8.1 Data Output File Data output files are created using the SystemOpenTestPoint command which creates a file named and stored at /payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName is the parameter received in the SystemOpenTestPoint command and _x is optional to avoid duplicate files, where x = 1,2,3, etc. The file contains a two-line header. The first line has the date and time, documentation of the setup received in a SystemDefineSetup command, and the PMT gains. The second line has the column headings for the subsequent rows of data. The text of the column headings is defined by the Diagnostics/Header registry entry or the Diagnostics/BreHeader entry depending on whether the SystemDefineSetup command experimentType parameter was BRE or not.

source: Science Documents ACME non-imaging data file description
text: The column headings should match the data which is the following: - A timestamp in the format HH:MM:SS:mmm, where mmm is milliseconds. - 11 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-207 board in the order shown in Table 1. - 25 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-225 board in the order shown in Table 2. (The names of many of these values change depending on whether it is a BRE test or not, hence the two options for header.) - Channel AO-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board. This is the E-Field control voltage. Rows of comma-separated data is added to the file between DataRecordingStart and DataRecordingStop commands at a rate defined by the Diagnostics/SampleTimeMsec registry entry, see Error! Reference source not found., defaulting to 8 msec for 125 Hz sampling.

source: Science Documents ACME non-imaging data file description
text: 3 8.2 Message Log File Software messages are logged to files named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-DD_hh-mmACME.log, where YYYY is year, MM is month, DD is day of month, hh is hour, and mm is minutes. The date in the name is when the log file is created, soon after software startup. Each message line in the file begins with a timestamp and a logging category. The timestamp is of the format YYYY-MM- DD DDD hh:mm:ss:mmm, where DDD is day of the year, mmm is milliseconds, and the rest are self-explanatory. See section Error! Reference source not found. for information about the logging category and how to filter them out if desired. 8.3 Command Log File The message log file, section 8.2, includes messages showing commands received and their parameters. Command log files contain only the details of each command received. The files are named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM- DD_hh-mmACMECommands.log. The format is for each command received a timestamped line of text with the command name followed by timestamped lines of text showing each parameter name and parameter value, including header information.

Introduction The purpose of this report is to describe the data acquired for ACME’s BRE experiment to facilitate its analysis. The data is all digital , where the fuel was gaseous and the re was no collection of soot or the combustion gases. For each test, the key data consists of image files and a file with the non -imaging measurements.

Additional files such as chamber calculator output, camera metadata, and operational logs provide information that can support the analysis. It is recommended that readers interes ted in analyzing the BRE data begin by familiarizing themselves with the hardware and instrumentation, either through the overview in the BRE Final Report or the more comprehensive description found in the ACME Engineering Implementation document. Those seeking to analyze the data should next review this document. To interpret the non-imaging data, it is suggested that a sample data file be opened, named for example 19039A1_data.csv, which has comma-separated values and can be opened with spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel. The data is in raw voltages, where conversion to engineering units requires study of ACME’s Software Interface Design Description, i.e., ACME-DOC-010 (where the latest version at the time of this writing is revision D). Additional documents that may be important include: ACME-RPT-010 A Data Camera Characterization Report, Rev. A

Instead, BRE used the following radiometer arrays: First round of testing BRE array addressed in ACME-RPT-012 Second round of testing standard ACME array addressed in ACME-RPT-011 The offset radiometer was used throughout all of ACME, including both rounds of BRE testing, where it is addressed in ACME-RPT-011. 2. BRE Overview This text is the “Overview” from the ACME/ BRE Final Report, which also provides descriptions of the science, preliminary results, and more. It is strongly suggested that it be reviewed by those interested in analyzing the BRE data.

The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. James G. Quintiere of the Department of Fire Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The experiment has two Co -Investigators (Co-Is), namely Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, of the same U. Maryland department, and Dr. John L. de Ris (FM Global, retired). The ISS research also benefitted greatly from the work of Parham Dehghani, a doctoral student in the Fire Protection Engineering department. Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including BRE and the rest of the ACME investigations. In preparatory drop testing, etc. , Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University ( CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU.

The ISS operations were conducted in two separate rounds of testing during Increments 58-59 and 63-64. More specifically, the first round of testing was conducted from Feb. to April 2019, while the second round testing occurred from Sept. 2020 to Jan. 2021. The first round of tests was limited to ethylene and the 25-mm BRE burner, while the second round also included tests with methane and the 50-mm burner (although not together). 3. Tests Conducted This text is an excerpt from the “Results” section of the ACME/BRE – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 64 (which is included in the ACME/s-Flame Final Report). A minor correction was made to Table 1 in which 19094 is now identified as April 4. It had accidentally been identified as April 5 in the 30 -day reports, although the testing did extend past midnight in Cleveland, OH so the final tests

ACME/BRE Data Interpretation 4 August 2022 4 were conducted on April 5. Nonetheless, the BRE (and more generally ACME) test days and numbers are identified by the date on which the test day began, even if they occurred after midnight (whether on the ISS or in Cleveland). The first round of BRE tests began in Februar y 2019, during Increment 58, when a total of 45 flames were ignited. That round was completed in April 2019, during Increment 59, when an additional 17 flames were ignited. BRE’s second-round flame testing began in Sept. 2020, during Increment 63, in whi ch 47 flames were ignited. The second and final round of tests was completed in Jan. 2021, during Increment 64, when another 85 flames were ignited. As a result, 62 and 132 flames were respectively ignited in the first and second rounds of testing for a total of 194 flames. The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome.

However, the break was longer than had been planned because of combination of hardware issues and limited crew availability. As a result, BRE’s second round was rescheduled to occur after both rounds of the preceding ACME experiment, Structure and Respon se of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s -Flame), was completed, where that occurred in July 2020. A factor in that decision was the delayed start of commercial crew launches and understanding that crew availability would be limited until such crew launches entered an operational, rather than demonstration, phase. All first-round tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen. The tests were carried out at a range of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats. More specifically, testing was especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen. In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with nitrogen and any combustion products (e.g., water vapor and carbon dioxide) from preceding tests.

An exception is tests conducted after the chamber atmosphere was vented and refilled, s uch as the first test of the day. But during tests days, the atmosphere was typically refreshed once or twice between sets of tests. Second round testing was carried out including both BRE burner diameters, i.e., 25 and 50 mm, and on some days with methane (CH4) – again sometimes diluted with nitrogen. Therefore, the second round of tests featured a broader range of conditions than investigated during the first round. However, in contrast to the first round most of the round 2 tests were carried out at roughly 14.7 psia, although pressure has a secondary effect on flames. Meanwhile, the tests in this round were carried out at various oxygen concentrations as in the first round but were more often conducted with ~40% oxygen, where oxygen of course has a strong effect on combustion. BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is wel l understood.

Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting because of its carbon

ACME/BRE Data Interpretation 4 August 2022 5 double bond. Tests are con ducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen, where the fuel and nitrogen were premixed on the ground prior to launch for some cases. But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations. There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for BRE, where all ISS results are electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME experiments. Data Output File The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface Design Description ( ACME- DOC-010 Rev D). The test number is made up of the year (2-digts), day of year (3 digits), and test (a letter and single-digit number). As such, the example, 19039A1 is test A1 conducted on the 39th day of 2019. But the test could also be early on the next (e.g., 40th) day because the day portion of ACME test numbers is not changed when operations continue past midnight (whether GMT or Eastern) into the start of the next day. Tests numbers that only differ by the final digit (e.g., 19039B1, 19039B2, and 19039B3) are typically similar and occasionally identical, where the number is indicative of the variant or repeat. Letters I and O are not used because of their similarity to 1 and 0.

While initially used in ACME testing, t he letter E ceased to be used because Excel software (for example) by default interpreted it as representing an exponential which was inconvenient. As a related aside, ACME tests are often not conducted in order and some planned tests are regularly not conducted at all. The latter results in additional letter gaps if the tests from a day are sorted alphabetically. However, ACME testing often begins with test A1, where the final digit begins with 1 and is increased from there with variant or repeat tests for the same letter. The basic data is in a CSV format, i.e., with comma-separated values, which can be opened by spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel. The first row is a header and provides a limited summary of the hardware and operational conditions. The header is explained in Section 10.1 Metadata Header of ACME-DOC-010 Rev D, which begins on page 126.

Image Files Image data and files discussed in this section are associated with the following cameras: Analog, operations (ops), internal camera ACME Data Camera (DataCam) Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package The Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera is not addressed herein because it was not used for BRE or most of the current ACME experiments. Of the ACME investigations, the LLL-UV camera was only used by the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) study. 1. Analog, internal, operations (ops) camera This color analog camera is mounted on the ACME chamber insert, and as such is within the combustion chamber and is sometimes referred to as the internal camera. Its primary purpose is to support the operations, e.g., to visualize the burner and igniter, an d as such is also often referred to as the operations or ops camera. The NTSC video (named for the National Television System Committee) from the ops camera is at 29.97 frames per second (fps) or nominally 30 fps.

It is not recorded on the space station but is streamed to the ground in near real time and is recorded on CIR consoles at the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center ( GIPOC) in a Transport Stream (TS) format using VLC Media Player which can be freely downloaded from https://www.videolan.org/vlc/. That software has a snapshot function allowing for convenient extraction of still images, e.g., for making measurements of flame dimensions. 2. ACME Data Camera (DataCam) ACME’s primary camera is a high-definition (1360 x 1024), 12 -bit color camera mounted outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench. It is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. It has a filter barrel with a fused silica window (for color imaging), a blue -green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for imaging CH* and CH2O (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence.

The priority in the NASA conversion was to make the images more readily accessible, not to meet all needs.

Most ACME investigators are processi ng the raw HOBJ files using the OMA2 software developed by Prof. Marshall Long (Yale U.), the lead for ACME’s CLD Flame experiment. The OMA2 software is freely available in both Mac and cross -platform (Qt) versions, where the latter can be used with both PC and Linux operating systems. A tutorial was prepared by Dr. Jesse Tinajero on the use of OMA2 to process ACME’s HOBJ image files, where it can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RMtu3KEXNiI. A tutorial for this function may be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4wbgWeJSilc. The HOBJ files can also be readily viewed and processed using ImageJ or its preloaded Fiji variant, where both can be freely downloaded. In either software package, the HOBJ files can imported (rather than opened) as raw files with the following settings: Image type 16-bit unsigned Width 1360 Height 1024 Offset to first image 6244 However, imported DataCam image s will be monochrome unless a Bayer filter (e.g., as described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayer_filter) i s subsequently implemented. It should be possible to install a plug-in to accomplish that color conversion. As another option, Python and Matlab both have image demosaicing functions. To use the ACME DataCam for quantitative measurements, it is critical to avoid saturation, for example by using a camera gain of zero.

Another employed approach was to not use the camera’s white balance which by default multiplies the red and blue by 1.41 and 1.68, respectively, because that could inadvertently lead to saturation. Such multiplication can be done after the HOBJ file is converted and the colors demosaiced, where in OMA2 the white balancing is accomplished with the commands: *rgb 1.41 1 1.68 clip 4095 In summary, the white balance, if desired, needs to be done after the fact through software because the color balancing was at least generally not done with the hardware to avoid the risk of saturation. However, in carrying out color-ratio pyrometry calculations for the ISS data from ACME’s CLD Flame experiment, the investigators determined that the three color ratios (e.g., blue/red) didn’t result in the same temperature profile until the green channel was adjusted by 10% . This notably differs from the camera’s default of multiplication by 1 (i.e., no multiplication) for the green color plane.

For Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP): “After rigorous testing, it was determined [by Tinajero and Long] that a modified version of the bilinear method could be used to optimize the conversion of raw fiber images to full resolution color images. This modified version biases the linear interpolation along the length of the fiber. This method combined with moderate use of defocusing was found to reduce artifacts created by standard de mosaicing algorithms and was used in all of the fiber measurements described below.” Jesse Tinajero and Marshall Long. “Dilution Limits of Coflow Laminar Methane and Ethylene Flames in Microgravity Versus Normal Gravity,” 12th U.S. National Combustion Meeting, 24-26 May 2021. Note that the ACME images will be naturally dark because of the use of the 16-bit file format with 12 -bit image data. As such, adjustments to the image brightness will generally be necessary even if the images are not demosaiced . Fu rthermore, cameras’ CCD arrays are

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 20 September 2021 15 susceptible to radiation damage while in orbit. As a result, the images feature hot pixels which increase in number over the months and years in space. As such, it will appear as if there is a star field within the combustion chamber. Therefore, the images should ideally be processed to remove the bright outlying hot spots. Radiation damage is also obvious in the ops camera imaging. Although the DataCam was typically set for imaging at 30 fps, that is trumped by the exposure settings which were often long because of the dim nature of the microgravity flames. As a result, the framing rate was typically far less. Different exposures are often selected fo r different phases of the tests, e.g., prior to ignition and during the test , so the framing rate may not be consistent . Bracketed imaging could also be employed, where a repeating sequence of different exposure durations is used to enable appropriate photography under uncertain or varying flame intensities.

Bracketing can also used to simultaneously accomplish multiple imaging objectives, e.g., to appropriately image both brightly glowing soot (or TFP fibers) as well as the much dimmer blue portion of the flame. In interpreting the image data, it may be helpful to check the ACME DataCam metadata file which should be available for each successful flame test, e.g., to verify the exposure duration. These files are in a comma -delimited (CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet software or alternately as a text file. Column headings are found in the first row of such files. Due to the use of a turning mirror, the DataCam images should be flipped vertically if upright images are desired, i.e., where the burner is at the bottom and the flame extends upward. In this regard, note that the DataCam provides images in a ‘landscape’ format with the image’s long dimension orthogonal to the burner and chamber axis. This is contrary to an ACME science requirement specifying that the long dimension be aligned with the experimental axis to provide images in a ‘portrait’ format. In this regard, the science requirements were not always met, e.g., because of design tradeoffs. There is some variation in the ACME camera zoom, where its setting is not completely reproducible. Therefore, the scaling of the image data should ideally be established for each subset of tests if more than one zoom setting was used within a test day.

The scaling can typically be carried out using images regularly taken of the ceramic fibers for Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP), where such imaging is normally made at two fiber array positions. Meanwhile, the other cameras used in ACME testing had fixed lenses. 3. Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera During ACME testing, t his intensified camera was typically configured with a CH* bandpass filter and was generally archived at 23 fps. The grayscale image files are in a Tagged Image File Format (TIFF) format and can be opened readily, where brightness/contrast adjustment may again be required. Note that this camera’s Field of View (FOV) is partially blocked by the arms of the fiber array for Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) when it is moved to position the fibers across the flame. As with the ACME DataCam, it might be useful to check the metadata for the CFI intensified camera, which is in a comma -delimited (CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet software or alternately as a text file.

High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package The HiBMs camera was used in combi nation with an opposed backlight, i.e., the CIR ’s collimated illumination package. The resultant imaging was used in preceding droplet combustion experiments for measuring droplet diameter , but it may also be useful for determining the soot volume fractio n via light extinction. However, the camera’s red filter , corresponding to the red illumination, appears to be broad enough to permit significant soot incandescence to pass through the filter. As a result, this imaging is unlikely to be useful for soot volume fraction measurements for all conditions. After post-processing on the ground, the images were made available in the TIFF format and as such are readily opened . The grayscale images were typically archived at 15 fps. It is important to understand that this camera’s images are of limited value for BRE because of the general lack of soot with exception of ignition .

But even considering that, the soot volume fraction can be computed using images from the ACME DataCam as discussed in that camera’s section. In initial ACME testing with the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, this monochrome camera was used without a filter, but that was abandoned because the camera is nearly insensitive to blue. The red filter was installed on 5 March 2018 and used throughout all subsequent ACME testing. C. Test Parameters and Other Files Files discussed in this section include the following: CIR chamber calculator file Test parameter file Notes Test timing Logs 1. CIR chamber calculator file In great contrast to other file types, there is just a single file for each of BRE’s two rounds of testing: Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2019-01-31 to 2019-04-09.xlsx Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2020-07-22 to 2021-02-03.xlsx which provide estimates of the composition of the combustion chamber before and after each BRE test, and more generally for every Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) action involving gas flow into or out of the chamber.

As a result, this includes filling and venting operations, plus recirculation of the chamber contents through the adsorber cartridge filled with 13x molecular sieves. More specifically, t he chamber calculator provides the chamber pressure before and after each operation involving flow into or out of the chamber. While the standard ACME data output files (discussed in section 4.A.1) provide the chamber pressure throughout each test,

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 20 September 2021 20 that measurement is from a pressure transducer that hasn’t been calibrated in years. Meanwhile, the calibrations of the corresponding CIR pressure transducers are checked every six months and those calibrations are updated if needed. Therefore, the chamber calculator is the more reliable source of the chamber pressure. The pressure in the C IR chamber is measured by four different CIR pressure transducers, of which one (PT29) is a different model used for safety. The output of the other three transducers were used to obtain an average chamber pressure. However, the output of one of those (PT28) was clearly an outlier from the other two (PT16 and PT17) as well that of PT29. Therefore, the average pressure recorded in the chamber calculator file was later based on just PT16 and PT17.

For BRE, the chamber calculator also provides concentration estimates of the following gases within the chamber before and after each test and FOMA operation: Oxygen & nitrogen: O2, N2 Fuels: CH4, C2H4 Combustion products: CO2, H2O The latter are based on telemetry from the three Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) on the ACME chamber insert for the flow of fuel, oxygen (or inert), and nitrogen. In a test, the chamber calculator assumes either complete combustion or no combustion, where in the former case the reactant flowing from the burner is tr ansformed into carbon dioxide and water vapor (or water vapor alone if the fuel was hydrogen). Failed or unsustained ignitions were typically set to assume no ignition. Short-lived flames were often treated as having complete combustion , even if a signif icant fraction of the reactant didn’t burn. However, adjustments can be made to account for partial combustion by appropriate selection of the ‘Burn Fraction’ in column AL. With recirculation of the chamber contents, the calculator assume s that the carbon dioxide and water vapor are completely adsorbed, i.e., removed from the chamber.

Meanwhile, it assumes that any unburnt fuels are not adsorbed. Researchers can of course make their estimates of the chamber contents where the chamber calculator should nonetheless be referenced for its record of fills, venting, and recirculation . Note that the chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed hardware. Unfortunately, it is not yet possible to compare chamber calculator estimates with measurements that were sometimes made with the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). Concentrations from the latter are not yet available as explained in section 4.A.3 of this document. 2. Test parameter file Each BRE test was controlled by a software script and corresponding parameter file, named for example ‘as run21028C1.txt,’ specifying settings for imaging, ignition, gas flow, and more. The parameter file and script are discussed extensively in the ACME/BRE Experimental Procedure document, which should be referred to for information on this file type. But note that the ACME.log files should be the best way to verify the as-run test parameters, where the separate parameter files are unfortunately not completely reliable.

Notes Notes of various types are available for test days, where not all types were collected or necessarily prepared for each test day. It is important to understand that the notes, whether handwritten or typed, may include mistakes. It is better to rely on automated logs, metadata files, and parameter files or of course the measurements themselves when possible. The daily test point logs, with names such as ‘19039 daily test point log.pdf,’ chronologically list the tests and the image data acquired which was to be downlinked. Typically, image data was not downlinked without successful, i.e., sustained, ignition. As an example, image data wasn’t downlinked if the test aborted prior to ignition. However, the reverse is not always true. Image data was sometimes downlinked when ignition was unsuccessful and as a result the test point log is only a clue as to what transpired.

Furthermore, note that image data from certain selected cameras, e.g., the HiBMs camera, was sometimes not downlinked due to the limit of how much data could be reasonably downlinked in a subsequent two-shift day. Notes with names such as ‘19039 flow traces.pdf’ include preliminary plots of the flow rates (as seen on a console during testing) and other flame diagnostics, typically along with additional information about the tests. The test parameter notes, with names such as ‘19039 test parameter notes.pdf ,’ show the parameter values which were planned in advance of the test day and the changes made during the test day. The test sheets, with names such as ‘19039 test sheets.pdf ,’ are summary notes about the conduct of each tests conducted that day. 4. The ACME.log files should be the best way to verify the test parameters, where the separate as-run parameter files are unfortunately not completely reliable. source: Science Documents BRE science concept RDR 201306
text: In general • The goal of this study is to establish the burning conditions for materials in a quiescent environment. • We seek to define the burning in terms of the heat of gasification L by using a burning rate emulator (BRE), which is a burner with controlled fuel supply. 3

source: Science Documents BRE science concept RDR 201306
text: Operational Objectives Build and operate a gas-fueled burner for studying steady burning • Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) • Demonstrate – Wall fires in 1 g – Pool fires in 1 g • Explore flat surface burning in microgravity • Establish fuel properties able to support burning in microgravity Examples to be discussed 4

source: Science Documents BRE science concept RDR 201306
text: Relationship to NASA Flammability Tests 1 and 2 • The Upward Flame Propagation (Test 1) is the dominant test for material flammability by NASA. – It tests the flame propagation of a vertical sample 30 × 6.4 – 7.5 cm wide, under a small electric source heat flux of 75 kW/m2. – The atmospheric conditions are controlled. – Burn length and time are recorded. – It is considered a pass-fail type test. • The NASA Test 2: Cone Calorimeter with external heat fluxes of 25 – 75 kW/m2 to supplement information gained from Test 1. 9

source: Science Documents BRE science concept RDR 201306
text: 11 Background of Combustion in Microgravity • Experiments in Skylab (Ross, 2001; Kimzey, 1974) indicated sustained burning of thin paper and plastics. • More recent experiments indicate flame spread on thin paper and plastic thin cylinders in microgravity (Ross, 2001). • Opposed flow spread in a quiescent atmosphere has been shown to depend on material, thickness, and oxygen concentration (Ross, 2001). • The burning of candle flames on the MIR (Ross, 2001) last for periods ranging from about 100 s to more than 45 minutes. A spherical flame formed around the wick. • Droplet experiments by Kumagai and others (Ross, 2001). • Small diameter jet flames of 0.4 – 2.7 mm yielded spherical flames of durations from 150 – 300 s (Ross, 2001). • Sunderland et al. (1999) recorded flames for port diameters up to 3.3 mm, and Re from about 10 – 1700 in microgravity. • Brahmi et al. (2005) used a gaseous burner to simulate burning in g. They burned ethane over a 60  60 mm sintered bronze plate in O2-N2 flowing at velocities of 10 – 150 mm/s. • Bustamante (2012) aircraft and drop data on flat liquid-fueled wicks.

source: Science Documents BRE science concept RDR 201306
Science Documents BRE science concept RDR 201306
text: 37 Knowledge Lacking and Knowledge to be Gained by Flight Tests • The proposed tests aboard the ISS will establish the range of steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in microgravity. We will identify the associated material properties and the real materials that are represented. • Once established based on fuel properties, NASA Test 2 could be used as a basis for establishing comparable properties for real materials. This could elevate the role of NASA Test 2 over Test 1. This would close the loop of using a ground-based test to assess the true flammability of materials in microgravity.

text: Science Data End Products 38 Objective 1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. Emphasize conditions that can be related to diverse condensed fuels. 2. text: BRE Operational Sequence Action Approx. Time 1. Ensure that the appropriate burner is installed. Preflow the burner fluent gas at the composition of the upcoming test point to flush the plumbing system. 2. Establish chamber conditions. These consist of a set point pressure and species compositions, as specified in the test matrix. Conditions are obtained in four ways: from cabin air (desired); from the preceding test; from scrubbing and replenishing; or from a complete evacuation and recharge. 3. Allow chamber contents to reach equilibrium. A hold time of 5 minutes is required for quiescent, isothermal, and well-mixed conditions. 4. Take reference images (if applicable). Establish framing rates for video cameras. Begin color imaging. Begin monitoring measurements and wait 15 s. 68

source: Science Documents BRE science concept RDR 201306
text: BRE Operational Sequence Action Approx. Time 5. Commence fluent flow at a value to be uplinked. The initial value should correspond to about 1 g/m2-s of hydrocarbon fuel. Energize igniter to ignite the flame and then retract the igniter. If ignition does not occur within 5 seconds, shut off the flow. A new value of flow rate will be specified by uplink. If the flame ignites, proceed to Step 6. Otherwise proceed to Step 7. 6. Set the flow rate to the test flow rate. Anytime during this step, if the flame extinguishes, or either heat flux sensor exceeds a critical temperature, stop the fuel flow. Continue until the surface burner temperatures become quasi-steady. Then reduce the flow rate in 10% increments of the test flow rate, hold for 15 s, and continue such reductions until extinction. 7. Stop fluent flow. Record reference images (if applicable). After 60 s terminate color imaging and monitoring measurements. Select data for downlink and downlink data. 0 s 5 s 60 s 69
