text: ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have unfortunately not always performed adequately. The fuel and especially nitrogen flows sometimes oscillate. Furthermore, the MFC used for the ‘air’ coflow behaves as if it is sticking in a few places, where the flow rate won’t linearly ramp when commanded (as required for the CLD Flame experiment) . It tends to stick in some places and then abruptly overshoot where that has sometimes been seen to extinguish the flame. As a result, mass flow controllers are tested - without flames - after they are first installed. Adjustments are often then made to (1) the settings that control when the valves open and (2) the Proportional -Integral-Derivative (PID) settings. This activity has involved significant testing, separate from flame tests, and has taken place during CLD Flame operations on 17333, 17334, 17347, 17354, 18008, 18022, 18038, 18046, 18143, and 18241. In this regard, there are an assortment of MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gases. While the MFC tuning

It was seen that nitrogen oscillations te nd to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre -flow was implemented so that the oscillations would typically end before the flame measurements. That approach has been partially successful and was introduced during E-FIELD Flames’ first round. Later, a procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to each test was also implemented during E-FIELD Flames’ second round. A replacement MFC for the ‘air’ coflow is being prepared for spaceflight, where a limited third round of CLD Flame testing is being planned to accomplish its extinction limit objective. The final day of testing during E-FIELD Flame’s first round was conducted with highly sooty ethylene flames and a positively charged mesh, which tends to push the flame down toward the burner. Additional evaluation tests were performed on May 31 (18151), and the decision was made to have the crew clean the soot from the burner because it was clear that the gas flow from the burner was affected by the soot buildup . A cleaning procedure was developed, approved, and carried out by astronaut Ricky Arnold on June 19 (18170). The cleaned burner was imaged with the CIR cameras on June 21 (18172), but the evaluation testing was deferred because of a cable mating issue. The key measurement for the E-FIELD Flames experiments is the ion current as a function of applied voltage, i.e., the voltage-current or V-I curve. This curve provides information on the flames ability to produce chemi -ions based on its saturation ion current, and it provides a measure of combustion performance in that ion production is a function of carbon influx into the flame and the vigorousness of the combustion process. More compact, higher temperature flames produce more chemi -ions than do larger more diffuse reaction zones of lower overall temperature for the same fuel flow. The first effect (i.e., the relationship between carbon influx and peak ion current) can be seen in Figure 2, where the flow of 15 cm/s methane produces slightly above 2 microamps of ion current at the peak (1.5 kV/cm) and the flow of 19 cm/s methane has a peak of 2.75 microamps.

Traditional electrical aspects of flames studies look for a saturation ion current plateau, where the ion current remains fixed despite an increase in applied electric field. For these microgravity flames, there is a pronounced peak in the ion current at saturation and then a gradual decrease to a global saturation plateau. This is a strikingly different behavior than is seen in 1-g, and the behavior is even more pronounced for the case where there is zero coflow. Figure 2. text: Since these are diffusion flames , essentially all of the fuel is being burned independent of the flame’s shape and the applied electric field, but it seems clear that the electric field is affecting the chemi -ion production capability of the flame. As is apparent from the flame images, the flame is most compact at the voltage consistent with the peak ion current. With increasing voltage, the flame becomes less compact and the ion current decreases. We presume that the flame remains at saturation throughout this period (that is, the fla me is producing as many ions as it can, and those ions are being removed from the reaction zone as soon as they are created) so the decrease in ion current results from a change in combustion intensity. We can explore this hypothesis further using the PMT data collected in the experiments.

(2) In microgravity, the ion current does not smoothly increase to saturation nor does it show a gentle peak with a mild decrease as is seen in the normal gravity results. Instead, in microgravity there is a distinct peak in the ion current with a severe decrease throughout the saturation condition, with a final saturation plateau observed at voltages substantially above the voltage at peak ion current. That is, the microgravity final saturation is not the maximum ion current observed. This difference is more dramatic when there is no coflow, which suggests that entrainment plays an important role whether caused by buoyancy or a forced coflow.

text: ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 1 1 June 2019 30-day Operational Accomplishments Report … for the International Space Station (ISS) Increments 57 and 58 ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments E-FIELD Flames Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames E-FIELD Flame s is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The investigation was carried out in two rounds of tests, where the first (with ACME’s coflow burner) occurred in Increment 55 and the second (with a gas-jet burner) began in Increment 56 and ended in Increment 57. As a result, there is nothing to be reported for Increment 58. Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project Scientist, who is the primary contact for E-FIELD Flames and ACME information. Principal Investigator (PI): Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin, University of California, Irvine, CA PI project scientist: Dr.

Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH PS team member: Dr. Uday G. Hegde, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH I. Introduction The Electric -Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E -FIELD Flames) experimen t wa s conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this experiment, an electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts was established between the burner and a flat, circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner . The motion of the charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong electric field. The resulting ion -driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flame.

text: Measurements we re made of electric -field strength, the ion current passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allow ed for great simplifications in the analysis of ion -driven convection and flame interaction , enabling new understanding and the development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth.

text: ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 2 An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer. The purpose of the E -FIELD Flames experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical benefit. For example, electric fi elds can enable stable burner operation at fuel -lean conditions with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the electric field. As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic. It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields.

text: More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi -ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of iner t (nitrogen) in the fuel. B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (n itrogen) added to the fuel stream. D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the combustion behavior of near -limit lifted flames and use the associated ion -driven wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of flame and electric field conditions.

text: The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, elect ric-field voltage and polarity were the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. Tests were conducted with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of soot-producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting. They were carried out with both a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. Tests with the coflow burner were conducted with and without a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas -jet burner to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame. The coflow burner also provided a different electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane). In a typical test, the mesh electrode was en ergized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner), where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field strength was measured. The field strength was changed in repeated steps or was instead smoothly ramped.

text: ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 3 driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Therefore, the flicker in the E -FIELD Flames was a result of electric body forces alone . Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, wh ich are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.

text: For example, c hemi-ion species, electronically excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include t he gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.

source: Reports 2019 - E-FIELD Flames 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 20190601
text: However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or soot limit. This was not done during Increments 5 5-56 or 57 -58, where the console commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

text: ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 4 III. Results A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E -FIELD Flames expe riment, with 142 and 77 respectively ignited during Increments 55 -56 and 57-58. Note that the investigation’s testing was completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 58. The first and second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and September-November 2018 . The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited flames conducted with coflow and gas-jet burners, respectively. The coflow burner was developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Fla me (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD Flames’ second round occurred between the two rounds of the E -FIELD Flames experiment. The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome.

text: E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with two different gas eous fuels, methan e and ethylene. Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon double bond. For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions. For limited cases, the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch. ACME bottles were launched with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 50%, and 100%, again with a balan ce of nitrogen (on a volume basis) . But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.

text: The first test of the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been sufficiently primed. Ignition was sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite. This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (P MT) module. The OH* chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum. However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to false ignition detection. ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have unfortunately not always performed adequat ely. The fuel and especially nitrogen flows sometimes oscillate.

text: It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests. As discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination package. Those are not critical for E-FIELD Flames, so tests continued without their use. Furthermore, recorded image data i s sometimes deleted withou t downlinking. This i s done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted. This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the project constraints. Data quality is of co urse dependent on the experimental hardware. But neglecting that limitation on data quality , the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually become ‘hot’ over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, they are a degradation of the image quality.

In this regard, note that the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS). text: ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 8 D. Status of Data Analysis Data from the tests making up the E-FIELD Flames experiment includes video recordings from the operations camera for general flame behavior, high resolution images from the ACME data camera at various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame luminosity, intensified camera images, and non-imaging data at 125 Hz. The non-imaging data file is processed using Matlab scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame researchers) to separately show trends of ion current and flame luminosity as a function of the applied field, and the flame parameters (fuel, flowrate, burner type). The PMT data is also extracted to evaluate flame luminosity oscillations. Image data is processed using the OMA software (also developed and used by CLD Flame researchers). The overall data volume is large with a storage limit of 127 ,000 MB per test day. All of the data has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine.

text: A t this stage, the data has been sorted into appropriate segments so that comparisons can be made between burner geometries (jet versus coflow from the prior round of testing), fuel type and dilution (methane versu s ethylene; no dilution, modest dilution, high dilution) and fuel flow velocity. The fuel flow velocity and dilution conditions were sometimes selected to hold total carbon flux into the flame constant. At this stage, the analysis remains comparative and qualitative, to show the major differences in behavior in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames, and to show particularly how buoyancy modifies the electrical response of the flames. E. Preliminary Research Findings Distinctly different results were seen in E-FIELD Flames’ second round tests with the gasjet burner when compared with the first round tests with the coflow burner. For example, the ion current response to the electric field strength with an upward ion driven wind in microgravity is a clear parabolic trend (which is similar to the trend observed in 1-g flames with the coflow burner as presented in the prior report).

source: Reports 2019 - E-FIELD Flames 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 20190601
text: The parabolic behavior is evident even with the strong oscillations observed during the rise. This rising trend is not observed with the coflow burner. The behavior of the soot and its charge state are complicated since in the regions of high field strength, particularly near the fuel tube where the field lines converge, soot can emit or collect free charges. Hence, the soot transport is driven directly by the field and by the ion-driven wind (and thermophoresis) which means it can travel differentially to the bulk flow. These various transport elements can push the soot through the flame to burnout, hold it in stasis in the flame for additional growth, or drive it to the burner where it accumulates. More work is needed to sort through these elements. text: ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 10 that maximum, the soot is almost gone (as seen in Figure 1). The flame base starts rising slightly around the current peak and lifts higher, with one side of the reaction wing attached to the tube, as the electric field increases further. The flame is not always lifted at the same edge of the burner tube; therefore, the attached reaction wing sometimes rotates along the tube edge with approximately the same lift angle under the same electric field strength. Otherwise, the lifted edge flame remains relatively stable. With further increases in the electric field strength , the flame starts fluctuating and a distinct dancing phenomenon can be seen from the i -v curve where the ion current oscillates strongly at the same field strength . The fluctuation crosses more than 3.5 A (between ~1.2 to 5 A) and reach es 5.0 A for the 24 cm/s case. Similarly, this oscillation at the same voltage is observed for 19 cm/s with the ion current spanning around 2.5 A (~1.4 to 4 A) and reaching 4.0 A; corresponding flame images are shown as 1.86 and 2.16 kV/cm in Figure 1.

The flame geometries and soot distribution under the electric field influence clearly differ when comparing the gas-jet burner results with those from the earlier coflow burner tests without a coflow (i.e., with the same jet flow for each), where the annulus of the coflow burner acted as a planar electrode. But the maximum amount of ions pr oduced within the flame (as evidenced by the ion current reaching the plateau) is similar for the case where the fuel flow velocity matches at 19 cm/s. The current also peaks around the same field strength per unit distance. Moreover, the oscillation behavior only exists in the jet burner experiment and further more influences the ion current monitoring due to the unstable flame behavior responding to the high field strength.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 3 1. Overview The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames ( E-FIELD Flames ) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack ( CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Derek Dunn -Rankin of the University of California, Irvine ( UC Irvine). Dr. Yu -Chien (Alice) Chien , also of UC Irvine, served as the Project Scientist at the university. Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is NASA’s Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including E-FIELD Flames and the rest of the ACME investigations. In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. The experiment had two Co-Investigators, the first of which was Prof. Felix Weinberg of London’s Imperial College. Prof.

Weinberg was a pioneer in researching the effects of electrical fields on flames in microgravity, but unfortunately died in 2012 (see http://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/117808/tribute-felixweinberg/) before the hardware was built and the tests were conducted on the ISS. The second Co - Investigator was Dr. Sunny Karnani who did his doctoral research in preparation of the spaceflight experiment and afterward worked for ClearSign Combustion Corp. , which markets Electrodynamic Combustion Control (https://www.clearsign.com/technology/electrodynamic-combustion-control/). The corporation provided some support to the E -FIELD Flames research effort, but Karnani left ClearSign to conduct research for the U.S. Army , effectively ending his intimate role in the project prior to the spaceflight operations. He remains a collaborator. E-FIELD Flames operations were conducted in two rounds of testing during Increments 55-57, which were more specifically in March -May and September -November 2018 .

The break in testing (from May to September) was intentional and planned years in advance to allow the research team to analyze early results and use the insights obtained from the analysis to plan the second round so as to maximize its scientific output. 2. Science Overview A. Background With minor editing, t his background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document (SRD) of March 2010. This project utilizes electric fields in microgravity combustion science to establish a fundamental understanding of chemi -ionization and ion -driven convection in flames. It also uses this understanding to demonstrate electrical manipulation of sooting behavior and stability limits in the absence of buoyancy. This work is based on prior foundation studies that included simulating zero-g combustion of small gas jet diffusion flames in an earth-gravity laboratory, and the electric field control of flame electrodynamics. The current SRD proposes to use the extended -duration microgravity environment to further develop an understanding of electric fie lds in combustion processes and their potential applications.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 4 The research centers on the fact that electrical forces, acting on charge carriers created through chemi-ionization, can provide for measurement and manipulation of flames in microgravity environments. For example, using the drag exercised on flame ions, electric fields have demonstrated observable influences on flame shape, sooting behavior, burning velocity, extinction, and stability. The source of these influences almost certainly resides in ion wind effects. In microgravity, where there are no density -driven buoyant effects to contend with, ion winds represent an important (and perhaps the only) body force that can be applied to manipulate combustion systems. This project includes both academic study of electric field effects and aspects for practical utilization of electrical control of combustion processes.

The prior laboratory experiments have shown that electrical properties of flames can be used to produce enhanced combustion performance by: (a) manipulating flame ions in order to change flame chemistry – this is generally considered a minor influence because flame ion concentration is typically small, but it may be critical at near -limit conditions; (b) creating a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front – this process can provide a local actuator for flame convection control; (c) using electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions; and (d) using electrical properties to characterize flames – e.g., there is a relationship between flame temperature, the carbon content of a fuel, and the ion current it can produce at saturation. In 1-g, the above -mentioned processes are confounded by complex buoyancy interac tions that cannot be unraveled.

Hence, to evaluate them in detail, we propose the following experimental objectives for an extended microgravity environment: (A) determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel; (B) compare the time response of the flame’s chemiluminescence and ion current to rapid cha nges in electric fields; (C) determine sooting behavior in relation to the electric field influences; and (D) manipulate the limit behavior of lifted flames using electric fields. The experimental approach includes a simple gas jet diffusion flame and a c o-flow burner. The basic variations in the tests are in the burner type, the fuel type (nomina lly nonsooting and sooting), and in the level of inert dilution of the fuel to vary the flame strength. The co-flow or environment gas will have a nominal molar composition of 21% O2 and 79% N2. The experimental concept is to ground the burner to the test chamber and to install an electrically active planar mesh electrode downstream of the burner mouth.

The potential of the mesh electrode can be either positive or negative, with a steady voltage or with a time varying potential (including a rapid step change) to examine the flame’s steady state response and time response. The data to be recorded include the applied voltage, the ion current, the flame broadband lumin osity, the CH* luminosity, flame images of OH* and visible light showing the flame shape as a function of electric potential and flame shape changes during transients in the electric field. In addition, a desired measurement of temperature in and near the flame will monitor the thermal field as a function of the electric field conditions. The data from these measurements will allow a chemical and physical understanding of flame ion production and information showing the potential to use these ions to electrically control the flame both via modification of the local chemistry near extinction limits and through changes in the local convection using the ion driven wind. For example, a lifted diffusion flame near its blowoff condition is sensitive to mixing at the flame anchor point. Therefore, electric fields acting

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 5 on near-limit flames can exert a large influence because they can affect the local mixing behavior. The role of electric fields on soot formation will be dramatic under conditions where the ion driven wind has a large influence on flow residence time (or on ion residence time, if chemical ef fects are found important) in sooting flames. Generally, the convective flows driven by electric fields acting on flame ions and those driven by buoyancy have been found to be of the same order of magnitude in earth gravity. In addition, raising the temperature often increases the ion production rate and the response to an electric field, but increasing temperature also increases the buoyancy effect, making it difficult, on earth, to separate ion wind effects from those due to buoyancy. In the zero -g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and develop sufficient understanding to predict the response of flames to electric fields under all conditions.

Extended run times are crucial for all of the studies because the timescales of flame property changes (which includes chemi -ionization) are dominated by convection (length scale/velocity) and past studies have shown that soot studies require high quality zero gravity timescales longer than is available in aircraft and drop towers. In addition, exploring instabilities and extinction behavior in near -limit flames requires experiments lasting tens of seconds. Overall, the goal o f this zero -gravity study is to understand chemi -ionization behavior and the resulting ion driven winds suffic iently well so that electrical properties of flames can be used to characterize (by monitoring ion current) and control them (via direct chemical or local convective influences). Electric field effects on flames have been documented for decades (even centuries), but flames in 1-g all include buoyancy influences that affect ion generation behavior. For flames near transitions and limits, buoyant influences always confound any understanding of the role of ion driven winds in using electric fields to characterize and manipulate flames.

The proposed study removes this confounding influence and allows definitive measurement and analysis of the electric field effects on jet diffusion and co-flow flames. B. Rationale for Microgravity This is the ‘Justification for Extended-Duration Microgravity’ section of the experiment’s SRD from March 2010. See the SRD itself for the references, etc. as they are not included in this report. As described in the Background and Overview (Section 1.1), electric field effects and buoyancy effects have been found to be of the same order of magnitude. In addition, in some cases, raising the flame temperature will increase the O atom concentration, thereby increasing the ion production rate and increasing the response to an electric field . At the same time, increasing temperature increases the buoyancy effect, making it difficult to separate ion wind effects from buoyancy. In the zero-g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and develop sufficient understandin g to predict the response of flames to electric fields under all conditions.

For electrically driven flames, microgravity is also necessary to create conditions that produce symmetric flames suitable for Abel inversion and steady-state analysis. While in general natural convection can enhance symmetry relative to non -buoyant flames, a flame at 1 -g in an electric wind experiences buoyancy as a disruptive influence on symmetry. Even when buoyancy effects can be minimized, we have found that there are periodic disturbances that disrupt the ideal symmetry. Highly symmetric conditions of extended microgravity are also useful for numerically simulating these various effects by our electrokinetic model or more comprehensively by others.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 6 Finally, in order to fully evaluate the potential for control, it is important to examine the effects separately. An example of the importance of microgravity for the electric field effects studies is shown in Figure 2.6. This figure compares the capillary flame used for 1-g experiments (which has some similarities to the jet -flame companion study) when it i s oriented vertically to when it is oriented horizontally relative to gravity. These flames behave differently in shape, size, and ion production demonstrating the substantial in fluence played by buoyancy even in the relatively small capillary flames. Grav ity effects in the co -flow flames have been described in the SRD for the CLD Flame experiment, and the same influences will be important when we apply electric fields. Only in ex tended microgravity will it be possible to separate the ion driven wind effects from buoyant wind effects. Figure 2.6. Effect of orientation on combustion of 1.8 mm jet diffusion flames in 1-g.

Extended run times are crucial for all of the studies beca use the timescales involved extend beyond drop tower capabilities and the microgravity quality required for symmetry and stability exceeds aircraft microgravity. The electric -field flame interaction tests carried out in the NASA Glenn 2.2 Second Drop Tower tests by Yuan and Hegde [55] showed that the flame did not appear to re ach steady state during the 2.2 sec. drop. Furthermore, their results showed substantial differences in flame shape between cases where the electric field was activated half-way through the drop and at the beginning of the drop, again suggesting that stead y state was not achieved. Although, we varied the range of tests performed at the Drop Tower, our research group encountered similar obstacles. Drop times were insufficient to achieve a steady flame after voltage changes in one direction. Additionally, we were unable to capture the removal of soot from the ignition event and the subsequent response of the flame to the electric field. Furthermore, testing has shown path dependence in the response time of the flame when subjected to step voltages of varying polarities.

Properly mapping the steady-state ion current as a function of applied voltage requires that the flame stabilize at each applied voltage. Generally speaking, the timescale of flame property changes (which includes chemi-ionization) is dominated by convection (length scale/velocity), which is on the order of 0.1 second. In order to ensure quasisteady conditions of the VI characteristics for a single flame configuration with some fidelity (e.g., 50 steps of 200 V each, with 2 seconds between steps for settling after the change), requires more than 100 seconds of continuous high quality microgravity. Each condition and voltage cannot be

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 7 run individually (i.e., with separate drop tests) because the 2 second settling time requires that the flame begin at a settled initial condition before taking another relatively small voltage step. If we tried to step to the initial condition, allow settling, take the base measurement, then step the voltage and again wait the required settling time, we would exceed 5 seconds for each test in nearly all cases. To run a return voltage sweep to examine hysteresis might take a further 100 seconds. Furthermore, these times are based on 1-g results which under low ion wind conditions are likely to be faster than occ urs in microgravity since their the convective timescales can be substantially smaller (under low electric field forcing conditions, for example). Understanding the electric field effects on soot is another area that requires high quality zero gravity timescales longer than is available in drop towers. A variety of zero gravity diffusion flame experience has shown that quasi-steady soot formation requires many seconds [22, 56, 57].

The long du ration is necessary since we are exploring the relative importance of residence time modification of these processes in these flames. In addition, as mentioned above, instabilities and extinction behavior in near -limit flames generally have a stochastic ch aracter so that relatively long observation times are needed to quantify electric field effects. For example, lifted flames in electric fields can exhibit an oscillatory behavior where they alternately approach and recede from the burner exit until they finally reattach. Tens of seconds for this process is not unusual. Extended microgravity conditions will clarify the role of electric fields (via ion winds) on stability limits of flames. C. Science Objectives The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘Experimental Objectives’ section of the experiment’s SRD from March 2010. Although the objectives were not formally changed, the slow response time of the high-voltage power supplies (recommended in the ISRD) limited the ability to accomplish objective B.

To make up in part for this shortfall, the investigation was permitted to test with two different burner types (specifically gas-jet and coflow burners) , where th e use of multiple burner types was disallowed for ACME experiments to limit their scope. Note that the hardware shortcoming was identified during the hardware development (and thus prior to spaceflight operations) , but the project management decided to accept the shortcoming and proceed with the existing design to avoid the cost and schedule ramifications of a redesign. The ultimate objective of this experiment is to develop an understanding of the mechanisms of chemi-ionization in flames and to describe the interplay between convective flows driven by those flame ions and their generation rate. With this information it will then be possible to detect and control flame behavior electrically. In 1-g, laminar diffusion flames are often controlled to a large extent by natural convection, and particularly by the rate at which natural convection brings fresh oxidizer to the reaction zone. Hence, the vigor with which combustion proceeds depends on local convection.

As described in Section 1, an electric field acting on flame ions produces a body force and convection (analogous to buoyancy) which affects the combustion process. The change in the combustion process can in turn affect the ion production rate, which is responsible for the body force. This coupled interaction is very difficult to measure, study, and understand in 1-g because buoyant forces (of approximately equal magnitude) interfere. In microgravity, there is no such complication and the body force in the flame is associated entirely with the ion-driven wind. 1-g experiments have demonstrated clearly that electrically driven convection can be used to modify the local flow field in a manner that changes combustion behavior. For example, it can stabilize lifted flames or force them to reattach. Electric fields have been seen to change soot formation,

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 8 though whether solely by residence time ef fects or their combination with chemical alterations has not been confirmed. In addition, ions can attach to soot particles providing them with enhanced mobility that can be manipulated. Furthermore, the electrical properties of flames provide a measure of their charact er. For example, non -premixed flames exhibit different relationships between ion production and ion wind forces than do premixed flames. The hydrocarbon fuel, and in particular, the carbon/hydrogen ratio, also affects these interactions. The goal of this p roject is to clarify and quantify this range of electrical effects and to then demonstrate the electrical manipulation of flame stability and soot in flames using the information obtained. To accomplish this scientific goal, there are four fundamental experimental objectives, in priority order, using a jet diffusion flame burner and a co-flow diffusion flame burner. The jet flame is the more critical configuration because it has a large 1 -g data foundation and it can be more easily modeled as an ion and thermal source.

In microgravity, however, it will be primarily driven by ion wind convection (no buoyant contribution and at its low fuel flow rates, the injection momentum dies rapidly with distance from the injector) which may limit its operating range. The co-flow flame allows a forced convection component to provide a wider range of flow conditions (fuel dilution and exit velocity) and a reproducible lifted flame for stability and soot behavior studies: A) Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel. For the above determination, a low -sooting and highly sooting fuel are included, and the inert weakens the flame sufficiently to permit near-limit conditions at moderate flow velocities, where the effects of electric fields will be most acute.

As shown in Figure 1.10, the resulting voltage current (VI) curve (also known as the voltage current characteristic - VCC) from these experiments will identify the voltage and current at which the ion current first saturates, the voltage at which the current begins to increase beyond saturation, indicating a change in combustion behavior, and the voltage at which the flame extinguishes. These data can be analyzed further to provide the ion production per carbon atom of fuel flux which describes the flame character (i.e., diffusion to partially premixed), and the ion wind strength for each condition. In addition to the ir direct interpretative value for calculating ion-driven winds and body forces, these data can also be used in electrokinetic simulations to compute ion mobility values consistent with measured ion currents and to help validate the numerical simulations o f oth er researchers that include ion species and electrical effects in their flame calculations.

B) Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (met hane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. These data provide the dynamic system behavior of the flame. This information comprises the time response of the flame (i.e., its surface area and luminosity) as compared to the time response of the ion current. These timescales can temporally separate the direct chemical effects of electric fields from ion diffusion and ion wind convective forcing. In addition, the system response is required to eventually build flame mo dels suitable for active electrical control, assuming linear behavior over small ranges. C) Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 9 The interaction between soot and electric fields is very com plex because it combines the direct influence of electric fields on the chemis try, the ion wind effects on residence time and mixing, and the electric forces on the charged soot particles themselves. The zero -gravity environment, using the combination of the jet diffusion flame and the co -flow flame provides a wide range of conditions where these different influences can be allowed to dominate individually. For example, the forced convection environment of the co-flow burner will minimize the influence of the axial ion-driven wind, which helps to distinguish the direct electrical eff ects on ion chemistry in soot formation. In addition to demonstrating the direct control of soot behavior by electric fields, separating the influences can help distinguish between neutral molecule addition mechanisms of soot formation and those that presu me the importance of ionic species. For example, changing the strength and polarity of the electric field can change the availability of ion precursors, and electric convection can manipulate reactants’ time/temperature history.

In addition, charges will accumulate onto soot, and the electric field can then act directly on the soot particles to change their residence time and path through the flame. D) Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the combustion behavior of near -limit lifted flames and use the associated ion -driven wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. Because the chemi-ion current per unit flame area can be used as an indicator of flame strength, its measure (both average and fluctuating properties) with low electric field voltage can be used to detect flames approaching their limit condition. By adjusting the electric field , 1 -g studies indicate that an ion driven wind can be used to reduce the liftoff height and stabilize the flame. This is an example of open loop electrical flame sensing, analysis, and control.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 10 D. Science Success Criteria The success criteria is from the E-FIELD Flames’ portion of the ‘Success Criteria’ section of the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (IS RD, ACME-SRD-001.B) from Sept. 2013, which is revision B of the version prepared for the Requirements Definition Review (RDR). 6.2.1. Minimum Success - Obtain V-I curve in quasi-steady conditions for undiluted methane fuel on either diameter of the gas jet burner or the co-flow burner - Simultaneously capture color images of flame responding to electric field during V-I sweep 6.2.2.

High Success All of the above plus: - Obtain V-I curve in quasi-steady conditions for both fuels (methane and ethylene) on one gas jet burner and the co-flow burner with a range of inert dilution of fuel - Simultaneously capture flame images during volt age sweeps to allow measurement of liftoff height has a function of applied voltage - Measure soot luminosity (radiometer measurement) as a function of applied voltage during VI sweeps and step changes - Capture color images and soot luminosity (radiometer measurement) as a function of coflow velocity during the Electric Field Effects on Soot experiment. 6.2.3. Complete Success All of the above plus: - Demonstrate open loop control of flame near sooting and stability limits using ion current and luminosity as sensors by determining the decrease (or increase) in soot luminosity and by evaluating the extent to which stability limits can be extended using an electric field - (Desired) Obtain thermal field information for the gas jet or coflow flame to visualize ion driven wind 3. Hardware Overview A. General Description This text is from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of the following conference paper: Y.-C. Chien, J.

Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn -Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. See the paper itself for the references, etc. as they are not included in this report. As a minor note, the sizes of some figures were adjusted in this report, but none were cropped. The E-FIELD Flames experiment is being conducted in 2018 within the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) [15], which was launched in 2008 and us ed from 2009 to 2017 for a series of droplet combustion experiments [16]. The CIR facility is similar in size to a vending machine as can be seen in Figure 1. It includes a 100-liter combustion chamber capable of operation at pressures of up to 300 kPa. The chamber features a ring of 8 sapphire windows and is equipped with a set of reconfigurable imaging systems. The CIR was designed with gas delivery, venting, thermal control, electrical power, data handling, image processing and storage, and vibration isolation to enable combustion research with gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels.

E-FIELD Flames is one of the six unique experiments featuring non -premixed laminar flames of gaseous fuels which currently make up the ACME project [17]. The 0.4 -m diameter ACME chamber insert provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and a retracting resistively -heated igniter. T he igniter has a crew -exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and stepper-motor drive for radial positioning.

The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the far left of Figures 2-3 behind an orange hose and b lack cables) for delivering fuel, oxidizer (or an inert), and nitrogen to the burner or chamber. The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate accuracy for the desired flow ranges. ACME’s gas delivery system enables on-orbit dilution of the gaseous fuel or oxidizer with nitrogen (available from the space station), but not both simultaneously. However, bottles of premixed fuel and oxidizer are also used, where the CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1 .00, 2.25, and 3.80 liters. Fuels are stored in 1 -liter bottles, while the 21/79 oxygen/nitrogen mixture (on a volume basis) used by E-FIELD Flames comes in 3.80-liter bottles. The ACME experiments are constant volume studies, where the chamber’s free volume, with the insert installed, is about 90 liters. Burner flows are generally constrained to limit the pressure rise and vitiation of the atmosphere, where typical ACME tests are only 0.5-2 minutes in duration.

In this study, a high-voltage electric field is generated between the burner and a copper electrode mesh located above (i.e., downstream of) the burner outlet, as can be seen in Figure 4(b). The circular mesh is energized at up to 10,000 volts w ith either polarity, where the bur ner serves as the electrical return and the flow of flame -produced ions completes the circuit. The ion current between the burner and electrode mesh is measured from the voltage drop across a known resistor and application of Ohm’s Law. With and without the copper ring, the electrode mesh is 8.9 and 8.4 cm in diameter, respectively. The square copper weave has 7.1 wires/cm, a wire diameter of 0.43 mm, and a 48% open area. The mesh permits gas to pass through while also acting as an electrical element.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 14 accommodate an alternate electrode position of 52 mm above the coflow burner tip, but the closer position is being used to produce the highest field strengths. ACME’s non -imaging measurements are recorded at 125 Hz. The measured test conditions include the chamber pressure and temperature, the three gas flow rates, and th e electrical potential of the elec trode mesh. Acceleration measurements are provided by the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) [18], which is the primary instrument for such measurements on ISS and previously served that role for the space shuttle. The flame behavior is observe d optically with a variety of instruments. For most ACME experiments, including E -FIELD Flames, the radiant emission is measured with 6 thermopile detectors with a spectral range of nominally 0.2 -11 microns. Five radiome ters are in a crew exchangeable linear array that is mounted parallel to the chamber axis. The other detector is downstream and off axis from the burner. Chemiluminescent emission is measured with a set of three Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules. Their spectral range is 230-700 nm, i.e.

in the visible and near ultraviolet, but two are equipped with narrow bandpass filters for measurement of OH* and CH* emissions, respectively. The third PMT is equipped with a neutral density filter to prevent saturation, although the gain values for all three PMTs are independently and readily adjustable. Like many of the components, the array of PMT modules can be removed from the chamber insert by the crew. In addition to their scientific value, PMT measurements are used operationally to detect igni tion and automatically deactivate and retract the igniter. The radiometer or PMT measurements can similarly be used to detect extinction and automatically end the gas flow and test. Imaging measurements of the flames complement the optical sensors descri bed above. Color imaging is provided by an analog color camera within the chamber and a high -definition (1360 x 1024), 12-bit color camera mounted outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench. The latter is equipped with a motorized lens with independent c ontrol of the zoom, iris, and focus.

It has a filter barrel with a fused silica window (for color imaging), a blue -green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for imaging CH* and HCHO (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence. The digital color camera was characterized prior to launch for color-ratio pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, via the techniques of [19, 20]. The camera makes soot pyrometry possible as well as Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP), where the chamber insert is equipped with a translating array of silicon-carbide (SiC) fibers. A 14-micron fiber array can be seen at the top of Figure 4(b). However, the fibers interfere with the electric field preventing the use of Thin Filament Pyrometry in the E-FIELD Flames experiment. Two intensified monochrome cameras mounted outside the combustion chamber are available for ACME use, although only one is being used by E -FIELD Flames. It is a high -definition (1390x1040), 12-bit camera equipped with a filter barrel similar to that used by the digital color camera discussed in the preceding paragraph, although it doesn’t have a blue -green filter. The CH* filter has been used in the intensified photography of the E-FIELD Flames tests.

While unused by E-FIELD Flames, the CIR is also equi pped with a high -definition (1024x1024) camera with an intensifier extending into the ultraviolet which can be equipped with a bandpass filter and corresponding optics for OH* imaging. Finally, a high -definition (1024x1024), 12 -bit monochrome camera is mo unted outside the chamber opposite a collimated light source with two fiber-coupled laser diodes emitting red light

This camera has a bandpass filter corresponding to the illumination source, allowing for determination of soot volume fracti on through an extinction technique previously employed in microgravity research [21 -23]. Unfortunately, because of trade -offs demanded by limited chamber volume and large number of instruments and components, th e collimated light is obstructed substantially by the electrode mesh mount, limiting the utility of this camera for the E-FIELD Flames experiment. Hardware Shortcomings As previously discussed, t he s low response time of the high -voltage power supplies (recommended in the ISRD) did not meet the requirements necessary to achieve the requested time response performance, and as such inhibited determination of the flame’s response time to rapid changes in the electric field strength. The negative and positive high-voltage power supplies were to have been coupled, as described for example in Appendix C of the ISRD. However, switching between the two high-voltage power supplies led to excessive Electrom agnetic Interference (EMI) so the power supplies were completely decoupled, where only one was installed at a time. As such, testing was limited to a single polarity at a time. The imaging for soot volume fraction via light extinction was largely blocked by the bracket holding the electrode mesh, where this was a design trade -off necessitated primarily by ACME’s large number of cameras and other optical instruments. However, Prof. Marshall Long (Yale

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 16 University), who is also an ACME investigator, has an alternate technique for determining the soot volume fraction from ACME’s data camera (DataCam) imaging. The DataCam is unfortunately not as sensitive as had been hoped to the dim microgravity flames. Therefore, the imaging with that camera has typically been at a long exposure time, e.g., 0.65 s, even though it is a video camera capable of 30 frames per second (fps). The principal exception has been when making soot pyrometry or Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) measurements. Between its thickness and the anti-reflection coating, the DataCam’s blue-green filter excessively attenuates the red light making its use undesirable. The filter’s purpose intended was to balance the intensity of the three colors in flame imaging to facilitate pyrometry. The accurac y of the pyrometric temperature measurements was diminished as result of this shortcoming. It is expected that lesser shortcomings will be addressed in the envisioned document describing the ACME hardware in greater detail than presented here. 4. Preliminary Results A.

Changed Test Plans To limit their scope, ACME investigations were limited to a single burner type and the E -FIELD Flames tests identified as required in the ISRD were with a gas -jet burner. However, during the hardware development (and thus prior to spaceflight operations) it was determined that the slow response of the high-voltage power supplies (suggested in the ISRD) inhibited determination of the response time of the flame to the electric field, i.e., objective B. To make up for that science loss, the experiment was permitted to conduct a portion of its test s with ACME’s coflow burner, where such tests had been identified as desired in the ISRD. The gas-jet burner used for the E- FIELD Flames investigation matched the inner tube of the coflow b urner. Therefore, the tests conducted allowed assessment of both the coflow and jet entrainment, where tests with the coflow burner were carried out with and without a coflow. It had also been conceived that some tests would be conducted in which the pol arity of the electric field was varied. However, the switching be tween the two high-voltage power supplies led to excessive Electromagnetic Interference (EMI).

Therefore, the electrical design was altered such that the power supplies were completely decoupled, where only one was installed at a time. This avoided the excessive EMI but prevent ed changes of polarity within a test , as had been planned for the step response procedure described in Table 4.2.2 of the ISRD. It also led to the need for crew to swap the power supplies to enable testing at each polarity. To be clear, these significant changes to the experiment were made prior to the spaceflight operations where the decisions were made by the project management to manage the budget and schedule. In addition to the above hardware -driven changes to the test matrix, a series of other smaller changes ensued as choices for more consistent scientific outcomes were sought. All adjustments were based on finding more effective ways to utilize the space ti me experiments. The change history included the following.

September 2017: Changed tests with 30% CH4 to 40% CH4 - This change occurred because ground testing with the coflow burner indicated that the more dilute methane flames were not stable at similar conditions. Therefore, to ensure stable starting co nditions, the slightly higher fuel concentration was chosen. January 2018: Changed tests with 80% CH4 to 70% CH4 - This modification was made in order to better span the dilution range ; we decided that changes of 30% dilution in two steps (i.e., 40%, 70%, 100%) was more consistent. December 2017: Added parameters to the draft script (i.e., software) - Parameters were added to make it convenient to adjust the P hotomultiplier Tube (PMT) gains and thus maintain useful PMT signal strengths over the wide range of flame conditions.

Parameters were also added to provide more flexibility in the step response script, where independent specification of on and off step durations was implemented so that testing wasn’t restricted to square waves. Before operation in 2018: Added script parameters for the initialize voltage and duration - The parameters were helpful in clearly defining the starting point for the electric field strength. During operation in 2018: Took actions to improve gas flow performance - A nitrogen ( N2) priming time was added to the script to allow the flow to stabilize . Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance was improved by remote adjustment of the cracking and Proportional, Integral, and Derivative (PID) settings. During operation in 2018: Implemented improved control of the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) settings - More detailed camera settings were added to the script . This importantly included specification for camera bracketing to allow photography with a set of exposure times.

All of these changes gave more control over the camera and improved the data quality; the changes to camera settings were designed to help get images over a wide dynamic range (where part of the flame was bright with soot and other parts were dim). The bracketing was only partly successful as the hardware was unable to maintain reliable shutter times when the request was shorter than the maximum framing rate of the camera, but the brackets were effective when long exposures were used. During operation in 2018: Did not use open loop and step response script - During testing we discovered that the standard sweep and ramp scripts could be use d to provide the kind of information that would have been possible wi th the open loop and step scripts because of the hardware limitations on the power supplies described earlier. That is, the time response and single polarity features of the power suppli es meant that a creative sweep design could mimic what would be obtained for a single target voltage with fixed step duration. (a) Setting the electric field to a zero voltage in the step response procedure deactivated the High-Voltage Power Supply (HVPS) between steps.

The recovery time of the HVPS between two steps during shut offs is more than two seconds, while there is limited fuel flow time (999 seconds without resetting it by evacuating the chamber). Hence, testing the flame response

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 18 time to various sudden electric field changes in voltage would require more than 20 seconds of precious fuel time for 10 voltages (for example). If there are 10 test points planned for the test day, the recovery time alone will consume more than 200 seconds of the fuel time. These numbers neglect the time required for the fuel to fill the lines from the bottle , which is another 20-30 seconds depending on the tes t points. These facts would lead to the actual experiment duration being cut by half. Therefore, after evaluating the trade off, we made the decision to not use step response procedure to save the valuable fuel time and we instead expanded the voltage sweep tests. As a future remedy, we would conduct step response tests by using a low non-zero voltage instead of turning off the HVPS. Overview of Experiment Test Operations The narrative description of the operations is from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of the following conference paper: Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. See the paper itself for the references, etc. as they are not included in this report. As a minor note, the size of some figures was adjusted in this report, but none were cropped. The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Thus far, ACME’s activity has included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities. Most often the astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips. In the latter case, the igniter tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the crew already has changes to make changes in the interior of the insert.

While these activities may seem mundane, the crew play a critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment. As an extreme example, there were crew activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. In contrast, only two crew days were required to reconfigure the hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner. Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the testing. The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console.

Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many pre- and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and e vening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM. A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks. On intervening weekdays, the image data is downlinked a nd the crew often swap one or both gas bottles. Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2 -shift day for the RO and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew activity. As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week. A team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console s taff, and the daily operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing.

The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding. In the case of E -FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters. That team does not see t he telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e -mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Pa yload Operations Center (GIPOC). While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files. In advance of the test day, the

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 20 UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in th e voltage sweep script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings. It i s also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low rate results from several unavoidable factors. After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz nonimaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team. A small sample of images are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples. The review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for t he given flame conditions.

After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed. Midway through a day’s E -FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only conducted when b oth Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) System. Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic communication outages with a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite to another) or can last as long as 30 minutes. A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis. The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material flammability. That follow -on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing.

Although it requires additional crew time, these allotments are split into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from testing for careful review of the early results so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of their second round. This paper reports on early results from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. While nitrogen is available fr om the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests. For E -FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010. At that time, NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited obj ectives rather than comprehensive experiments. As such, the general target was 50 tests per experiment. For most ACME experimen ts, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber.

This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing). The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion chamber. Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant). For E -FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 10 tests typically completed per day. Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, such as the video downlink, are planned for a limited numbe r of hours. When necessary for the

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 21 research, NASA does have continuous 24 -hour/day operations for some non -CIR experiments. But as discussed, the ACME tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is almost always limited to the planned durations. Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on -orbit hardware can store a limited amount of data. More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two shift transfer and downlink day. Therefore, tests da ys are limited to this amount of data, where image data from select cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge. Nonetheless, the limit sometimes forces decisions to abandon recorded images. This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME experiments are conducted. Their complexity makes the flame conditions seem trivial in comparison. It is a simple coflow flame, with just a small jet of fuel surrounded by a weak coflow of ‘air’ which also fills the chamber, but where tests are also conducted with no coflow.

A test includes starting the gas flows to prime the system, energizing the igniter to initiate a flame, retracting the igniter, and allowing the flame to steady slightly before energizing the electric field to its initial value. The flame is again allowed to steady before beginning a voltage sweep over a specified range with steps or smooth ramps of specified voltage changes and durations. The sweep can be in one direction or can include cycles of sweeps. After each test, a duplicate field sweep is made to ensure that there are no current leaks, i.e., other than the ion current through the flame. The first phase tests in E -FIELD Flames em ploy the coflow burner geometry shown in Figure 4, with the fuel tube extending slightly above the burner surface. The results shown in this paper are for tests conducted with 100% methane in a chamber atmosphere and coflow (when used) of synthetic ‘air’ (i.e., 21/79 oxygen/nitrogen by volume) at a nominal pressure of 100 kPa. The mesh is held at a negative potential relative to the burner in these tests. The sweeps shown in this paper extend to at least -7 kV, where the voltage is increased in small steps (e.g., of 100 V) lasting 1-2 seconds.
