Pyrometry on the simple gas jet tube could give simi-lar information when the view of the fuel tube is unobstructed. 2.3 Science Data End Products Having defined the objectives and the experimental approach of this investigation it is now possible to define a group of final data products that is sufficient to fulfill each ob-jective. Final data products are the graphs, analyses, and figures that will be reported in the archival literature. These final data products are referred to as the “Science Data End Products” (SDEP). The science requirements and the experiment success criteria de-scribed below are developed from this list of SDEP. Before defining the SDEP, we re-view briefly the independent (or manipulated) variables and the dependent (or respond-ing) variables that will form the raw data from the experiment. A description of the SDEP then follows. 2.3.1 Independent Variables Co-flow condition (i.e., burner type) – two types of burners are used.

A simple gas jet burner that has no co-flowing gas and a co-flow burner that includes an annular sheet of oxidizer flow around the inner circular cross-section fuel jet. The co-flow condition af-fects the relative importance of the ion-driven wind relative to the forced convection in controlling flame behavior and can produce a steady lifted flame. Both burners have a large 1-g data foundation; the former with and without electric fields (e.g., [8,9,33]) and the latter without electrical effects but with comprehensive modeling and detailed diag-nostics (e.g., [49-51]). There are two gas jet flame burners (without coflow) to be used, the only difference being their diameter. One matches the current 1-g jet flame studies and the other (desired) matches the fuel tube of the co-flow burner so that direct compari-sons can be made with regard to any changes in entrainment affected by the co-flow an-nulus. We will also run experiments (desired) using the co-flow burner but without any co-flowing gas because entrainment effects will be different for flames in this configuration compared to the simple gas-jet flames even when the fuel tube has the same diameter.

Fuel type – two fuels: methane and ethylene are used. The former is a low sooting fuel with a low C/H ratio of 0.25. This fuel is predicted to produce a clean burning flame with relatively low ion production and ion driven wind strength. It also has the broadest earth gravity data set associated with electrical aspects of flames. Ethylene is well-known to have high sooting tendencies, with a C/H ratio of 0.5. Its higher carbon content also pro-duces higher ion production and larger potential for ion driven winds. This fuel will al-low broad exploration of the potential for electric fields to control flame soot. Our earth gravity studies confirm that the two proposed fuels behave differently (e.g., [9]). These two fuels are also those being proposed for the CLD Flame experiment (with the same coflow of air) allowing comparisons with flames not influenced by electric fields.

28 Total flow rate of fuel (including inert) – the total fuel flow rate sets the exit jet velocity and thereby the relative importance between jet momentum and ion driven convection. The electrical effects will dominate under conditions of low ejection momentum. How-ever, in the co-flow burner, even when the exit jet velocity is fairly high the momentum match between the fuel stream and the co-flow sheath means that the cross flow momen-tum can be low, so radial electrical influences may still be important. This total flow rate parameter also controls the liftoff height of the flame. Dilution with inert (nitrogen) of fuel – ion production mechanisms predict higher concen-trations of chemi-ions under conditions that create higher concentrations of oxygen radi-cal. In a premixed flame, this variable can be manipulated by adjusting the equivalence ratio and reducing the flame temperature. In a simple non-premixed flame, however, the reaction zone coincides with the stoichiometric condition and so dilution of the fuel with an inert can serve this purpose. In addition, dilution with an inert can weaken the flame by reducing the heat release rate per unit of fuel inlet flow mass.

At their limit, these flames are most susceptible to the forcing flows and entrainment that can be driven by flame ions. Voltage (V), polarity, and distance between electrodes – as shown in Section 1, the ion wind body force is a direct function of electric field strength and ion concentration. The electric field strength is a function of voltage and distance between the electrodes, as well as any space charge effects. Switching the polarity of the voltage source is important for changing the role of charge carriers during electric field forcing of flames. The direction of the ion driven wind does not always change dramatically with electric field polarity because the wind generally flows in the direction of the most distant electrode. This in-teresting uni-directionality occurs because the active ion polarity switches to accommo-date the change in field. That is, the ion wind is driven either by negative ions produced by electron attachment to neutrals beyond the flame or H3O+ ions surviving beyond the flame. Because their distance to the electrode is generally short, the oppositely charged ions or electrons do not create a significant opposing wind.

This behavior may not hold when the flame is lifted a substantial distance from the burner surface. Even if the wind direction does not change, however, its strength changes substantially because of the rela-tive concentration and mobility differences between the ion species responsible. In addi-tion, direct effects on charged species within the reaction zone will be different for differ-ent polarities. We have observed clear indications of these directional wind changes in microgravity from our recent results obtained in the 2.2 s drop tower. 2.3.2 Dependent Variables Chemi-ion current (I) – the ion current is a primary indicator of chemi-ionization in the flame, and varies depending on flame character, reaction zone size, and combustion in-tensity (heat release rate). This is a global measurement of current flowing through the shunt resistor. A current measurement without the flame present provides the baseline leak current and ensures that there is no corona discharge or conducting pathway contrib-uting to the measured current. Our 1-g studies show that the experimental configuration

29 described previously has essentially zero leakage current. Excessive leakage current with no flame may indicate significant soot buildup and be an indicator of cleaning required. Flame shape and size – in order to determine the effects of ion wind on the reaction zone, images of the flame are needed. Images of the flame reveal the flame area, provide evi-dence of combustion intensity, identify locations of soot formation, and show how the ion wind (local convection) changes the flame shape for the various input flame parameters and electric field strength. These line-of-sight integrated images will be Abel-inverted to provide the true reaction interface size and location. Color video images provide infor-mation regarding the location of luminous soot and the visible reaction zone interface. UV images with a filter for OH* provide a sharp determination of the reaction zone. The images of CH* chemiluminescence (desired) can be related to the local rate of heat re-lease, which also correlates to chemi-ion production. This last measurement is “desired” because the combination of the visible images and the OH* images are expected to pro-vide approximately equivalent information.

Soot volume fraction – quantitative evaluation of the effects of electric fields on soot formation, transport, and burnout require this information over the flame zone. We ex-pect this measurement to be made by extinction followed by Abel deconvolution. Soot volume fraction is also needed to estimate mean soot particle size from the Dushman equation as described at the end of Section 1. Spatially integrated luminosity – Broad spectrum flame luminosity, which includes the chemiluminescence and soot radiation collected over a large solid angle (not imaging) provides a rapid global response variable of how the flame reacts to changes in the elec-tric field. Laboratory studies (see, for example, Figure 1.5 and 1.19) have shown that this luminosity signal can be correlated to flame appearance and ion current. Spatially integrated chemiluminescence (CH*) – CH* chemiluminescence can be related to heat release rate and its collection over a broad solid angle (not imaging) provides a rapid response variable of how the flame reacts to changes in the electric field.

Normal gravity studies have shown that this chemiluminescence signal can be correlated to flame appearance and ion current and can be used as a sensor in controlling and monitoring combustion [30]. Burner temperature (desired) – The temperature of the burner surface, provides the inlet thermal boundary condition of the flow. This temperature is important to show how much the flame interacts thermally with the burner. The burner/flame interaction has been shown to affect flame stability for very small jet flames [48] and it can also change the inlet conditions for coflow flames when the lift-off height is very small. This meas-urement is desired because it is likely that the burner temperature effect is much more significant in 1-g where a rising buoyant plume from off the burner can interact at the flame base. In zero-g, this will not occur and so the effect involves only thermal aspects. Gas temperature in and near the flame (desired) -- Measuring the temperature field be-tween the flame and the electrode shows the shape and structure of the thermal plume. In

30 the jet diffusion flame, 1-g experiments show that this boundary coincides with that of the ion-driven wind region. Schlieren imaging (e.g., as in Figure 1.5) provides an indica-tion of the boundary and distributed temperatures (such as would be provided by shadow deconvolution and soot pyrometry in sooting regions). Unfortunately, laboratory studies have shown that silicon-carbide thin filaments in the flame change the electrical behavior substantially, so we cannot use thin filament pyrometry in soot free regions. The thermal information is valuable however, as it allows the current density, the ion mobility, and thereby the electric body force, to be calculated most accurately. In laboratory studies, for example, we have seen evidence of substantial differences in ion mobility and ion wind depending on the thermal field the ions traverse. In the case of the co-flow flame, the thermal plume is governed by a combination of the ion driven wind and the forced convective flow.

Comparison between the temperature fields with and without the elec-tric field can be used to estimate the ion driven wind contribution in this case, which helps resolve the controversy alluded to earlier regarding the relative importance of chemical and physical effects in electric field resistance to liftoff. These results also al-low comparison with 1-g studies of electric control of heat transfer in flames, as dis-cussed in 1-g by Sandhu and Weinberg [31]. SDEP (Objective B) – time response of flames to electric forcing Time resolved measurements after step changes in voltage are necessary to determine the temporal response of flames to electric forcing.

In particular, the time resolved ion cur-rent, as shown in Figure 1.20, provides the ion flux timescale given by any time delay beyond that of the natural capacitive decay time for the experimental apparatus. In 1-g studies, the system electrical response is dominated by the slow capacitive timescale, which may also be the case in microgravity. Time resolved measurements of spatially integrated luminosity (including soot) and CH* filtered light from the flame in concert with the ion current measurement monitor changes in the flame behavior for comparison with the capacitive timescale. As shown in Figure 1.19, the steady-state flame luminosity changes with electric field. The timescale of this change is a combination of any rapid chemi-ion transport effects and the slower convective timescale effects arising from changes in the ion driven wind. Computational and experimental studies show that at 1-g, the convective effects can require hundreds of milliseconds to first influence the flame and a longer time to reach quasi-steady state (e.g., [52]). The longer secondary timescale response appears to result from the development of a quasi-steady convective flowfield driven by ions.

Our recent drop tower microgravity tests show that the time response be-havior is significantly different in zero-g, with less dependence on the timescales associ-ated with buoyant flows. In addition, by comparing the broadband luminosity response to that of the CH*, it will be possible to separate the soot development timescale from the ion flux timescale and from the fluid/chemical timescale in the electrically driven flame. Luminosity timescale comparisons between different flame conditions will characterize these dynamics. SDEP (Objective D) – electric field sensing and control of near-limit flames There are two main elements to this objective. One is to use the ion current as a sensor for identifying the incipient extinguishment of lifted flames and the other is to increase the flame’s resistance to blowoff. Diffusion flames near their blowoff limit in 1-g gener-ally exhibit an unstable fluctuation just before extinguishing. The fluctuation appears in the chemiluminescence, in the location of the flame base (liftoff height), and in the chemi-ion current.

The data products are, therefore, the mean and RMS ion current at low voltages as functions of fuel flow rate and inert dilution in the fuel. Near limit flames are identified from data in Objective A where the fuel flow rate and the inert con-centration are increased to flame extinguishment. Extended time at microgravity is nec-essary for these experiments because the blowoff process is stochastic and can involve long periods of fluctuation. The second element of this objective is open-loop control, using the ion driven wind to restabilize near-limit co-flow flames. This phenomenon has been observed by Won, et al. [46,47] as manifested by a resistance to flame lifting. They find, for example, that a higher velocity is needed to maintain a fixed liftoff height when the flame is under the influence of an electric field. There is a question, however, whether the effect is simply due to an additive ion wind to the jet flow or if there is a more subtle influence of local

34 mixing that changes the flame propagation velocity. By measuring the liftoff height, the fuel flow rate, and the ion current, it is possible to distinguish these influences. For ex-ample, a substantial change in liftoff height accompanied by a modest ion wind (deter-mined from the ion current and flame surface area) relative to the flow rate would suggest a local mixing effect whereas when a larger ion wind is involved we would likely identify a broader mean flowfield influence. Extended microgravity conditions are necessary to establish the relationship between electric fields and liftoff height behavior because the flame’s liftoff height can oscillate slowly for several cycles before it either blows off or reattaches [54].

Hence, we begin by mapping the electrical response of a wide range of flames and then concen-trate on particular conditions of interest, particularly those near limit and transition condi-tions in diffusion flames. For example, the saturated ion current is a characteristic of the carbon flux into the flame so long as the flame character does not change. As the ion driven wind begins to influence the reaction zone, the saturation current can change dra-matically. We are interested in the flame condition near this transition. Similarly, a lifted diffusion flame near its blowoff condition is sensitive to mixing at the flame anchor point. Electric fields acting on such flames can exert large influence because they can affect the local mixing behavior. We are interested, therefore, in these near-limit flame conditions. Finally, the role of electric fields on soot formation will be most dramatic under condi-tions where the ion driven wind has the largest influence on flow residence time (or on ion residence time, if chemical effects are found important) in sooting flames.

The explanation of the knowledge gaps associated with electric field effects in diffusion flames have been described in the foregoing sections. It is worth making some general statements in this regard, however, to summarize. The goal of this zero-gravity study is

35 to understand chemi-ionization behavior and the resulting ion driven winds sufficiently well so that electrical properties of flames can be used to characterize (by monitoring ion current) and control them (via direct chemical or local convective influences). Electric field effects on flames have been documented for decades (even centuries), but flames in 1-g all include buoyancy influences. For flames near transitions and limits, buoyant in-fluences always confound any understanding of the role of ion driven winds in using electric fields to characterize and manipulate flames. The proposed study removes this confounding influence and allows definitive measurement and analysis of the electric field effects on sooting, saturation current, and dilution on coflow and jet diffusion flames. 36 2.5 Justification for Extended-Duration Microgravity As described in the Background and Overview (Section 1.1), electric field effects and buoyancy effects have been found to be of the same order of magnitude. In addition, in some cases, raising the flame temperature will increase the O atom concentration, thereby increasing the ion production rate and increasing the response to an electric field. At the same time, increasing temperature increases the buoyancy effect, making it difficult to separate ion wind effects from buoyancy. In the zero-g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and develop sufficient understanding to predict the response of flames to electric fields under all conditions. For electrically driven flames, microgravity is also necessary to create conditions that produce symmetric flames suit-able for Abel inversion and steady-state analysis. While in general natural convection can enhance symmetry relative to non-buoyant flames, a flame at 1-g in an electric wind experiences buoyancy as a disruptive influence on symmetry.

Even when buoyancy effects can be minimized, we have found that there are periodic disturbances that disrupt the ideal symmetry. Highly symmetric conditions of extended microgravity are also useful for numerically simulating these various effects by our electroki-netic model or more comprehensively by others. Finally, in order to fully evaluate the potential for control, it is important to examine the effects separately. An example of the importance of microgravity for the electric field effects studies is shown in Figure 2.6. This figure compares the capillary flame used for 1-g experiments (which has some simi-larities to the jet-flame companion study) when it is oriented vertically to when it is ori-ented horizontally relative to gravity. These flames behave differently in shape, size, and ion production demonstrating the substantial influence played by buoyancy even in the relatively small capillary flames. Gravity effects in the co-flow flames have been de-scribed in the SRD for the CLD Flame experiment, and the same influences will be im-portant when we apply electric fields.

Only in extended microgravity will it be possible to separate the ion driven wind effects from buoyant wind effects. Extended run times are crucial for all of the studies because the timescales involved ex-tend beyond drop tower capabilities and the microgravity quality required for symmetry and stability exceeds aircraft microgravity. The electric-field flame interaction tests car-ried out in the NASA Glenn 2.2 Second Drop T ower tests by Yuan and Hegde [55] showed that the flame did not appear to reach steady state during the 2.2 sec. drop. Furthermore, their results showed substantial differences in flame shape between cases Figure 2.6. Effect of orientation on combustion of 1.8 mm jet diffusion flames in 1-g.

37 thermore, their results showed substantial differences in flame shape between cases where the electric field was activated half-way through the drop and at the beginning of the drop, again suggesting that steady state was not achieved. Although, we varied the range of tests performed at the Drop Tower, our research group encountered similar ob-stacles. Drop times were insufficient to achieve a steady flame after voltage changes in one direction. Additionally, we were unable to capture the removal of soot from the igni-tion event and the subsequent response of the flame to the electric field. Furthermore, testing has shown path dependence in the response time of the flame when subjected to step voltages of varying polarities. Properly mapping the steady-state ion current as a function of applied voltage requires that the flame stabilize at each applied voltage. Gen-erally speaking, the timescale of flame property changes (which includes chemi-ionization) is dominated by convection (length scale/velocity), which is on the order of 0.1 second.

In order to ensure quasi-steady conditions of the VI characteristics for a sin-gle flame configuration with some fidelity (e.g., 50 steps of 200 V each, with 2 seconds between steps for settling after the change), requires more than 100 seconds of continu-ous high quality microgravity. Each condition and voltage cannot be run individually (i.e, with separate drop tests) because the 2 second settling time requires that the flame begin at a settled initial condition before taking another relatively small voltage step. If we tried to step to the initial condition, allow settling, take the base measurement, then step the voltage and again wait the required settling time, we would exceed 5 seconds for each test in nearly all cases. To run a return voltage sweep to examine hysteresis might take a further 100 seconds. Furthermore, these times are based on 1-g results which un-der low ion wind conditions are likely to be faster than occurs in zero-gravity since their the convective timescales can be substantially smaller (under low electric field forcing conditions, for example).

Understanding the electric field effects on soot is another area that requires high quality zero gravity timescales longer than is available in drop towers. A variety of zero gravity diffusion flame experience has shown that quasi-steady soot formation requires many seconds [22,56,57]. The long duration is necessary since we are exploring the relative importance of residence time modification of these processes in these flames. In addi-tion, as mentioned above, instabilities and extinction behavior in near-limit flames gener-ally have a stochastic character so that relatively long observation times are needed to quantify electric field effects. For example, lifted flames in electric fields can exhibit an oscillatory behavior where they alternately approach and recede from the burner exit until they finally reattach. Tens of seconds for this process is not unusual. Extended micro-gravity conditions will clarify the role of electric fields (via ion winds) on stability limits of flames.

38 3. EXPERIMENT REQUIREMENTS 3.1 Requirements Discussion This section does not include any requirements, but instead describes their importance in achieving the experiment objectives. The requirements have been incorporated into the ACME-SRD-001 Integrated Science Requirements. 3.1.1 Ambient Environment The experiments are to be conducted in the chamber described in the combined ACME science requirements. The gas fill for the gas jet tests and the coflow gas for the coflow burner tests is nominally nitrogen (79%) and oxygen (21%) by volume. For the coflow burner tests, the fill gas is as specified in the CLD Flame experiment SRD (as is the com-position of the co-flow gas). Oxygen composition should not fall below 19% during the tests. Oxygen makeup gas can be added as it is consumed to maintain an appropriate overall oxygen concentration. The makeup oxygen is based on the assumption of com-plete combustion of the fuel flowing into the system. Because there is no direct oxygen concentration measurement, we expect that the chamber will be flushed and refilled ap-proximately every 7-8 tests based on how much uncertainty has developed regarding the ambient oxygen concentration.

We want to ensure that the oxygen level does not leave the window between 19 and 21%. 3.1.2 Burner Material The gas-jet and coflow burners shall be electrically conductive and able to withstand a constant temperature of 1000 ºC. The burner temperature requirements reflect the maxi-mum temperature observed at the burner tips in past laboratory 1-g experiments. The burner material requirement stems from the necessity of the burners to serve as electrodes in the high voltage circuit. Figure 2.4 illustrates how the burners complete the electrical pathway for measuring the flame’s ion current by forcing electric current into a shunt re-sistor for measurement. The magnitude of the current is simply determined with Ohm’s law and dividing the voltage drop across the resistor by the known value of the resistor. 3.1.3 Burners Two different burner types are to be used. One is the simple gas jet burner. The second type is the coflow burner as specified in the CLD Flame experiment SRD.

Two different nozzle diameters are included (one required and one desired) for the gas-jet burner to vary the exit velocity of the fuel mixture without altering the flow rates specified in each experimental test series and to match prior 1-g studies. The precise dimensions of all burner nozzles must be known to ensure accurate velocity computations and conditions for later numerical simulations by others if desired.

39 3.1.4 Electric Field The electric field shall be produced between a copper mesh electrode and the burner. Copper mesh is an ideal electrode because its open surface area allows combustion gases to flow through preventing interaction with the flame. The range of mesh screen densities in the ACME science requirements have been used successfully in past experiments. Another desired capability is to place the mesh electrode at a range of axial positions to achieve a desirable charge distribution in the electric field while preventing contact be-tween the flame and the mesh. If the flame and mesh come into contact while the electric field is active, a short circuit will result, and the flame will allow electric current to flow between the burner and mesh electrode. Because the flame height and lift-off heights will vary across the two burners and the vast experimental conditions, variable positioning is highly desirable. A preliminary estimate of coflow burner lift-off heights suggests that the mesh be placed approximately 5 cm away from the burner nozzle, preferably at two different heights no less than 1 cm apart.

The mesh diameter should be no less than 8 cm to collect sufficient ion current from the flame based on our electrokinetic calculations of ion flow. The electric field potential should be controllable in 50V or smaller increments and should be able to reach 10kV across the electrode space for both polarities. 3.1.5 Ion Current Measurement The proposed method of ion current measurement involves measuring the voltage across a shunt resistor connected between the burner and the high voltage ground. Based on our past experiments, the resistor and data acquisition system should have a resolution better than 0.05 microamperes with an expected maximum current of 25 microamperes. For example, we suggest that the shunt resistor value shall be 100 kΩ, and will measure cur-rents on the order of microamperes. The resulting voltage will be on the order of 0.1 Volt with an expected range of ± 4 Volts to be read by a 12-bit A/D converter. The resistor tolerance should better than or equal to ± 0.1%, and have the lowest possible temperature coefficient for precise measurements.

The resistor should also be placed sufficiently far from the burners to prevent changes in the resistance value due to heat conduction through the connecting wire. To ensure that the total ion current is measured at the shunt resistor, it is required that the mesh electrode and burner be electrically isolated to prevent current leakage. Current leakage should be less than 25 nanoamps at maximum voltage. The mesh electrode should withstand +/- 20kV without breaking down. In addition, it is suggested that a cop-per ring with a cross-sectional diameter of 2-3 mm be soldered to the perimeter of the mesh to reduce the likelihood of break down at the tips of the mesh wires at high voltages.

40 3.1.6 Flame Imaging and Chemiluminescence Measurements Color images of the flame will reveal the flame area, provide evidence of combustion in-tensity, identify locations of soot formation, and show how the ion wind (local convec-tion) changes the flame shape for the various input flame parameters and electric field strength. UV images with a filter for OH* are required to provide a sharp determination of the reaction zone. Images of CH* chemiluminescence are desired for observing spatial changes in heat release rate due to electric field actuation, and may also be used as a sen-sor for quantifying the electric field control effect. Density imaging is highly desired as this provides a secondary indication of the reaction zone location but more importantly shows the path of the convected hot gases driven by the ion wind for comparison with our electrokinetic modeling. It is also possible to extract temperature from density images in the soot-free regions of the flame, which is valuable for ascertaining electrical mobility. Density images should be at no less than 15 Hz.

3.1.7 Soot Measurements Soot volume fraction and soot temperature are needed to show the effects of electric fields on the location, mean size, and amount of soot in the flames. Soot temperature provides information regarding the thermal field in highly sooting regions of the flame. The mean size of the soot is to be determined from assessing the presumed thermionic current from the soot. The ion current is related to soot surface area and so the mean size can be determined from the ratio of soot volume to soot area.

41 3.2 Operational Sequence As described in Section 2, the E-FIELD experiment consists of 4 objectives correspond-ing to 4 series of tests using 2 different diffusion flame burner configurations. The first three test series provide the key fundamental information regarding the electrical charac-ter of diffusion flames and the influence of electric fields on soot formation; the final se-ries focuses on electric field sensing and control of flames. General Operations -- preparatory actions -- before any of the electric field experiments, the high voltage mesh should be installed (or moved into position). Leak current should be measured by sweeping the voltage from 0 to 10kV and 0 to -10kV with no flame pre-sent. A steep rise in current under these conditions indicates corona discharge and sets the upper limit on the potential. The test sequence involves a complete repeat voltage sweep with no flame to provide a point-by-point current leak measurement. A similar sweep should be completed following flame extinguishment at the end of a test set. The leak current allows a baseline for higher precision in the flame ion current determination.

In addition, excessive leak current at relatively low voltage may indicate electron emission from carbon buildup on the gas jet flame tip. If the leak current exceeds 10% of the flame ion current, cleaning of the gas jet tip is requested. Cleaning consists of a manual wiping or possibly burning off the carbon with a modified flame condition. We expect this to be a rare request, but the continuous monitor of flameless ion current provides a reliable in-situ monitor. We assume that the chamber will be emptied and refilled approximately every 7-8 tests to minimize the oxygen concentration uncertainty in the test chamber. We further assume that our test series will start with the co-flow burner if it is already in-stalled to minimize replacement time. After the co-flow experiments, a gas jet burner would be installed. The gas jet flame experiments duplicate our laboratory-based studies. The exact times for settling and voltage steps may vary (they should be reconfigurable from the ground), but a nominal expected operational sequence for one chamber fill and the key measurement data sets are shown below.

(A) Voltage Sweep – collection of VI curves (or VCC curves) -- where the voltage is swept from 0-±4kV (or until flame blowout) and the ion current is monitored and re-corded. The sweep should be a series of discrete steps, where a settling time is allowed after each voltage change. At the same time, color and OH* video records the flame shape and luminosity (both broadband flame and soot luminosity and OH* chemilumi-nescence) throughout the sweep. Discrete steps in the sweep allow a system settling time and higher voltage resolution at some parts of the curve to effectively map the current transition points. A typical step sweep might comprise: 15 second ignition & stabiliza-tion; 100 V/step, 0.5 sec settle between steps, and a 0.3 sec. ion current measurement at each point, to ±5kV or blowout. It is important to keep in mind that the short measuring time is only possible because the changes are developing from a prior quasi-steady condi-tion. If tests were attempted with a pair of voltage steps from a zero voltage initial condi-tion (as in a drop test, for example), the settling time would more than double. Blowout can be detected by a sharp drop in ion current.

49 3.5 Post-Flight Data Analysis The post-flight data analysis will use many of the tools and follow many of the proce-dures established in our 1-g experiments, as shown in Section 1. In particular, we will employ electrokinetic modeling based on measured flame shapes and total ion currents, along with established relationships between flame area and ion flux to evaluate the links between flame behavior and chemi-ionization. Analysis of test results will be conducted both concurrently and at the conclusion of the flight experiment. Concurrent analysis is required at key points in the E-FIELD Flames test matrix to determine the specific test conditions and parameters necessary for a following set of related tests. Specifically, an analysis of ion current saturation, luminosity, and blowout will be conducted at the con-clusion of the voltage sweep test sets (described in Section 3.2) to determine the best flow rate and nominal voltage range for soot effect tests and open-loop control tests. An analy-sis of step response experiments is also required to determine time constants for modeling the flame and designing the control parameters for open-loop experiments.

Finally, an analysis of the near-limit test results in the E-FIELD Flames test matrix (and, desirably, the results of CLD Flame near-limit experiments) is required to determine the flow rate and mixtures that are most suitable for the stability experiments. It is important to note that while tentative conditions for soot effects and control tests have already been identi-fied in the test matrix, the ability to select conditions based on analysis of previous tests will enhance the probability of success, and will ultimately maximize the value of the science product. The final analysis of all experimental data will be conducted at the conclusion of the flight experiment until each objective (listed in Section 2.1) is achieved. Video, imagery (luminosity), thermal field information, and ion current data will be analyzed together to evaluate the ion wind strength, ion flux, ion production rate per unit carbon, and effects of electric fields on soot—completing Objectives A and C. Ion concentration will be de-termined from the saturation ion current: the point where ion collection and production are equal.

The mobility can be determined from numerical methods previously discussed in Section 1 (see, for example, Figure 1.9) and in reference [52]. Once mobility is deter-mined, we can ascertain the convective effects on the flame due to electricity. One feature of the co-flow burner which makes this test unique is that axial convection on the flame is dominated by the forced flow (buoyant convection is removed). Hence, by reducing exit flow velocity and adjusting the magnitude of the electric potential at the mesh, it is possible to create an equivalent local flow velocity with different electrical effects. Adjustable flow configurations such as these would enable us to determine whether the electrical effects on soot are residence time based or chemical in nature. Open loop control measurements allow us to understand the dominant factor in flame re-attachment and extended blowout limits: is it the mean ion wind or mixing effects at the base? Analysis of the variation in ion current and luminosity time response in the step voltage experiments will be conducted to distinguish chemical effects of the electric field

50 from diffusion and ion wind since their timescales are sufficiently well separated. This analysis will fulfill Objective B. Objective D will be achieved by analyzing the effective-ness of the electric field to vary soot luminosity, vary lift-off heights, and delay extinction of a near-limit flame. All analyses completed during and after the flight experiment will be documented in anticipation for future disclosure.

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 1 16 Dec. 2020 30-day Operational Accomplishments Report … for the International Space Station (ISS) Increment 63 ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments s-Flame Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames The s-Flame investigation is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The first round of s-Flame tests was conducted during Increments 60 and 61, wh ile the second round was conducted fully within Increment 63. There were no tests conducted in Increment 62 because of limited crew availability. Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project Scientist, who is the primary contact for s-Flame and ACME information. Principal Investigator (PI): Prof. C.K. (Ed) Law, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ Co-Investigator (Co-I): Prof. Stephen D. Tse, Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ Lead collaborator: Dr. Vladimir V. Gubernov, P.N.

Lebedev Physical Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences , Moscow, Russia NASA Project Scientist (PS): Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH I. Introduction Tests for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment were conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The purpose of s-Flame is to advance the ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction and instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames. The results may contribute to the development of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth. The spherical flames are ignited at non -steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally towards steady-state or extinction. Tests are conducted with various inert diluents in both the fuel and chamber (oxidizer) atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames.

One experimental objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative and chemical kinetic extinction, i.e., where the flame extinguishes from radiative heat loss or is “blown out, ” respectively. Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in flames with certain fuel/inert mixtures at near-limit conditions.

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 2 More specifically, s-Flame has the following experimental objectives: A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non -steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot -free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. B. Determine the quasi -steady convective/chemical -kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical -kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot -free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty). A. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number, at near-limit conditions.

As suggested by the experiment’s name, s-Flame features a spherically symmetric diffusion flame, which is generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a still oxygen/inert atmosphere in microgravity. The one-dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mapping and characterization of the motion (e.g., expansion) of spherical diffusion f lames subsequent to ignition and at extinction because of the finite-rate chemistry and radiative heat loss. The study is focused on the thermal radiation, the adequacy of the detailed chemistry and transport submodels used in computational modeling, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries. (2) Studies of the response of cha racteristically sooty flames to ignition, the onset of soot in the expanding flames, the soot radiation, and the soot’s effects on the flame spread, extinction, and instability. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal -gravity studies.

For example, the natural flicker of flame s, which is a buoyancydriven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum -dominated flames, whi ch are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environme nt valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry.

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 3 II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The s -Flame investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on th e modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the test s were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. As expected, no s-Flame tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value.

Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. III. Results A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight A total of 276 flames were ignited for the s-Flame experiment, with 29, 116, and 131 respectively ignited during Increment s 60, 61, and 63 . These numbers neglect some flames which quenched promptly after ignition. In this regard, science testing began at the end of Increment 60 and the first round of tests were completed during Increment 61. No tests were conducted in Increment 62 d ue to a lack of crew time , where the second round of tests were fully conducted during Increment 63. The tests were conducted in two rounds, where the first was conducted in increments 60 and 61 featured 145 flames (nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen (i.e., in the chamber atmosphere) were diluted with nitrogen.

The second round conducted in increment 63 featured 131 flames (nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen were instead diluted with helium. The s-Flame experiment does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are i ndependently conducted with various gaseous fuels, including hydrogen,

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 4 methane, hydrogen/methane blends, and ethylene. These are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is relatively well understood. No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for s-Flame; all of the ISS results were electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME experiments. ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 5 B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 1. Mission anomalies While there were certainly issues with testing discussed in the next section, there were no significant anomalies during s -Flame’s Increment 63 testing. However, anomalies did occur during Increment 60 and 61 which led to corrective act ions and/or make-up testing. 2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data Ignition of the flames presented a significant challenge to the experiment during this increment. All of the flame tests were conducted where the fuel and chamber atmosphere were both diluted with helium rather than the nitrogen used in Increments 60 and 61. The two gases’ properties are dramatically different making comparison testing very desirable for ma nifestation of different phenomena . Helium’s thermal conductivity is notably several times greater than that of nitrogen, so considerably more energy and power was required to ignite the flames.

The power level was slowly increased from test to test unti l ignition was finally achieved on the ninth test, where only seven flames were ignited of the 15 tests conducted on May 11 (20132), the first day for flames in Increment 63. The cautious approach was taken because of concerns that the igniter tip might f ail (i.e., burn out) if too much power was applied. An igniter failure would have likely halted testing for weeks given the need to schedule the commander’s time to replace the igniter tip. After that first test day, the decision was made to have the igniter replaced with a coil rather than loop design which was believed to be more robust because of the thicker wire. Furthermore, the igniter tip had not been replaced in months, and the tips do degrade with time, especially when they are not quickly retracted from the ignited flames. The coil igniter was used successfully but still with caution, where flames were not always ignited successfully. Subsequently, some tests were co nducted in atmosphere with ~30% oxygen (by volume) instead of the planned ~21%. As one would expect, that proved to be helpful for achieving ignition.

But the end result was that some tests were conducted with 21% oxygen, some at 30%, and some at both nominal concentrations. Fortuitously, this mixture of conditions may provide deeper insight into the mechanisms of flame dynamics and response. Tests are also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite, where that occurred , for example, during Increment 61 in tests 19304A4, 19304A6, 19308C1, and 20006A1. That can be corrected by adjusting various test parameters and other settings. In this case, adjustments were subsequently made to the ignition position (e.g., after 19304A4 and 19304A6), the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation (e.g., after 19308C1), and the duration of the igniter activation (e.g., after 20006A1). As another example, failed ignition can result from false ignition detection and deactivation resulting from the combina tion of settings for ignition and detection, e.g., the gain for the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module measuring the OH* chemiluminescence. The latter, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 6 ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum. Testing on June 3 (20155) was cut short due to a combination of issues. The final test was aborted due to an error with an Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU). Consoles needed to be reset for the new increment, and there was an issue with the Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) Control Unit, i.e. the FCU. Rebooting the FCU inadvertently set the valve safety timers to zero, which cannot be reset without venting and refilling the combustion chamber with the intended atmosphere. Those issues combined with an extended loss of commanding prevented further science operations on that day. Therefore, an additional test day ( July 8, i.e., 20190) was added to make up for lost science , e.g., whe re only one test was successfully conducted at ~21% oxygen on June 3. The FCU was off nominal because of a high carrier gas pressure in the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP).

Imaging of the hydrogen flames was often an issue, where they were not apparent or hardly visible to the operations camera and ACME DataCam, where the latter is the primary camera for ACME testing. The testing with the extremely dim flames was limited to that conducted on Dec. 18 (19352), Jan. 24 (20024), June 3 (201 55), and July 8 (20190). This shortcoming unfortunately inhibits assessment of the three -dimensional flame symmetry as the two intensified cameras were opposite of each other. The flow ranges of the selected Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) was found to be a challenge, where it was discovered that the goal of studying both kinetic and radiative extinction was not always satisfactorily achieved because of flow rate constraints. At high flow rates, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner.

In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. When at a small fraction of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during s-Flame testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed from that desired. However, this was not a surprise to those familiar with the hardware. Flow perturbations have been noticed in some s -Flame tests, where ACME’s MFCs used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer have unfortunately not always performed satisfactorily. In tests conducted using the 1 -slpm fuel MFC (where the flow range is on a nitrogen basis), the flow has been seen to overshoot and undershoot when first opening. Small flow irregularities have been most ap parent

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 7 through their effect on the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) measurements, e.g., of OH* and CH* chemiluminescence. A momentary increase in fuel flow, as has occurred in some s-Flame tests, naturally leads to increased light from the flame. The MFCs are tested - without flames - after they are first installed. Adjustments are typically made to (1) the setting that controls when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral- Derivative (PID) settings. This ACME activity has involved significant testing , where there is an assortment of MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gas types. While the MFC adjustments have been beneficial, they have not eliminated all gas flow problems. It was seen in prior ACME testing that nitrogen oscillations (if any) tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre -flow can be used so that such oscillations might end before the flame is ignited. As another measure, the MFCs are re -zeroed prior to each test, where that was another measure adopted in earlier ACME testing.

As mentioned previously, s-Flame tests have sometimes automatically aborted (because of the controlling software script), where that is normally prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter – which is typical for other ACME experiments . As a result, there was little lost other than the available experimental time in the failed test attempt. ACME aborts normally occur because of communication issues with an IPSU, which for example happened for tests 19304A5, 19352D3, 19352P1, 20024N1, and 20024J1. A few other tests aborted because flow rates were accidentally specified outside of the range of the installed mass flow controller(s), where that included for example 19352A1, 19352D2, and 20013 C2. ACME aborts are infrequent, but there are sometimes days when they occur repeatedly as can be seen here. C. Completeness/Quality of Data During Increments 60 and 61, nine days of tests were conducted during which 145 flames were ignited for the first round of testing . In contrast, only 29 tests were specified as required or highly desired in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Documen t (ISRD) for that round.

Therefore, a wealth of data was obtained for this round of testing which featured gaseous fuels diluted by nitrogen. However, there was a significant loss of data. Most importantly, the first fuel bottle appeared to leak on installation (in Increment 60) and later on-orbit testing (in Increment 61) with other hydrogen/methane blends suggests that its fuel mixture would have been ideal for achieving science success. Furthermore, there was significant image data loss on two different test days, specifically Sept. 13 (19256) and Dec. 18 (19352). As a result, those test days were nominally repeated on Jan. 29 (20029) and Jan. 24 (20024), respectively (i.e., in a reversed order). For these reasons, a simple comparison of the total number of flames ignited (145) with that specified as required or highly desired (29) for the first round of testing is somewhat misleading. As discussed in the preceding section, the hydrogen and diluted -hydrogen flames were not apparent or extremely dim in imaging from the operations camera and ACME DataCam. Neglecting that factor, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 8 gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, they are a degradation of the image quality. It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there is not obvio us indication of this ; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). D. Status of Data Analysis [provided by Prof. Stephen Tse, Rutgers U.] Image files are currently being processed. Radial position s of maximum CH* chemiluminescence is being plotted against time. Different radii are being considered and plotted together, as some flames are not completely symmetric. MFC and PMT data are being compared with video images to assess and confirm experimental settings. Radiometer data is being reviewed. Analy ses of the fiber pyrometry data are ongoing. MATLAB code is used to isolate fiber images, which are then color assessed for temperature. Computational simulations with detailed chemistry and transport of the test cases are underway.

Time -dependent simulations will be compared with the time-dependent experimental data , where tracking of the flamefront location is based on chemiluminescent emission . Stea dy-state simulations will produce the Isola curves mapping flame response versus system Damkh öler number for given fuel mixtures. The experimental cases will then be pin -pointed on the computational mapping s to assess whether the experimental conditions are in quasi-steady state or near extinction limits, either kinetic or radiative. Oscillation behavior will be correlated to possible pulsating oscillations found in the simulations. E. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by Prof. Tse and lightly edited by Stocker] The s -Flame experiment utilize s spherically-symmetric diffusion flames and their dynamics and responses to investigate fundamental processes, such as extinction, instability, and soot formation. The tests conducted on 19254 (near the end of Increment 60) revealed that a quasi-steady flame could be attained for extended duration at low flow rate, i.e., 3 cc/s for 20% C2H4/80% N2 (on a volume basis) .

The flame was shut down by the automated system because the burner reached a cut -off temperature of 250°C. Although the flame oscillated near the end of the test, it was likely due to influence of the burner tube. Comparisons with computation simulations will help to clarify the involved processes. For higher flow rates, e.g., 5 -10 cc/s, with the same mixture, radiative extinctions were observed. Generally, the flames showed unstable behavior near the burner tube prior to extinction, likely because o f lack of fuel mixture and heat loss in that region. Other mixtures, e.g., 25% C2H4/75% N2 and 30% C2H4/70% N2, also showed radiative extinctions at higher flow rates. For some cases, the pyrometry fiber interacted with the flame, allowing determination of temperature in on -going analyses. Soot was observed only

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 9 during ignition, which went away as the flame established itself. To assess whether these nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames are non-sooty or sooty, cases were run where mixtures were ignited and established at low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents (e.g., 25 -30% C2H4) and then ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5 -10 cc/s) with higher ethylene contents (e.g., 40 -50% C2H4). The flames all radiatively extinguished, but no sooting was observed. Observations of such radiative extinction behavior at high flow rates is an achievement because such phenomen on was not observed in our ground based studies, given the limited microgravity durations. Radiative reabsorption extends flame size a t extinction. In ISS testing, radiative extinction has been found to be a common event, which was predicted computationally, but not observed previo usly for our flame conditions. The 19256 tests (in Increment 60) were aimed at examining kinetic extinction.

Similar to the radiative extinction cases , sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observe kinetic extinction because a near steady flame needs to be established first, before ramp down in flow rate to find properly the chemical kinetic extinction limit. High flow rate cases (e.g., 13.5 cc/s, 15 cc/s) showed asymmetrical flames which radiatively extinguished. Flow rates were lowered so that quasi-steady flames could be established before ramp down in flow rate. The 15% C2H4 mixtures were not strong enough to sustain a quasi-steady flame at 3 cc/s before ramp down. However, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20-30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions were observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. Radiative extinctions for ramp up cases were also examined. Similarly, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20 -30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and radiative extinctions were observed during ramp up before reaching 8 cc/s. Testing on 19304 investigated 45% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into an air atmosphere. The results indicated that the flow rates specified by the fuel MFC (0.5 slpm) were in the regime of kinetic extinction.

Quasi-steady flames could not be established. Furthermore, larger flow rates could not be provided by the MFC, so observations of radiative extinction could not be achieved. Even with a larger capacity MFC, characteristically larger flames would be expected to be asymmetric. As such, nitrogen-diluted methane flames were planned to be reexamined in increased oxygen atmosphere, i.e., 30% O2/70% N2. Consequently, the 19308 tests investigated nitrogen-diluted methane flames in 30% O2/70% N2 atmosphere. Various methane concentrations from 45% down to 15% were examined. For 45% CH4/55% N2, relatively long duration flames of ~15 s and ~10 s were established at flow rates of 2 cc/s and 3 cc/s, respectively. At larger flow rates of 5 and 9.4 cc/s, the flames expanded to large radii and then extinguished. These flames appeared to demonstrate radiative extinction. Reduction of flow rate from 2 cc/s to 1 cc/s resulted in extinction during ramp down, indicating kinetic extinction.

For 30% CH4/70% N2, flow rates of 3, 5, and 10 cc/s produced flames that expanded to extinction (assumed radiatively); while reduction of flow rate from 3 to 1 cc/s resulted in presumably kinetic extinction during ramp down. For 25% CH4/75% N2, flow rates of 5 and 10 cc/s

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 10 yielded flames that expanded to extinction. For 20% CH4/80% N2, constant flow rate of 10 cc/s created a flame that expanded until extinction (assumed radiatively) ; while reduction of flow rate from 10 cc/s to 1 cc/s resulted in wavering extinction during ramp down, suggesting kinetic ex tinction. For 15% CH4/85% N2, flames were ignited, but extinguished very quickly. These tests of 19308 suggest that they could manifest both radiative and kinetic extinction for the conditions specified. The 19352 tests examined various concentrations of H2 (45%-70%) diluted with N2 issuing into air. The installed fuel MFC had a maximum output of 0.1 slpm, which unfortunately provided a less-than-sufficient flow range where its use may have precluded the study of radiative extinction corresponding to larger flame sizes. Imaging the diluted hydrogen flames was a challenge, especially since the hobj image files from the ACME DataCam were mis-formatted.

Furthermore, little could be seen in the analog ops imaging, e.g., where it, like the DataCam and Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, cannot image the ultraviolet OH* flame emission (at 310 nm). Analysis of images from the Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL -UV) camera and its OH* filter is ongoing. And as one might expect, little could be seen with the CFI intensified camera using its broadband CH2O filter. Quasi-steady flames seem to be present at low flow rates (e.g. , 2.4 cc/s for 70% H2), as inferred from PMT, pyrometry fiber emission, and b urner temperature observations. Kinetic extinction seems to occur a s the flow rate is ramped down. There were various problems with the IPSU and some tests aborted. Using the 100% H2 bottle with a higher flow rate MFC was later performed for tests of 20024 (see below), which was a make-up test day added because of the mis-formatting of the DataCam image files. The tests conducted on 20006, using the 44.4% H2/55.6% CH4 bottle, examined 20% H2/25% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Flames extinguished, some with wavy oscillating behavior prior to extinction.

However, it seems that even for very small flow rates, e.g., 2 cc/s, extinction was by the radiative mechanism during flame expansion. There was too little parameter room in terms of flow rate and burner size to identify conclusively kinetic extinction durin g ramp down for these mixtures. In short, radiative extinction (with local flame extinction and re -ignition seemed to occur prior to ultimate extinguishment) during flame expansion after ignition was observed. However, it is unclear whether ramping down the flow rate resulted in kinetic extinction. Detailed analyses of the data are needed. The various cameras seemed to capture the tests well. The 20013 tests, which used the 66.7% H2/33.3% CH4 bottle, mainly investigated 30% H2/15% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Radiative extinction was difficult to identify conclusively because flames with larger flow rates, e.g. 15 cc/s, seemed to last, although with patchy ex tinction areas, until time out. Larger flow rates could not be examined either because of limited MFC range or distorted flame shape cause by burner limitations at high flow rat es.

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 11 The 20024 tests using the 100% H2 bottle repeated and augmented conditions for those of 19352 where the 0.1-slpm fuel MFC range was too low to examine radiative extinction and the analog and intensified cameras did not pick up t he flame images at all or well. Here, the 0.5-slpm fuel MFC was used and only a fused silica filter was used for the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera. 45%-15% H2/N2 balance mixtures were investigated. The flames at high flow rates, e.g., 10 cc/s, did not extinguish, appearing quasi-steady until time out. The pyrometry fibers glowed, perhaps making good flamestructure measurements, which will be evaluated subsequently. The flames seemed to extinguish during ramp down, but further analysis is needed to assess kinetic extinction. The tests conducted on 20029 used 50% C2H4/50% N2 and repeated and augment ed conditions of 19256, when the images were not good. Again, the results indicated both kinetic and radiative extinction phenomena under corresponding conditions .

However, no sooting flames were established, necessitating 100% C2H4 and an enriched oxygen atmosphere to facilitate sooting behavior in possible future tests. The 20132 tests kicked off a round of tests with helium -diluted fuel and oxidizer. The ambient was 21% O2 and 79% He. The fuel was composed of 25% H2, 20% CH4, and 55% He. Using He as inert made igniting the mixture much more difficult compared to that for the N2 inert cases of Round 1, using the same ignition parameters. The reason is believed to be due to the 6X higher value in thermal conductivity of He versus that of N 2. As a result, ignition parameters were varied, e.g., with a longer preheat time and higher power, to achieve ignition for the He-diluted mixtures and ambient. The tests produced flames at 3, 5, 7, and 10 cc/s that expanded outwardly quickly and extinguished. For 5, 7, and 10 cc/s, the flames seemed to disappear and 're -ignite' with a "flash" before final extinction. We are currently investigating the flash phenomenon. Moreover, the radiation mechanism is not conclusive, as it appears different than for the N 2-diluted cases.

We did not have a chance to examine lowering of flow rates to assess kinetic extinction. The 20136 tests examined 20% H2/25% CH4/55% He issuing into 21% O2/He. For 5 cc/s and 7 cc/s, the mixture ignites but imme diately extinguishes, with almost no observable flame-front expansion. For 10, 13, 15, and 17.5 cc/s, the mixtures ignite, expand quickly, and extinguish. We believe that the extinction mechanism is radiative and will compare with computational simulations. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, the flames seemed to extinguish before ramp down. Thus, we were not able to assess purely kinetic extinction. Ignition parameters were varied to investigate thresholds for igniting the mixture for differe nt flow rates. Only flow rates above 7 cc/s showed flame -front expansion leading to extinction, with 17.5 cc/s showing a flash or wavering of the flame before final extinction. The test s conducted on 20142 investigated 30% H2/15% CH4/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He. Elevated oxygen was approved for study, since ignition and extinction limits in previous testing were affected by the high thermal conductivity of He. For 5, 7, 10, 15,

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 12 13, and 16.5 cc/s flow rates, nice flames were established that expanded to wavy/oscillating extinction at the end, indicative of radiative extinction. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, the flames seemed to extinguish during the ignition flow rate stage before ramp down. Thus, we were not able to assess kinetic extinction. The 20155 tests examined 45% H2/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. Previous tests using He as inert had shown that much larger energy and power are needed to ignite the mixtures. For the 30% O2/H2 atmosphere, the tests produced flames at 10 and 14 cc/s (MFC limit of 1 SLMP) that expanded after ignition, but were extinguished by the automated protocol because the burner reached the 250°C temperature limit before any self-extinction could occur. The flames were not too large at the end. Presumably, the thermally-conductive He diluent facilitates heat transfer to the burner. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, i.e., starting at 10 and 14 cc/s and ramping down, the flames seemed to self-extinguish during ramp down.

Flow rate at 5 cc/s results in flames that only existed briefly. Extinction at this lower flow rate is probably due to heat loss to the burner, rather than pure kinetic extinction. Ramp down from 14 cc/s towards 5 cc/s resulted in the burner reaching the 250 °C limit during ramp down. More analyses are needed. Tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere were limited. Fuel flow of 5 cc/s showed flash ignition, but no sustained flame. Meanwhile, 10 cc/s resulted in a flame that seemed to expand to self-extinction. Testing on 20160 investigated 45% CH4/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. Without H 2 in the mixture, even larger energy and power were needed to ignite the mixtures. For the 30% O2/H2 atmosphere, the 5, 10, and 15 cc/s flow rates were sooty only at ignition; and the subsequent non-sooty flames expanded to self-extinction. At 3 and 4 cc/s, the mixtures flashed at ignition, and extinguished almost immediately. It was not clear whether extinction was due to kinetic extinction or heat loss to the burner. At 6 and 7 cc/s, flames ignited with less soot, expanding with no soot to self-extinction.

The case with a ramp down in flow rate could not conclusively identify kinetic extinction. More analysis is needed. Tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere needed even more energy and power for ignition. At 5, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, flames ignited with soot, and expanded quickly to extinction. The 20164 tests began study of ethylene-based flames, where 20% C2H4/80% He issued into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He atmospheres. For 5 cc/s, the flame expanded and remained quasi-steady until the burner limit temperature (250°C) was reached. At 6, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, the flames expanded to extinction, with the higher flow rates (i.e., 10 and 15 cc/s) exhibiting sooty ignition. Fuel flow of 5.5 cc/s seemed to correspond to a condition where the onset of oscill ating extinction was simultaneous with the burner reaching the 250°C temperature limit. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, the flames seemed to extinguish during ramp down, but heat loss to the burner may be the mechanism of extinction. Althoug h 13 tests were conducted with the 21% O2/He atmosphere, ignition was not achieved.

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 13 The tests performed on20170 investigated 25% C2H4/75% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. At 5 and 5.5 cc/s, nice blue chemiluminescent flames were ignited, but eventually were cut off because of the burner temperature limit being reached. At 6 cc/s, a nice blue flame was ignited which expanded slowly to extinction. At 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, sooty ignition occurred, but as the flames expanded, the soot went away, e ventually resulting in radiative extinction. By ramping the flow rates up, starting at 5 cc/s, soot at ignition was minimized, and the flames could expand to extinction. Ramp down of the flow rate resulted in almost immediate extinction. For tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere, cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s resulted in flames that expanded quickly to extinction. Less soot was present at ignition compared with that for the 30 % O2/He atmosphere cases. Consistent ignition was not always achieved for the same conditions, which is puzzling. Testing on 20176 explored 30% C2H4/70% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He.

At 5 cc/s, a long duration flame was established that eventually reached the burner temperature limit. At 6, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, the flames were sooty at ignition, but the soot dissipated; and they expanded to extinction. Ramping up the flow rates, starting at 5 cc/s, minimized soot at ignition and resulted in flames that slowly expanded to extinction. For tests at 21 % O2/He atmosphere, cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s resulted in flames that expanded to extinction. At 4 cc/s, the flame lasted a while before eventual e xtinction. The 3 cc/s case did not ignite. Ramp down of the flow rate seemed to result in flames that extinguished quickly before the protocol could ramp down the flow rate. The last testing of Round 2, which was a makeup of 20155, occurred on 20190, with 45% H2/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21 % O2/He. For both oxygen concentration environments, flow rates resulting in expanding flames lasted for a while, but were cut off by automated protocol before self-extinction when the burner temperature limit was reached. As for cases where the flow rates were ramped down, extinction detection was observed for both oxygen concentration environments.

We are currently analyzing the data to determine if extinction was kinetic or due to heat loss to the burner. A last set of tests were conducted with a reduced oxygen concentration atmosphere, i.e., 17.5 % O2/82.5% He. Some cases indicated that radiative and kinetic extinction were possibly observed. In summary, selected preliminary findings from this testing include: o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames and in air seemed to indicate kinetic extinction at low flow rates and radiative extinction at high flow rates. As previously mentioned above (and in our report for the pr eceding increment pair ), such phenomena were not observed in our ground -based research, given the limited microgravity durations. Nevertheless, comparisons with computational simulations are needed to assess better the extinction behavior. o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames seemed to show kinetic extinction at ramp down. However, for the mass flow rates that could be accommodated, radiative extinction was not observed.

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 14 o Cases run for nitrogen -diluted hydrogen/methane mixture flames manifested extinction, which are presumed to be radiative. However, kinetic extinction at low flow rates could not be identified. More analyses of the data are needed. o Cases for helium -diluted cases shifted the extinction limits with respect to the nitrogen-diluted cases. In general, kinetic extinction was difficult to observe for the conditions examined.
