ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 3 1. Overview The Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments ( ACME) project for which tests are conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Chung K. Law of Princeton University. The experiment has two Co-Investigators (Co-Is), namely Prof. Stephen D. Tse of Rutgers University and Dr. Kurt R. Sacksteder of the NASA Glenn Research Center . While Sac ksteder was actively engaged in defining the experiment, he had t ransitioned to other NASA work long before the spaceflight operations limiting his overall contributions. Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NA SA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including s-Flame and the rest of the ACME investigations. In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University ( CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist . For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs.

Vedha Nayagam and Uday G. Hegde who are also with CWRU. The s-Flames operations were conducted in two rounds of testing during Increments 60-63, where there was no testing during Increment 62 due to limited crew availability. M ore specifically, the first round of testing was conducted from Sept. 2019 to Jan. 2020, w hile the second-round testing – featuring helium rather than nitrogen dilution - occurred from May to July 2020. 2. Science Overview A. Background This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document (SRD) of Jan. 2010. Recognizing that most combustion engines and devices operate on the basis of diffusion flames, the proposed program aims to characterize and gain predictive capability of the structure and dynamics of diffusion flames in simple, well -defined flow f ields such that the phenomena of interest can be studied without being unduly complicated and compromised by complex and sometimes non-quantifiable flow field effects.

The basic flame configur ation adopted for the investigation is the spherically symmetric diffusion flame generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a quiescent, oxidizing ambience in microgravity. The one dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The primary goals of the program are two -fold and strongly interdependent. The first objective is to interrogate the fidelity of the chemical kinetic mechanisms and transport submodels used in the simulation of aerothermochemical phenomena, and conseque ntly identify possible modifications. The second objective is to characterize and gain predictive capability on spherical diffusion flames.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 4 The space flight program consists of two main parts : (1) Mapping and characterization of the movement of spherical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition from a non-steady-state condition and their extinction boundaries due to direct finite-rate chemistry and indirect radiative heat loss. The emphases ar e on the relative importance of radiative emission and re -absorption, the examination of the adequacy of the detailed chemical kinetics mechanism and transport sub models used, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the extincti on boundaries. Results of the study are of relevance to the de velopment of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions. (2) Studies of the response of characteristically sooty flames to a non-steady-state initial condition with respect to the aspects given in (1). The studies will include characterizing soot onset as a function of residence time for expanding flames, as well as soot radiation and transport contributions in spreading, extinction, and instability.

The project involves microgravity experimentation, computational simulation, and, where appropriate, theoretical analysis. Interpretation of all phenomena will emphasize the simultaneous and coupled influence of chemistry and transport. B. Rationale for Microgravity This is the ‘Justification for Extended Duration Microgravity Environment’ section (2.5) of the experiment’s SRD from Jan. 2010. See the SRD itself for the references, etc. which are not included in this report. 2.5.1 Limitations of Terrestrial (1g laboratory) Testing We seek to make observations of truly one -dimensional flames whose structure can be studied without complications due to uncertainties in the flow pattern caused by buoyancy. Such fundamental study of flame structure and dynamics is best served via the elimination of buoyancy through the reduction of gravity. The minimum sizes of these flames imply that buoyancy would be significant if the experiments were conducted in normal gravity. Previous experimentation on earth has amply demonstrated this influence.

Although studies of spherical diffusion flames were conducted in normal gravity using the low-pressure, inverse-flame arrangement (see §1), the conditions are limited for small flames, low pressures, low molecular weight fuels. Indeed, on ly the hydrogen flame can be considered to be nearly buoyancy free. With such constraints, normal -pressure, micro-gravity, hydrocarbon-based experiments are requisite. One-dimensional spherical flames allow for the unambiguous study of such fundamental f lame phenomena as the dynamics and extinction of diffusion flames (including the mechanisms of flame front unsteadiness), soot suppression/formation, and flame front instabilities, without gravity-induced baroclinicity and buoyancy, on the flame responses.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 5 2.5.2 Limitations of Drop Towers and Aircraft Extensive experimentation has been conducted in the 2.2 -s drop tower, 5 -s drop tower, and parabolic aircraft, as reviewed previously in §1.3. Although experimental data of good quality were obtained on the transient response of spherica l diffusion flames in the 2.2 -s drop tower facility, the duration was insufficient to observe radiative extinction. The numerical simulations indicate that, for the characteristic flames under study, more than 2.5s of microgr avity time is needed. Subseque nt parabolic aircraft experimentation afforded the additional low -gravity duration (up to 10s by free -floating the apparatus), as well as an experimental package incorporating rainbow schlieren (which cannot be contained within a package for the 2.2 -s drop tower), although radiative extinction was still not observed. The unavoidable g-jitter associated with the facility, however, renders the observation less definitive. Note that even though the package was free -floated, umbilical restrictions could not be avoided. This g -jitter effect was substantiated by accelerometer data.

5 -s drop tower experiments for a mixture composition of 20%H2 / 25%CH4 / 55%N2 did show events with local extinction toward the end of the drop (see Fig. 1.11). While these new resu lts are extremely encouraging and suggest that radiative extinction can indeed be experimentally observed, the 5-s duration is still insufficient. To obtain spherical symmetry for small burners (in order to minimize heat loss to the burner), as well as to ensure quasi-steady flame evolution up to radiative extinction (for the flame sizes to be studied), low mass flow rates are needed, which increase the characteristic time needed. Moreover, for other mixture compositions (suc h as 50%H2/10%CH4/40%N2 45%H 2/55%N2), more than 5s of microgravity duration has been computationally predicted to be needed to achieve radiative extinction (see Fig. 1.12). Additional time is also needed to employ multi -staged flames (where the mass flow rate is changed) so that such phenomena as kinetic extinction can be studied (for example, by establishing a quasi-steady flame at a given flow rate and then reducing it so that the flame front moves inwardly and quasi -steadily until kinetic extinction).

Fi nally, given the characteristic time for diffusion flame oscillation (see Fig. 1.14), which does not occur until the flame nears the quasi-steady extinction limits, extended microgravity duration becomes essential in order to study the phenomenon. 2.5.3 Justification for Space-Flight Facility As explained above, extended microgravity duration, of high quality, is needed to make all necessary flame structure measurements, allowing for the study of transient phenomena (such as flame oscillations and fuel vap or accumulation) and extinction processes. Moreover, at present, the advanced diagnostics found on the space-flight facility cannot be utilized in the drop tower facilities. Numerical simulations indicate that about 25s of microgravity is needed for nonextinguishing flames to reach 80% of their steady-state radius, for the fuel mixtures and flow rates examined. It is expected that within this duration, the aforementioned phenomenon can be duly investigated. The total experimental duration for a single case would be 25s .

This duration is within the 25s bound imposed by constant volume combustion within the specified CIR dimensions (see §Appendix 5.1) regarding oxygen depletion for a “penetration depth” of 20cm. C. Science Objectives The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘Experimental Objectives’ section (2.1) of the experiment’s SRD from Jan. 2010. Current experimental and theoretical capabilities make detailed, quantitative descriptions of laminar flames situated in well -defined flow fields conceivable provided that comprehensive

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 6 chemical-kinetic and transport mechanisms are available. The comprehensiveness of these mechanisms has been extensively tested for premixed but not diffusion flames, especially in simple, well-defined flow fields not complicated by buoyant flows. A burner-generated spherical diffusion flame provides a simple, one -dimensional flame geometry that permits a rigorous comparison between detailed theory and experimental verification. Existing theory and limited low-gravity experimental results suggest that quasi -steady spherical diffusion flames can exist with some combinations of fuel mixture supply rates and quiescent ambient oxidizers. With respect to the steady flame conditions, altering fuel sup ply rates to limit f lame residence time induces a convective -kinetic extinction limit. Alternatively, very large residence times allow radiative heat losses and diffusive transport mechanisms to quench the flame. Near these dual flammability boundaries of quasi-steady flames, flame-front instabilities may appear before the flame is quenched.

We seek to investigate and improve the fidelity and comprehensiveness of the chemical kinetic mechanisms and transport submodels used in the simulation of aerothermo chemical phenomena, and consequently identify possible modifications, by characterizing important unit combustion processes, including: (1) the dynamics and extinction of diffusion flames, with emphases on fuel vapor accumulation, radiation heat transfer, flame pulsation, and flame kinetics; and (2) the structure and response of characteristically sooty flames, with emphases on flame front stability and soot formation. Comprehensive predictive capability can be achieved by employing the simple flames of Process (1) to interrogate and suggest modifications of the kinetic and transport data bases, and then validate their adequacy in the chemically and aerodynamically more complex situation of Process (2). A series of experiments is proposed with the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and sooty flames, to compare with detailed computational simulation to assess transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence): Objective A.

Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. Objective B. Determine the quasi -steady convective/chemical -kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical -kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/dil uent ratios (soot -free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty). Objective C. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.

As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners. Besides the chamber insert, other ACME-unique hardware includes a high -definition color camera and an avionics package, which is for data acquisition and control. Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 10 ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow b urner (where the two concentric tubes have inner di ameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and ea ch BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter wil l have a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to accommod ate the various burners) and its stepper -motor drive will allow for precise positioning. Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment.

Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm. However, only the larger gas -jet burner was used during the s paceflight tests. The burners are addressed in detail in section 3.C. Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching. Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been co nducted using a loop igniter tip like those w hich had been successfully used in the droplet combustion experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with a coil igniter tip, where that included the second round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s -Flame) experiments, with the exception of the latter’s first day testing.

The CFI -G investigation will also use the coil igniter tip. For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), w hereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames,

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 11 although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments. Gases can also be delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as the blending of different fuel gases. CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) that can be released into the combustion chamber. Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent. Furthermore, the fuel diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer flows of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a maximum of 5 slpm. ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control. ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems, of which three cameras ar e part of the CIR facility and are already in use on orbit.

All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot volume fraction; and o perational support. However, it is unlikely that all functions would be exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high -definition digital camera mounted outside of the cham ber and a standard analog camera mounted on t he chamber insert (with a turning mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operati ons. Lightemitting diodes within the chambe r can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging.

Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, w hich balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23 -24]. Alternately, CH* imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430 -nm bandpass filter with a 10 -nm full width at half -maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450 -nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame conditions. The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, is not archived in space. The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. Its gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 12 antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it doe s not balance the intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature determination. Meanwhile, rather than the 450 -nm bandpass fi lter described above, the high definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions. For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A). Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment was particularly challenging with these, if not all, cameras. Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band. This camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frame s per second (fps). Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss through the LCTF.

More information about this camera can be found in its characterization report, CIR-RPT- 4600. The ACME chamber insert will also be equipped with non -imaging optical diagnostics including both thermopile radiometers and Photomultiplier Tubes (PMTs). There is a crew -exchangeable linear array of radiometers of which there are two versions supporting the initial set of

The array has a fixed position which is parallel to the chamber axis and cen tered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows and thus most of the other instrumentation. One array is equipped with a single wide -view radiometer with two narrow view radiometers that are downstream and two more that are upstream, wher e all view s are orthogonal to the chamber axis, as depicted in Figure 4. This detector is primarily intended to support the spherical flame experiments and will have a quicker response than the more sensitive detectors that will used in the linear arrays. Like the radiometers on the two linear arrays, it will have a spectral range of nominally 0.2 -11 micron and its field of view will be established by an appropriately selected aperture. The FOV of the off-set radiometer is also shown in section 3.F. Learn more about this sensor from the Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-011). To detect the quenching of dim flames, the chamber insert will be equipped with a set of three PMTs.

Each PMT will have a wide-angle view, a sight line that is orthogonal to the chamber axis, and will be centered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows so that it is aligned with most o f the other instrumentation. The PMTs’ spectral r ange will be 230 -700 nm, i.e., visible and near ultraviolet, but one will have a 310-nm bandpass filter and another will have a 430-nm bandpass filter (where both are with a 10-nm FWHM). Hardware Shortcomings Key s-Flame shortcomings include image acquisition, limited imaging sensitivity (especially to the hydrogen flames), and the flow asymmetry from the burner (especially at high flow rates). Other shortcomings are discussed in this section and Appendices B to D, but the reader may want to refer to the ACME Engineering Implementation document for additional information. At high flow rates, the porous spherical burner used for s -Flame did not produce spherically symmetric flames.

While they wer e nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center bec ame increasing offset from the burner center when testing with higher flow rates . More specifically, the flame shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the sintered sphere. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non -spherical, where it can appea r to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. When s-Flame’s first fuel bottle was installed on 30 July 2019 (19211), it was at the expected pressure, but the fuel pressure was observ ed to drop with time, indicating a leak. Troubleshooting, including testing with other fuel bottles, was carried out and it was concluded that the leak was related to the bottle’s quick connection and potentially caused by foreign debris. The bottle was returned to Earth unused and tested in the ground copy of the CIR, but a leak was not found in that ground testing.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 18 When a fuel or diluent Mass Flow Controller (MFC) was used at a small fraction of its maximum flow rate, the actual flow rate sometimes differed from that desired. More importantly, small flow perturbations were observed in some s-Flame tests, where the flow irregularities were most apparent through their effect on Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) measurements, e.g., of OH* and CH* chemiluminescence. For example, a momentary increase in fu el flow, naturally leads to increased light from the flame. Steps were made to mitigate such behavior, e.g., by zero-ing the MFCs prior to each test, but they were not completely successful. Ignition of the flames in the second round, with helium rather than nitrogen dilution, presented a challenge. The properties of the two gases differ dramatically; for example, helium’s thermal conductivity is several times greater than that of nitroge n. A cautious approach was taken in increasing the igniter power on the first test day with helium (11 May 2020, i.e., 20132) because of concerns about potential failure of the igniter tip and the stalled operations that would result.

The number of tests accomplished with that day’s conditions were limited as a result. The standard igniter tip was subsequently replaced with a replaced with a coil, rather than loop, design which was believed to be more robust because of the thicker wire. The coil igniter was used successfully in subsequent testing, but still with caution where flames were not always ignited successfully. As a result, some tests with helium dilution were conducted in atmospheres with ~30% oxygen (by volume) instead of the planned ~21%, which as one would expect facilitated ignition. As a result, tests were conducted with an inconsistent mix of oxygen concentrations, which may yield valuable insights, but limits the planned test-to-test comparisons. The CIR’s Image Processing and Storage Unit for Gigabit Ethernet cameras (IPSU-G), which is used with the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) and Cool Flames Inve stigation (CFI) intensified camera, didn’t properly archive all of the image data on 13 Sept. 2019 (19256), where a large fraction of the image data was lost while flames were burning.

After troubleshooting attempts, the IPSU-G was removed and replaced by astronaut Jessica Meir on 24 October 24 (19297) where subsequent check-out on Oct. 28 (19301) confirmed normal archival of the image data. The DataCam images were mis-formatted on 18 Dec. 2019 (19352), where the cause is unknown but there were repeated operational issues with the CIR’s Image Processing and Storage Units (IPSUs) on that test day. Fortunately, the mis -formatting was not seen on subsequent test days and the problematic test day was nominally repeated on 24 Jan. 2020 (20024) to make up for the lost science. The ACME DataCam , generally the primary camera for ACME testing, is unfortunately not as sensitive as had been hoped to the dim microgravity flames. A critical challenge for s-Flame was in imaging the pure hydrogen and diluted hydrogen flames, which were not apparent or hardly visible to the DataCam and analog operations camera. This unfortunately inhibits assessment of three-dimensional flame symmetry because the CFI intensified camera and Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) cameras were opposite of each other.

While infrequent, tests also sometimes aborted automatically, typically due to communication issues with an IPSU but sometimes because test parameters were accidentally assigned out -ofrange values. Fortunately, such aborts occurred before the start of gas flow so little was lost other than the time in which the aborted tests were conducted.

The s -Flame investigators accordingly planned within that target limit whereas each of the other ACME experiments exceeded it , significantly so in most cases.

T o improve the balance between the ACME investigations, the decision was made to treat s-Flame’s highly desired tests, featuring diluted ethylene, as required. This was proposed by Dennis Stocker in 2015 (if not earlier) and adopted by 2016, where s -Flame was conducted on the ISS in 2019 - 2020. Long in advance of the launch of the ACME hardware, Stocker proposed that each experiment be conducted in two separate rounds to allow the investigators to dig into the results from past tests so that they could make the best use of the remaining testing and thereby maximize the scientific return. Clarifications and additional information, not in the conference paper, are included in boxed notes like this. The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Thus far, ACME’s activity has included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities. Most often the astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips. In the latter case, the igniter tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the crew already has changes to make changes in the interior of the insert. While these activities may seem mundane, the crew play a critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment. As an extreme example, there were crew activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. In contrast, only two crew days were required to reconfigure the hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner.

Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. Similarly, the s -Flame exp eriment was conducted using the same burner as the Flame Design investigation which preceded it . However, there was hardware reconfiguration for s -Flame to enable use of an addition al intensified camera for imaging OH* chemiluminescence , namely the Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera. All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically , four to six people staff four consoles during the testing. The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console. Two shifts of per sonnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because th ey typically last 14 hours with the many pre - and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Clev eland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM.

A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks. On intervening weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew of ten swap one or both gas bottles.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 21 Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2 -shift day for the RO and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew activity. As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week. A team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing. The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding. In the case of E -FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure co mputer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters. That team does not see the telemetry d uring the testing, but is in communication via phone and e -mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC).

While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files. In advance of the test day, the UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings. It is also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are ch anged in response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. Provisions have been m ade to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely view the analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the operations center. Thus far, all ACME flame tests, including those for s-Flame and E-FIELD Flames, have been conducted in an automated manner using software scripts and extensive parameter files. Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low rate results from several unavoidable factors.

After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz nonimaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team. A small sample of images are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples. The review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for the given flame co nditions. After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosph ere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed. Midway through a day’s E -FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes th rough a filter cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay Satelli te (TDRS) System.

Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic communication outages with a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite to another) or can last as long as 30 minutes. In contrast to E-FIELD Flames, an average of 15 flames were ignited per test day for s -Flame, but they were of even shorter durations. The pressure rise with an s -Flame test was small and the chamber was rarely vented af ter a test unless the chamber atmosphere was being adjusted for

In this regard, the chamber atmosphere was sometimes scrubbed for the s-Flame investigation by recirculating it through the adsorber cartridge, but this was not a regular routine as in the case of E-FIELD Flames. The chamber was also sometimes partially or completely vented and refilled during s -Flame operations, for example to adjust the atmosphere’s oxygen concentration. Unlike E-FIELD Flames, the s -Flame experiment also ma de use of the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentational Package (GCIP) to measure species concentrations of the atmosphere in the combustion chamber. There is no sampling probe and measurements are only made before, between, or after tests when the chambe r atmosphere was ‘stirred’ through use of a fan. For s - Flame, the GC measurements were made on most but not all test days, but they were limited in scope because of the significant time required. The GC measurements were sometimes only made at the end of the test day but were occasionally made earlier in the day, for example prior to an adjustment of the chamber atmosphere.

A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis. The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material flammability. That follow -on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing. Although it requires additional crew time, these allotments are split into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from testing for careful review of the early results so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of their second round. This paper reports on early results from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. In contrast to earlier plans, the two rounds of the s -Flame experiment occurred sequentially because of limited crew availability. Due to delays in commercial crew transport, the space station had three rather six crew members through much of 2020. As a result of the reduced c rew size, the s-Flame investigators did get a 3 -month break (in Feb. to April) between their two rounds of flame tests allowing them to study early results and prepare for the second round.

Hardware issues also stretched out s-Flame operations in the latter half of 2019. While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests. For E -FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010. At that time, NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited objectives rather than comprehensive experiments. As such, the general target wa s 50 tests per experiment. For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber. This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing). The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion chamber.

Therefore, the timer limit combined with o ther constraints effectively corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant). For E -FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 10 tests typically completed per day. The second round of the s -Flame experiment featured helium dilution of both the fuel and the oxidizer, so its testing was also limited by the oxygen/helium bottles launched for that purpose.

Summary of Preliminary Results The s-Flame experiment aims to characterize and gain predictive capability of the s tructure and dynamics of diffusion flames in simple, well -defined flow fields such that the phenomena of interest can be studied without being complicated by various flow fi eld effects. The basic flame configuration adopted for the investigation is the spherically symmetric diffusion flame generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a quiescent, oxidizing atmosphere in microgravity. The theoretic ally one -dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduct ion, and computational simulation. The s -Flame experiment uses the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the ACME hardware in the Destiny module of the ISS.

Specifically, the s-Flame tests are intended to: (i) Advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free and sooty flames; (ii) Obtain experimental data in simple, well-defined flow fields and understand various key elemental diffusion flame processes; (iii) Identify the extinction limits for both radiative and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damköhler numbers, respectively); (iv) Determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number; (v) Validate and/or improve accuracy of computational simulation including detailed chemistry and transport. The project has completed two (2) rounds of microgravity experimentation. Currently, detailed analyses of the acquired data, computational simulation, and theoretical analysis are ongoing. Interpretation of all phenomena will emphasize the simultaneous and coupled influ ence of chemistry and transport.

Table 1, on the preceding page, summarizes the tests conducted for two rounds of tests, which are meant to address the scientific objectives listed above. All experimental data address transient phenomenon, as the flame e volves from localized ignition towards “steady” behavior. The flames then evolve in a q uasi-steady state manner (becoming history independent), after a short initial transient. Conventional gaseous fuels including hydrogen, methane, and ethylene are used. Hydrogen is the simplest fuel and its reaction mechanism is also reasonably establish ed. Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon, and extensive studies have been conducted on its combustion chemistry. Ethylene is a typical sooty fuel and is also an import ant intermediate for the oxidation of higher hydrocarbons. Diluents mixed with fuel inc lude nitrogen and helium to adjust mixture diffusivities and characteristic flame temperature. The rationale for the matrix of tests is to utilize various mixtures to assess both chemical and transport effects (including radiative) on flame behavior. Pur e H 2 and pure CH 4 are utilized to assess kinetic mechanisms associated with each.

Additionally, pure H 2 only produces H2O as its radiative product, thereby isolating its radiative properties. Mixtures composed of both H 2 and CH4 are used to examine their combined chemical and transport effects. N2 and He inerts which affect characteristic flame temperature and transport (molecular and radiative), in the same mole

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 26 fractions, are utilized for comparison. As seen in Table 1, the first round of tests exam ined nitrogen-diluted fuel burning in a nitrogen diluted oxidizing atmosphere. Test day 19254 examines nitrogen -diluted C2H4 issuing into 21% O 2 / 79% N 2 atmosphere. C 2H4 allows for the examination of a fuel with nominal unity Le number, setting a baseline standard for flame stretch and thermal diffusive stability effects. Additionally, its characteristic sooting nature (in normal gravity) directly addresses our basic science objectives focusing on spreading of flame sheets, dual extinction states, and flame-front instabilities. For a case of fuel-mixture of 20% C2H4 / 80% N2 at a flow rate of 3 cc/s, a seemingly quasi-steady flame is attained for extended duration. For the same mixture, higher flow rates of 5-10 cc/s result in radiative extinctions, corresponding to high system Damköhler number. Other mixtures of 25% C2H4 / 75% N2 and 30% C2H4 / 70% N2, also show radiative extinctions at higher flow rates. Since characteristic residence times will affect sooting tendencies, various flow rates a re investigated for different mixtures.

Soot is only observed during ignition, which goes away as the flames establish themselves, as seen for cases where low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents (e.g., 25 -30% C2H4) are ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5-10 cc/s) with higher ethylene contents (e.g., 40 -50% C2H4). Soot will also enhance flame radiation, but our non-sooty flames already extinguish as they spread outwardly. Observations of such radiative extinction behavior at high flow rate s is an achievement because such phenomenon was not observed conclusively in our ground-based studies, given the limited microgravity durations. Radiative reabsorption extends flame size at extinction. In ISS testing, radiative extinction has been found to be a common event, which was predicted computationally, but not definitively observed previously for our flame conditions. Test day 19256 uses nitrogen-diluted C2H4 issuing into 21% O 2 / 79% N2 atmosphere to examine kinetic extinction at low system Damkö hler numbers.

Similar to the radiative extinction cases, sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observ e kinetic extinction because a near steady flame needs to be established first, before ramp down in flow rate to find properly the chemical kinetic extinction limit. Surprises and New Discoveries Many discoveries are expected to arise as the data is analyzed and computational simulations are compared. Initial surprises and discoveries include: (1) Nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames in air seem to demonstrate kinetic extinction at low flow rates (low system Da) and radiative extinction at high flow rates (high system Da). Such phenomena were not observed in our ground -based research, given the limited microgravity durations. Nevertheless, comparisons with computational simulations are needed to assess better the extinction behavior. Radiative reabsorption extends flame size at extinction, making the chamber size an import ant parameter.

Surprisingly, radiative extinction has been found to be a common event in ISS testing, which was predicte d computationally, but not observed previously for our flame conditions. Similarly, sufficient microgravity duration is needed to obse rve kinetic extinction because a near steady flame

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 30 need to be established first, before ramp down in flow rate to find pr operly the chemical kinetic extinction limit. The nitrogen-diluted methane flames were tested in air and enriched O2 environments. Th e enriched O2 environments produce smaller characteristic flames; nonetheless, both extinction limits appear to have been observed. (2) Ethylene flames which tend to soot under normal gravity conditions did not soot under microgravity conditions. Sooting only occurred during forced ignition from the hotwire, but soon dissipated. Inherent sooting was also not found for enriched oxidizer conditions or for either of the inerts, i.e., N2 and He, examined. (3) Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames seem to need to be at very large characteristic sizes to selfextinguish. As such, radiative extinction was not observed for the cases run, despite lowering the H2 concentration. However, kinetic extinction during ramp down seem to be exhibited for hydrogen flames. (4) Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen/methane mixture flames manifested radiative extinction, as predicted by computational simulations.

However, kinetic extinction at low flow rates could not be identified conclusively. The characteristic extinction radius may be within the burner radius, precluding experimental identification. More analyses of the data are needed. (5) Helium-diluted cases had shifted extinction limits with respect to the nitrogen-diluted cases. In general, kinetic extinction was difficult to obser ve for the conditions examined. Ignition was also severely affected by using He as diluent. More analyses are needed to assess instability near the flame limits, which was predicted to occur computationally. (6) The He inert cases are meant to better is olate pulsating instabilities that are theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number. However, such instabilities were not conclusively observed in the ISS tests, at least from the video images. Radiometer and PMT data will need to be examined in detail.

(7) The highly thermal conductive nature of He seems to affect various processes, such as ignition and heat transfer to the burner (affecting isolation of kinetic extinction), despite higher characteristic flame temperatures. (8) Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength (or combustion intensity). E. G. Impacts, Benefits, and Products The impact of this work consists of both practical and fundamental aspects. Practically, with diffusion flame burning as the basis in many combustion engines and devices, understanding the underlying dynamics and chemistry of diffusion flames is important in improving performance in terms of power, efficiency, pollutant emissions, and reliability. Fundamentally, the unique buoyancy-free environment offered by mic rogravity affords simple aerodynamic flow fields to acquire diffusion flame data of high fidelity, with the prospect of understanding unit thermochemical processes as well as quantifying the associated physico-chemical parameters.

In analyzing and validating the data sets, the experimental data and corresponding computational simulations should yield quantitative and qualitative understanding of various elemental flame phenomena. In studying the transient motion of diffusion flames ignited from a non-steady-state initial condition, the significance of fuel accumulation will be evaluated, which was originally found to be important in droplet burning. Here, with no droplet surface regression nor coupling of fuel flow to heat transfer from the flame to influ ence flame-front motion, the effect can be better isolated and the far-field unsteadiness assessed. Quantitative predictability of the flame motion permits assessment of the parameters and mechanisms involved in radiation loss and reabsorption as well as other transport parameters. The m icrogravity environment greatly facilitates the examination of pulsating instabilities, which can be hidden or coupled to other processes in normal gravity. Moreover, involvement of multi-dimensional effects, rather than the nominally 1-D geometry here, would further complicate the manifestation of the phenomenon.

Near-limit phenomena, including extinction, is best evaluated and validated using our one dimensional spherical diffusion flame (as rea lized in the microgravit y environment), which is probably the most desirable flame configuration for study of this nature. Understanding extinction phenomenon is paramount to revealing basic flame processes, along with highlighting implications in fire safety. The results are of strong interest to other groups working on diffusion flames, including those also doing ISS -based experiments. The main products will be ( i) insights from fundamental characterization of transient dynamics and responses of such f lames, ( ii) categorizati on of processes that are either quasi -steady (e.g., expanding flame front motion toward steady state) or fully transient (e.g., pulsating instabilities prior to extinction), ( iii) quantitative and qualitative mapping of extinction boundaries and unstable regimes, (iv) clarification of the role of diluents in various processes, and (v) additional understanding of ignition in non-premixed flames. Engines and devices on Earth can be improved in efficiency, pollutant emissions, and depe ndability from such products. H.

Follow-On Experiments Although two rounds of testing have been completed, with no further testing planned, if a third round becomes available, there are two main types of experiments that we would like to implement. We would like to examine the same fuel mixtures (plus C3H8 as mentioned below) of the first two rounds, but with CO2 as inert, including that for the ambient. N 2 and He are radiatively transparent gases; while CO2 is an optically participating gas. Use of CO 2 should result in a characteristically lower flame temperature, increasing the Zeldovich number, Ze. At the same time, the highly reabsorptive CO2 species can minimize net radiative heat loss affecting flame dynamics and extinction. Objectives A, B, and C would be addressed by these experiments. Additionally, characteristically sooty flames were not observed in the first two rounds for the fuel mixtures tested. As such, we would like to investigate using C3H8 as fuel, which was originally specified in the SRD that was approved [in 2002, but which was not part of the s-Flame plan under ACME, which didn’t begin until 2006].

Specific knowledge origi nally sought in the first two rounds with respect to sooty flames, which were not achieved consist of: (a) the transient and steady state behavior and structure of sooting spherical flames, (b) residence time effect on soot formation, with only curvature effects and no strain, and (c) the effects of soot radiation and transport on extinction, at constant mass flow rate. The results so far will be compared with computational simulations to address deficiencies in fundamental parameters and models. The aforementioned CO 2 experiments are highly desired; however, experimentation with C3H8 is of utmost importance if we are to achieve our original objectives with respect to characteristically sooty flames, which were not attained for the fuel mixtures and conditions tested in the first two rounds.

Introduction Tests for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s -Flame) experiment were conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The purpose of s-Flame is to advance the ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction and instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames. The results may contribute to the development of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth. The spherical flames are ignited at non -steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally toward extinction. Tests are conducted with various inert diluents in both the fuel and chamber atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures for soot -free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames.

One experiment objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative and chemical kinetic extinctio n, i.e., where the flame extinguishes from heat loss or is blown out, respectively. Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 38 pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to oc cur in flames with certain fuel/inert mixtures. More specifically, s-Flame has the following experimental objectives: A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initi ally non -steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot -free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. B. Determine the quasi -steady convective/chemical -kinetic extinction limits (low syst em Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical -kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot -free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty). A. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich n umber, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.

As s uggested by the experiment’s name, s -Flame features a spherically symmetric diffusion flame, which is generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a still oxygen/inert atmosphere in microgravity. The one -dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mapping and characterizati on of the motion (e.g., expansion) of spherical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition and at extinction because of the finite-rate chemistry and radiative heat loss. The study is focused on the thermal radiation, the adequacy of the detailed chemistry a nd transport submodels used in computational modeling, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries. (2) Studies of the response of characteristically sooty flames to ignition, the onset of soot in the expanding flames, the soot radiation, and the soot’s effects on the flame spread, extinction, and instability. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal -gravity studies.

For example, the nat ural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics ar e important. For example, chemi -ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 39 With these advanta ges, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The s -Flame investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream.

But it is no t expected that such control, which might be used to approach a stability or soot limit, will be used for s -Flame. Thus far, that has been the case for this experiment, with the possible mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. III. Results A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight A total of 29 flames were ignited for the s -Flame experiment in its two days of flame testing during Increment 60. Mission anomalies When s-Flame’s first fuel bottle was installed on the CIR on July 30 (19211) it was at the expected pressure, but the fuel pressure was observed to drop with time, indicating a leak. Tro ubleshooting, including testing with other fuel bottles, was carried out and it was concluded that the issue was related to the first s -Flame fuel bottle, which contained a hydrogen/methane blend. It was concluded that the leak was related to the quick co nnection, where it might have been caused by foreign debris. The bottle was returned to Earth and tested in the ground copy of the CIR, but surprisingly a leak was not found in that testing. Preliminary Research Findings The s -Flame experiment utilizes spherically -symmetric diffusion flames and their dynamics and responses to investigate fundamental processes, such as extinction, instability, and s oot formation. ISS testing for 19254 and 19256 examined nitrogen diluted ethylene flames in air.

The experiments of 19254 revea led that a quasi -steady flame could be attained for extended duration at low flow rate, i.e., 3cc/s for 20% C2H4 / 80% N2. The flame was shut down by the automated system because the burner reached a cut -off temperature of 250°C. Although the flame oscillated near the end of the experiment, it was likely due to influence of the burner tube. Comparisons with computation simulations will help to clarify the involved processes. For higher flow rates, e.g., 5 -10cc/s, with the same mixture, radiative extinctions were observed. Generally, the flames showed unstable behavior near the burner tube prior to extinction, likely because of lac k of fuel mixture and heat loss in that region. Other mixtures, e.g., 25% C2H4 / 75% N2 and 30% C2H4 / 70% N2, also showed radiative extinctions at higher flow rates. For some cases, the pyrometry fiber interacted with the flame, allowing extraction of temperature in on-going analyses. Soot was observed only during ignition, which went away as the flame established itself.

To asses whet her these nitrogen -diluted ethylene flames are non -sooty or sooty, cases were run where mixtures were ignited and established at low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents (e.g., 25-30% C2H4) and then ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5-10 cc/s) with higher ethylene contents (e.g., 40 -50% C2H4). The flames all radiatively extinguished, but no sooting was observed. Obse rvations of such radiative extinction behavior at high flow rates is an achievement because such phenomenon was not observed in o ur ground -based experiments, given the limited microgravity durations. Radiative reabsorption extends flame size at extinction. In ISS testing, radiative extinction has been found to be a common event, which was predicted computationally, but not observed previously for our flame conditions. The experiments of 19256 were aimed at examining kinetic extinction. Similar to the radiative extinction cases, sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observe kinetic extinction because a near steady flame ne eds to be established first, before ramp down

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 44 in flow rate to find properly the chemical kinetic extinction limit. High flow r ate cases (e.g., 13.5 cc/s, 15 cc/s) showed asymmetrical flames which radiatively extinguished. Flow rates were lowered so that quasi-steady flames could be established before ramp down in flow rate. The 15% C 2H4 mixtures were not strong enough to sustai n a quasi steady flame at 3 cc/s before ramp down. However, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20 -30% C2H4, very nice flames were esta blished at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions were observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. Radiative extinctions for ra mp up cases were also examined. Similarly, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20 -30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s ; and radiative extinctions were observed during ramp up before reaching 8 cc/s. Future tests will investigate soot formation processes, which have not been observed for the fuel mixtures and conditions tested thus far. Introduction Tests for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusio n Flames (s -Flame) experiment were conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The purpose of s-Flame is to advance the ability to pr edict the structure and dynamics, in cluding extinction and instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames. The results may contribute to the development of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth. The sp herical flames are ignited at non -steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally towards steady-state or extinction. Tests are conducted with various inert diluents in both the fuel and chamber (oxidizer) atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 47 extinguishes from radiative heat lo ss or is “blown out,” respectively. Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in flames with certain fuel/inert mixtures at near-limit conditions. More specifically, s-Flame has the following experimental objectives: A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non -steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of di fferent H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot -free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. B. Determine the quasi -steady convective/chemical -kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical -kinetic extinctio n limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot -free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty). B. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e.

mode, f requency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number, at near-limit conditions. As suggested by the experiment’s name, s -Flame features a spherically symmetric diffusion flame, which is generated by discharging a fuel gas from a por ous spherical burner into a still oxygen/inert atmosphere in microgravity. The one -dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mappi ng and characterization of the motion (e.g., expansion) of spherical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition and at extinction because of the finite-rate chemistry and radiative heat loss. The study is focused on the thermal radiation, the adequacy of the detailed chemistry and transport submodels used in computational modeling, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries.

(2) Studies of the response of characteristically sooty flames to ignition, the onset of soot in the expanding flames, the soot radiation, and the soot’s effects on the flame spread, extinction, and instability. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal -gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum -dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exh ibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.

Th e absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 48 concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The s -Flame investigation and other AC ME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass fl ow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifi cally from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.

However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. But it is not expected t hat such control, which might be used to approach a stability or soot limit, will be used fo r s-Flame. Thus far, that has been the case for this experiment, with the possible mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. III. Results A. Introduction Tests for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s -Flame) experiment were conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The purpose of s-Flame is to advance the ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction and instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames. The results may contribute to the development of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth. The spherical flames are ignited at non -steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally towards steady-state or extinction. Tests are conducted with various iner t diluents in both the fuel and chamber (oxidizer) atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames.

One experimental objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative an d chemical kinetic extinction, i.e., where the flame extinguishes from radiative heat loss or is “blown out,” respectively. Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in flames with certain fuel/inert mixtures at near-limit conditions.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 58 More specifically, s-Flame has the following experimental objectives: A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffu sion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot -free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. B. Determine the quasi -steady convective/chemical -kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical -kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot -free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty). C. Determine the exis tence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number, at near-limit conditions.

As suggested by the experiment’s name, s -Flame features a spherically symmetric diffusion flame, which is generated by discharging a fuel gas from a por ous spherical burner into a still oxygen/inert atmosphere in microgravity. The one-dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mappi ng and characterization of the motion (e.g., expan sion) of spherical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition and at extinction because of the finite-rate chemistry and radiative heat loss. The study is focused on the thermal radiation, the adequacy of the detailed chemistry and transport submodels used i n computational modeling, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries. (2) Studies of the response of characteristically sooty flames to ignition, the onset of soot in the expanding flames, the soot radiation, and the soot’s effects on the flame spread, extinction, and instability. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal -gravity studies.

For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum -dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exh ibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. Th e absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy env ironment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 59 new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The s -Flame investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifi cally from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. As expected, no s-Flame tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream.

Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. III. Results A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight A total of 276 flames were ignited for the s -Flame experiment, with 29, 116, and 131 respectively ignited during Increments 60, 61, and 63. These numbers neglect some flames which quenched promptly after ignition. In this regard, science testing began at the end of Increment 60 and the first round of tests were completed during Increment 61. No tests were conducted in Increment 62 due t o a lack of crew time, where the second round of tests were fully conducted during Increment 63.

The tests were conducted in two rounds, where the first was conducted in increments 60 and 61 featured 145 flames (nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen (i.e., in the chamber atmosphere) were diluted with nitrogen. The second round conducted in increment 63 featured 131 flames (nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen were instead diluted wit h helium.

These are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is relatively well understood. No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for s -Flame; all of the ISS results were electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME experiments.
